_comment: Hand-authored node metadata, merged from per-namespace fragments by build/merge_overlay.py and validated against dist/ess.json. build/nodes.py combines this with ess.json to produce dist/nodes.json. Edit THIS file (or a fragment), never ess.json -- that one is regenerated from src/ on every build.

Ess.AIOrders.command.title: AI Orders: Command
Ess.AIOrders.command.desc: Gives a group of spawned units an order - move, patrol, defend, attack, follow and so on. This is the node most likely to look like it did nothing, and the cause is almost always the options: each behavior needs its own fields, and a move with no destination is thrown away entirely. Orders are forced through, so a fresh order overrides a hold or defend the units were locked into (without that, units coming off a guard order just keep standing there). An order aimed at a vehicle is handed to its driver for you. Walking destinations work by quietly spawning an invisible marker prop at the spot and sending the units to THAT - a bare coordinate is silently ignored by anyone on foot - so pass a tracker if you want those props cleaned up afterwards.

guids.desc: The units to order, as a Lua list. Wire in what a spawn node handed you, or look up a group you filed with the AI Orders: Set Group node. A name that was never filed gives an EMPTY list, and an order to an empty list commands nobody with no error at all.

behavior.desc: One of: move, patrol, defend, attack, hold, face, follow, flee, enter, deploy, animate. What each looks like in play - move: walk to a spot and stop. patrol: walk a route of points over and over. defend: walk to a spot then hold that area and fight anything that comes inside it. attack: hunt a target down. hold: stand still where they are and never give chase. face: turn to look at a point without moving. follow: tag along like a recruited buddy, keeping pace and climbing in and out of vehicles on their own. flee: run away from the player. enter: climb into a vehicle. deploy: a transport disgorges its passengers. animate: play a canned action such as cowering. Any other word is logged and nothing happens.

opts.desc: The settings for the chosen behavior, and the usual reason nothing happens. move, face and defend need at = {x, y, z} - without it the order is dropped and the units carry on with whatever they were doing. patrol needs points = {{x,y,z},{x,y,z}} and walks it forever unless you add loop = false. defend takes radius (12). attack, follow and enter take target, which is either a group name you filed or a unit/vehicle handle - and with NO target both attack and follow fall back to the nearest hero, which means they turn on the PLAYER. flee takes distance (120). animate takes action ('Cower'). enter takes role ('passenger', 'driver' or 'gunner') and gets the vehicle unlocked for you, which a freshly spawned vehicle needs before anyone can board it. Most behaviors also accept speed, priority ('hi', 'med' or 'lo'), and onComplete for a move or a non-looping patrol.

tracker.desc: Optional. Hand it an Ess.Track and the invisible destination markers this spawns get removed when you tear the rest of your setup down. Leave it blank and they sit in the world for the rest of the session.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order ran without a Lua error. It is NOT a promise the units accepted it - an unknown behavior name gives false, but a move with no destination still reports true even though nothing was ordered. If your units stand still, read the log rather than this.

Ess.AIOrders.group.title: AI Orders: Get Group
Ess.AIOrders.group.desc: Looks up the units filed under a name by the AI Orders: Set Group node, so you can feed them into an order or count them.

name.desc: The name you filed the units under.

returns.name: guids
returns.desc: The list of unit handles. An unknown or misspelled name gives an EMPTY list rather than an error, which is the usual reason an order aimed at a group commands nobody.

Ess.AIOrders.setGroup.title: AI Orders: Set Group
Ess.AIOrders.setGroup.desc: Files a list of units under a name, so later orders can point at the whole group by that name - 'attack the CONVOY group' - instead of wiring the list all over your graph. It is purely a label store: nothing spawns, moves or changes in the world when you call it.

name.desc: The name to file them under. Any word you like, but spell it the same way when you use it - an unknown name reads back as an empty group and orders aimed at it quietly do nothing.

guids.desc: The list of unit handles to file, as a Lua list. Normally wired straight from whatever spawned them.

Ess.Bones.aimVector.title: Bones: Aim Direction Between Two Hardpoints
Ess.Bones.aimVector.desc: Works out which way a mounted part is pointing by taking the line from one hardpoint to another on the same model - a turret's breech to its barrel tip gives you the barrel line, confirmed live on the Allied Destroyer's cannon. Use it to put a muzzle effect in the right place, send something flying along the barrel, or aim a camera down the gun. Gives you nothing if either name doesn't exist on that model, and note that a freshly spawned model's hardpoints read as nothing for about a third of a second - wait for it first.

uGuid.desc: The vehicle or character carrying both hardpoints. They must be on the SAME object.

hpBase.desc: Name of the hardpoint at the BACK of the part - where the line starts.

hpTip.desc: Name of the hardpoint at the FRONT - where the line ends. Base to tip is the direction the part is pointing.

returns.name: dx
returns.desc: East/west part of the direction. These three are a DIRECTION, not a place - add them onto the base hardpoint's position to travel along the barrel.

returns.name: dy
returns.desc: Up/down part of the direction - this is what tells you the barrel is raised or lowered.

returns.name: dz
returns.desc: North/south part of the direction.

Ess.Bones.attachFX.title: Bones: Attach Effect To A Bone
Ess.Bones.attachFX.desc: Glues a particle effect (smoke, fire, a glow) onto a named bone or hardpoint of a character or vehicle so it rides along as the model moves - a plume off someone's head, flames on an engine, a flash at a gun muzzle. Every bone on a person and every hardpoint on a vehicle is reachable by name, because the engine hashes the name rather than looking up text, so 'hp_' hardpoints and raw 'bone_' skeleton joints both work. TRAP: a model you have JUST spawned reports no bones for about a third of a second, so this quietly gives you nothing if you run it the instant you create something - put a Wait Until Model Is Ready node in front of it.

uGuid.desc: The character or vehicle to stick the effect to. Defaults to you, which is the easiest way to see that it worked.

bone.desc: The name of the bone or hardpoint to pin to. Bone_Head and Bone_Chest are confirmed human joints; vehicles use their own hp_ names like hp_barreltip_cannon. A name that doesn't exist isn't an error - you just get nothing back.

template.desc: The name of the effect to create. The default is a confirmed-working tall smoke plume. A blank name is refused on purpose - an empty name crashes the game outright, and that crash cannot be caught.

returns.name: uFx
returns.desc: The effect that was created. KEEP this - it is the only way to take the effect off again later, via the Detach Effect node. You get nothing back if the bone name didn't resolve, the name was blank, or the game refused to create it.

Ess.Bones.detachFX.title: Bones: Detach Effect
Ess.Bones.detachFX.desc: Takes an effect back off a bone and removes it from the world - the undo for Attach Effect To A Bone. Safe to run on nothing at all: that is a harmless do-nothing rather than an error, so you don't need to check first before cleaning up.

uGuid.desc: The character or vehicle the effect was glued to.

uFx.desc: The effect to remove - wire in the one you got back from Attach Effect To A Bone. Left empty, nothing happens.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if an effect was actually removed. False just means there was nothing to remove.

Ess.Bones.probeNames.title: Bones: Probe Bone Names
Ess.Bones.probeNames.desc: A discovery tool for finding out what a model's bones are called. You give it a list of name beginnings and a list of endings; it tries every combination and reports which ones resolved to a real point, with the coordinates it found. HARD CAVEAT, keep it in mind: bone names are hashed, so a nonsense string can collide onto a real bone and hand back real, valid coordinates. A hit proves the string is a usable handle for SOME node on that model - it does NOT prove that node is really called that. Use this to explore, never as the foundation of a finished mod.

uGuid.desc: The model to probe. The player character is the easiest thing to try it on.

prefixes.desc: A Lua list of name beginnings to try, each in quotes inside the braces.

suffixes.desc: A Lua list of name endings. Every beginning is joined to every ending, so 2 beginnings and 4 endings means 8 names tried.

returns.name: hits
returns.desc: The names that resolved - a list where each entry carries name, x, y and z as read at the moment of the probe.

returns.name: nTried
returns.desc: How many name combinations were tried in total (duplicates are only tried once), so you can see the hit rate.

Ess.Bones.waitForReady.title: Bones: Wait Until Model Is Ready
Ess.Bones.waitForReady.desc: The fix for the most common bone bug there is. A model you have just spawned reports no position and no bones for roughly a third of a second, so reading a bone the moment you create something silently does nothing and looks like your names are wrong. This checks ten times a second until the object's position can actually be read, then runs your code once. If the object never becomes readable it gives up after a set number of tries and runs your code anyway (writing a line to the log), so nothing can hang forever - your code should still check that the exact bone it wants exists.

uGuid.desc: The object to wait on - normally wired straight out of a Spawn node. The player character is already loaded, so with the default your code runs almost immediately.

cb.desc: Your code, run once the model is ready. It receives the object so you can act on it. If your code errors, the error is caught and written to the log instead of breaking anything else.

maxTries.desc: How many tenth-of-a-second checks before giving up and running your code regardless. 6 (about 0.6 seconds) is the default and comfortably clears the confirmed third-of-a-second window.

Ess.Camera.beginCinematic.title: Camera: Begin Cinematic (Takes Control)
Ess.Camera.beginCinematic.desc: TAKES OVER the player's camera and locks their look control away so you can frame a shot. Nothing from Place Camera, Look At or Hold shows up until this has run. You MUST give control back with End Cinematic - always build the way out at the same time as the way in. If you ever do get stuck with a frozen camera, the Panic Revert node always works and can be fired blind.

i.desc: Whose camera to take over. 0 is you; 1 is the co-op partner, which doesn't exist in single-player and simply fails.

nBlend.desc: Seconds to ease into the shot. 1 is a nice entry and 0 is a hard cut - but 0 is REQUIRED if you're going to move the camera every tick (an orbit, a chase, a dolly), because any other value restarts a whole new ease on every move and the shot rubber-bands. That rubber-band is the classic 'why is my camera jittery' bug.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the takeover happened. False means there was no camera to take over - almost always because player 1 was asked for in a single-player game.

Ess.Camera.blend.title: Camera: Set Blend Time
Ess.Camera.blend.desc: Arms how long the NEXT Place Camera takes to glide across, instead of cutting. Begin Cinematic sets this once at the start; use this to re-arm it for a later smooth move - swing the camera out to one side, then later swing it back. This is for one-off moves only, one Place Camera per blend. A camera you're moving every tick still wants 0 here or it rubber-bands.

i.desc: Whose camera. 0 is you.

nDur.desc: Seconds the next camera move takes. 1 is a gentle glide, 2 to 3 is stately, 0 is an instant cut.

Ess.Camera.endCinematic.title: Camera: End Cinematic (Gives Control Back)
Ess.Camera.endCinematic.desc: Hands the camera and the player's controls back, and stops any watch or orbit follow loop running for that player. This is the way out of EVERY camera takeover - make certain something reaches it, on every path through your script. If a shot is already running and you have no way to get here, use Panic Revert.

i.desc: Whose camera to release. 0 is you. Releasing a player who was never taken over is harmless.

Ess.Camera.fade.title: Camera: Fade Screen
Ess.Camera.fade.desc: Fades the whole screen to black, or back to clear - the standard bookend for a cutscene, and the trick for hiding a cut or a teleport. There is no duration on this call at any confirmed use, so it is a straight set: use two of them with a wait between for a fade out then in. Careful - a fade to black with nothing to clear it leaves the player staring at nothing, so always have a clearing step (the cutscene runtime clears it for you automatically when a scene ends).

nAmount.desc: How black the screen is: 0 is fully clear, 1 is fully black. Those are the only two values real game code is confirmed to use.

Ess.Camera.followHardpoint.title: Camera: Follow A Hardpoint
Ess.Camera.followHardpoint.desc: Keeps the camera glued to a named hardpoint on a MOVING object by re-reading that point's world position many times a second and pushing the camera there - the fallback for the cases where the engine's own object-and-bone camera form does nothing. IMPORTANT: a look-at binding must already be active (run Look At A Point (Anchor), or a cinematic look-at, first) or setting the camera's position silently does nothing, exactly as everywhere else in this namespace. This is not a fix for the vehicle GUNNER camera - while seated in a turret the camera you can reach isn't the active one at all, which is a known hard limit.

uGuid.desc: The object carrying the hardpoint to follow.

hp.desc: The name of the bone or hardpoint to sit the camera on. Bone_Head works on a person; vehicles use their own hp_ names.

i.desc: Which player's camera to move. 0 is you.

interval.desc: How often to re-read the point, in seconds. 0.05 (twenty times a second) is the default and looks smooth; bigger numbers are cheaper but choppier.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: KEEP this. Call it (or drop it into an Ess Stop node) to end the follow - otherwise it keeps dragging the camera around forever.

Ess.Camera.fov.title: Camera: Set Field Of View
Ess.Camera.fov.desc: Blends the camera's field of view to a new angle over a few seconds - a punchy zoom in, or a wide dramatic pull back. Heads up: this reaches a genuinely DIFFERENT engine system from every other camera node here (it takes a player slot number rather than a camera handle) - it lives with the camera nodes because it is a camera effect, not because it shares any plumbing. Always pair it with Restore Field Of View or the player is left zoomed forever.

i.desc: Which player slot. Every confirmed real use in the game's own scripts passes 0, the local player.

nAngle.desc: The new field of view angle. Smaller zooms IN (30 is a strong telephoto look), larger pulls back to a wide, warped view. The game's normal value isn't documented anywhere confirmed, so set a value, look at it, adjust.

nDuration.desc: Seconds to blend to the new angle. 1 is a smooth push; 0 snaps instantly.

Ess.Camera.hold.title: Camera: Hold Framing
Ess.Camera.hold.desc: Pins the shot exactly where it is now, so the camera stops easing and stays on the framing you set. Use it as the last step of a locked-off shot: place the camera, aim it, hold it. End Cinematic releases the hold along with everything else.

i.desc: Whose camera to pin. 0 is you.

Ess.Camera.lookAtAnchor.title: Camera: Look At A Point (Anchor)
Ess.Camera.lookAtAnchor.desc: The fix for the single biggest camera trap on this engine: moving the camera does NOTHING until the camera has been told to look at an OBJECT - not even a deliberately huge test teleport moves it without one. This spawns a tiny invisible marker at a spot and locks the camera onto it, which creates that binding for real. After that you re-aim the shot by moving the marker, and clean up by removing it. It uses a TinyGeometry marker on purpose: that one is confirmed safe during live gameplay, unlike the 'Verification Camera' prop, which the game calls in and despawns almost immediately unless the world is paused.

x.desc: East/west coordinate of the spot to look at. Usually wired in from a position node rather than typed.

y.desc: Height of the spot. Aim about head height on a person rather than at their feet.

z.desc: North/south coordinate of the spot to look at.

i.desc: Which player's camera to bind. 0 is you; 1 is the co-op partner and does nothing in single-player.

returns.name: uAnchor
returns.desc: The little marker that was created. KEEP it: move it to re-aim the shot, and remove it when you're done or it stays in the world forever. You get nothing back if that player has no camera.

Ess.Camera.lookAtObject.title: Camera: Look At An Object
Ess.Camera.lookAtObject.desc: Locks the camera onto a thing and KEEPS it framed as that thing moves - this is the 'watch the helicopter fly in' shot, and the engine does the panning itself, so it stays smooth for free. It also creates the look-at binding that Place Camera needs before it will do anything. Tracking a moving VEHICLE: aim at whoever is RIDING it and give the bone Bone_Chest, because object tracking works on character bones, not vehicle hardpoints. Needs a camera takeover (Begin Cinematic) to be in effect.

uGuid.desc: The thing to keep framed. Wire in whatever you spawned - a helicopter, a car, a person.

sBone.desc: Optional bone or hardpoint to frame instead of the object's centre - Bone_Chest keeps a rider or a talking character nicely framed. Leave empty to look at the object as a whole.

i.desc: Whose camera. 0 is you.

Ess.Camera.lookAtPoint.title: Camera: Look At A Fixed Point
Ess.Camera.lookAtPoint.desc: Aims the camera at a fixed spot in the world by coordinates. WARNING, confirmed trap: this coordinate form does NOT create the look-at binding the engine needs, so Place Camera afterwards can silently do nothing and leave the camera stuck on the player - with control frozen, watching yourself. If you are placing the camera yourself, use Look At A Point (Anchor) instead, which spawns a tiny marker and looks at that; the cutscene runtime routes all of its point shots that way for exactly this reason.

x.desc: East/west coordinate of the spot to aim at.

y.desc: Height of the spot to aim at.

z.desc: North/south coordinate of the spot to aim at.

i.desc: Whose camera. 0 is you.

Ess.Camera.panicRevert.title: Camera: Panic Revert (Escape Hatch)
Ess.Camera.panicRevert.desc: The always-works way out. Force-releases EVERY camera takeover, for every player, and hands control back. Even while a cutscene has the controls locked the Lua console still accepts commands, so this can be fired blind to rescue a stuck camera. Worth putting on a key while you're building shots - it is the difference between a bad shot and a quit-to-desktop.

Ess.Camera.placeCamera.title: Camera: Place Camera
Ess.Camera.placeCamera.desc: Puts the cinematic camera at a fixed spot in the world. Two things must already be true or it silently does nothing at all: the camera must be taken over (Begin Cinematic), and it must already be looking at an OBJECT - so run Look At An Object or Look At A Point (Anchor) FIRST, then place. Whether the camera cuts or glides there is set by the blend time, not by this node.

x.desc: East/west coordinate of the vantage point. Normally wired in from a position node, offset a bit so you're not standing inside your subject.

y.desc: Height of the vantage point. Adding 8 to 12 above ground level gives the classic looking-down establishing shot.

z.desc: North/south coordinate of the vantage point.

i.desc: Whose camera to move. 0 is you.

Ess.Camera.restoreFov.title: Camera: Restore Field Of View
Ess.Camera.restoreFov.desc: Blends the field of view back to the game's normal value after Set Field Of View. Nothing else undoes it, so every zoom needs one of these eventually.

i.desc: Which player slot - the same one you zoomed. 0 is the local player.

nDuration.desc: Seconds to blend back. 1 is smooth; 0 snaps.

Ess.Camera.shake.title: Camera: Shake
Ess.Camera.shake.desc: Rattles the screen - the instant way to sell an explosion, a crash or a heavy impact. The default preset is a one-shot medium shake that ends by itself, which is the safe choice for a single call. The other confirmed preset keeps going until something stops it.

i.desc: Whose camera shakes. 0 is you; 1 is the co-op partner and does nothing in single-player.

sPreset.desc: The named shake style. ShakeCameraMedium is a one-shot rattle that stops on its own. ShakeCameraConstantlyRandom runs until the Stop Shake node is used - left unstopped it shakes until the player leaves the level. Those two are the names confirmed to exist.

uSource.desc: What the shake is coming from, so the game can judge it against the camera. Point it at the explosion, or just at the player.

nAmplitude.desc: How hard the shake is. 6 is the default and reads clearly - push it up for a big blast, down for a background rumble.

nDuration.desc: How many seconds it lasts. Meaningless for the never-ending preset, which needs Stop Shake instead.

Ess.Camera.staleAxisDecay.skip_reason: A programmer's helper for hand-built freecam controls - it hands back an object whose update method must be called from inside every controller-input event, which a node graph has no way to do.

Ess.Camera.stopShake.title: Camera: Stop Shake
Ess.Camera.stopShake.desc: Switches off an ongoing ShakeCameraConstantlyRandom shake. The one-shot medium shake finishes by itself and never needs this - but a constant shake left running lasts until the player leaves the level, so always pair the two.

i.desc: Whose camera to settle. 0 is you.

uSource.desc: The same source you gave the Shake node.

Ess.Cinematic.active.skip_reason: Hands back the running scene's internal bookkeeping object, which nothing else in a node graph can use - Is A Cutscene Playing answers the real question, and Stop already targets whichever scene is running.

Ess.Cinematic.define.title: Cinematic: Define A Named Cutscene
Ess.Cinematic.define.desc: Registers a cutscene under a name so it can be played later from anywhere by that name - a mission intro, a trigger, a contract. Nothing plays until you use Play A Named Cutscene. Definitions are wiped every time the game loads a level, on purpose, so that a saved scene can never carry stale coordinates into a different map - re-register yours when your script loads.

id.desc: The name you'll play it by. Keep it short and recognisable - defining a second scene with the same name replaces the first.

steps.default: { { type = "orbit", target = "player", radius = 9, height = 4, speed = 45, hold = 6 }, { type = "banner", text = "Reinforcements inbound", hold = 2 } }
steps.desc: The storyboard, same shape as the Play node: a Lua list of steps, each with type =, its own settings, and hold = seconds to wait before the next one.

opts.desc: Default settings for this scene (camera, blend, skippable, skipKey, startFade, i, onDone). Play A Named Cutscene can override any of them for one particular play.

Ess.Cinematic.isPlaying.title: Cinematic: Is A Cutscene Playing
Ess.Cinematic.isPlaying.desc: Tells you whether a cutscene is running right now. Only one can play at a time and a new one cancels the old, so this is the guard to put in front of anything that starts a scene - a second press of the key then does nothing instead of cutting the first scene short.

returns.name: bPlaying
returns.desc: True while a cutscene is running, false otherwise.

Ess.Cinematic.play.title: Cinematic: Play A Cutscene
Ess.Cinematic.play.desc: Plays an ordered list of steps as a cutscene - camera cuts, dollies, orbits and chases, spawns, AI orders, narration, fades, shakes, music, teleports - each step waiting its own 'hold' seconds before the next. By default it TAKES OVER the screen and the player's controls, and it ALWAYS gives them back when the scene finishes, is skipped, or is stopped; a step that errors is logged and the timeline carries on, and the screen is always cleared of any fade at the end, so a cutscene can never strand the player. Pressing ESC skips: every remaining step still FIRES (so actors the scene was going to spawn or position all still end up in place), it just stops waiting between them. Starting a new cutscene cancels any one already running.

steps.default: { { type = "orbit", target = "player", radius = 9, height = 4, speed = 45, hold = 6 }, { type = "banner", text = "Reinforcements inbound", hold = 2 } }
steps.desc: The storyboard: a Lua list of steps in order. Each is a table with type =, its own settings, and hold = how many seconds to wait before the next one (hold 0 fires the next step on the same tick, so several things can start together). Types: camera, orbit, chase, wait, spawn, face, order, fly, say/banner, subtitle, hint, vo, music, sound, fade, shake, teleport, relations, func. A spawn step's name = registers that actor so later steps can refer to it by that label, and "player" always means the hero.

opts.desc: Scene settings: camera = false runs the timeline WITHOUT taking over the screen, blend (0 for instant cuts, the default), skippable (ESC fast-forwards - on unless you turn it off), skipKey, startFade = true to open on black, i for the player index, and onDone = a function that runs when the scene ends.

returns.name: seq
returns.desc: A handle for the running scene. You can leave this unwired - the Stop node with nothing wired already ends whichever scene is playing. You get nothing back if the steps weren't a proper list.

Ess.Cinematic.playNamed.title: Cinematic: Play A Named Cutscene
Ess.Cinematic.playNamed.desc: Plays a cutscene you registered with Define A Named Cutscene. Same behaviour as playing one directly: it takes over the screen, ESC skips it, and control always comes back at the end. If no scene by that name exists, nothing happens and a line is written to the log - check your spelling and that the define ran first, since definitions are cleared on every level load.

id.desc: The name the scene was defined under.

extraOpts.desc: Settings that override the defined ones for this play only - most often onDone, so the same scene can run different code each time it ends. Leave empty to use the scene's own settings.

returns.name: seq
returns.desc: A handle for the running scene. Safe to leave unwired - Stop with nothing wired ends whatever is playing. You get nothing back if no scene by that name was defined.

Ess.Cinematic.skip.title: Cinematic: Skip To The End
Ess.Cinematic.skip.desc: Fast-forwards the cutscene that's playing: every remaining step still fires straight away, so everything the scene was going to spawn, order or say still happens - it simply stops waiting between them. This is exactly what ESC does for the player; use this node to skip from your own code, such as a button or a trigger. To end a scene WITHOUT firing the rest of it, use Stop instead.

Ess.Cinematic.stop.title: Cinematic: Stop A Cutscene
Ess.Cinematic.stop.desc: Ends the cutscene immediately. Remaining steps do NOT fire. The camera and controls go back to the player, any fade is cleared so the screen can't be left black, any tutorial hint is hidden, anything the scene marked as temporary is cleaned up, and the scene's onDone code runs. Use Skip instead when you want the rest of the scene's actions to still take effect.

seq.desc: Leave this empty. With nothing here it stops whichever cutscene is currently playing, which is what you almost always want; it only exists so code holding one specific scene handle can end that one.

Ess.Color.hex.title: Color: From Hex Code
Ess.Color.hex.desc: Turns a web colour code like #ff8800 into the red, green and blue numbers (0-255) that Ess markers and UI panels expect. Accepts #RRGGBB, RRGGBB, or the three-letter short form #f80. Gives back nothing at all if the text isn't a valid colour, so check it before using it.

s.desc: The hex colour code, with or without the leading #.

returns.name: r
returns.desc: Red, 0-255 (nothing if the code was invalid).

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green, 0-255.

Ess.Color.hsv.title: Color: From Hue/Saturation/Value
Ess.Color.hsv.desc: Builds a colour from hue, saturation and brightness instead of red/green/blue - the easy way to make a rainbow, or to give every squad member a clearly different tint by stepping the hue round. Hue is degrees around the colour wheel (0 red, 120 green, 240 blue); saturation and value run 0 to 1.

h.desc: Hue in degrees, 0 to 360 around the colour wheel.

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green, 0-255.

Ess.Color.lerp.title: Color: Blend
Ess.Color.lerp.desc: Blends two colours together - the trick behind a health bar that slides from green through yellow to red. Each colour is typed as a { r, g, b } list; t of 0 gives the first colour, 1 gives the second, and anything outside 0..1 is pulled back in.

c1.desc: First colour as { r, g, b }, each 0-255.

c2.desc: Second colour as { r, g, b }, each 0-255.

t.desc: How far between them, 0 to 1.

returns.name: r
returns.desc: Red of the blended colour, 0-255.

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green of the blended colour, 0-255.

returns.name: b
returns.desc: Blue of the blended colour, 0-255.

Ess.Color.of.title: Color: By Name
Ess.Color.of.desc: Looks up a ready-made colour by name so you never have to remember numbers. Known names: red, green, blue, yellow, orange, cyan, magenta, purple, pink, lime, teal, white, black, gray (or grey) and brown. Capitals don't matter. An unrecognised name gives back nothing.

returns.name: r
returns.desc: Red, 0-255 (nothing if the name is unknown).

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green, 0-255.

Ess.Contract.Abort.title: Contract: Cancel Mission
Ess.Contract.Abort.desc: Stops the running mission immediately and counts it as failed - no reward, the fail callback fires. Everything the mission created is cleaned up: HUD objective lines cleared, mission-spawned units and markers removed, faction stances put back the way they were, special music stopped. Safe to call when nothing is running (it just does nothing). This is your panic button while testing a mission.

Ess.Contract.Accept.title: Contract: Start Mission
Ess.Contract.Accept.desc: Starts a registered mission and hands the player their first objective. Places the heroes if the definition has a `start`, sets faction stances, plays the intro cutscene if there is one, then runs the objectives (in order, or all at once in parallel mode) until they are all done or one fails. Only one contract runs at a time - accepting a new one aborts whatever was running. In co-op only the host runs missions; a joining client is skipped on purpose.

idOrDef.desc: The id you gave the mission when you registered it. (It also accepts a whole mission definition table directly, if you would rather skip registering.)

Ess.Contract.Chase.title: Contract: Chase Objective
Ess.Contract.Chase.desc: Build a runner: targets that are actively trying to escape. It finds its targets the same three ways Destroy does (spawn them, name placed ones, or sweep an area), marks them, then ORDERS each one to run or drive for the escape point at whatever urgency you set - for a vehicle it steers the driver, not the hull, so they actually go. Kill all of them to complete. If even one reaches the escape point, or the optional clock runs out, the mission fails. This is your fleeing convoy or escaping VIP.

t.default: { desc = 'Stop the fleeing convoy', spawns = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -514, -2.1, 2706, 0 } }, escapeAt = { -440, -2.1, 2620 }, escapeRadius = 20, haste = 2, time = 120 }
t.desc: The objective spec. Targets come from `spawns` (a list of `{template, x, y, z, yaw}`), `objects = {'name', ...}` or `where = {area={x,y,z,r}, kind=, faction=}` - same as Destroy. `escapeAt = {x, y, z}` is where they are running to and `escapeRadius` is how close they need to get to have escaped (default 15). `haste` sets how hard they run (1 is normal, higher is faster). `time` is an optional deadline in seconds.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Collect.title: Contract: Collect Objective
Ess.Contract.Collect.desc: Build a pickup run. It spawns each item you list as a physical object in the world and marks it, and the player collects one simply by walking up to it - get within the pickup radius and it vanishes and the count goes up. Completes once the quota is reached. Good for intel, crates, cash drops and fetch quests.

t.default: { desc = 'Collect 3 intel packets', items = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -512, -2.1, 2706, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -504, -2.1, 2712, 0 } }, quota = 3, radius = 4 }
t.desc: The objective spec. `items` is a list of `{template, x, y, z, yaw}` pickups to spawn (use whatever prop template reads as your collectible). `quota` is how many the player needs (default: all of them). `radius` is how close they must get to grab one, in metres - defaults to 4, which is roughly 'walk over it'.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Defend.title: Contract: Defend Objective
Ess.Contract.Defend.desc: Build a 'hold out and keep it alive' objective. A clock runs for the given number of seconds; when it runs out the objective is complete. If the thing you named as the target is destroyed before then, the whole mission FAILS. With no target it is simply a survive-the-clock objective. Pair it with reinforcement waves from the contract's `support` list to give the player something to actually defend against.

t.default: { desc = 'Defend the transmitter for 60 seconds', time = 60, target = 'transmitter' }
t.desc: The objective spec. `desc` is the HUD line, `time` is how many seconds to hold (defaults to 60), and `target` is the NAME of an object already placed in the level - if it dies, the mission fails. Leave `target` out for a plain timer.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Destroy.title: Contract: Destroy Objective
Ess.Contract.Destroy.desc: Build a 'wreck these targets' objective. It can SPAWN its own targets for you (`spawns`), point at objects already placed in the level by name (`objects`), or sweep everything of a kind inside an area (`where`) - or any mix. Every target gets marked on the radar, PDA and in the world, and the objective completes once enough of them are destroyed. Anything it spawned is removed automatically when the mission ends. If it resolves zero targets it just completes instantly rather than hanging the mission.

t.default: { desc = 'Destroy the 2 cars', spawns = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -510, -2.1, 2700, 0 } } }
t.desc: The objective spec. `desc` is the line the player reads on the HUD. `spawns` is a list of `{template, x, y, z, yaw}` targets to create (swap in your own coordinates - stand where you want them and read the numbers with Ess.Player.pose(0)). `objects = {'name', ...}` uses already-placed level objects instead. `where = {area={x,y,z,r}, kind='vehicles', faction='VZ'}` grabs whatever is there right now. `quota` = how many must die (default: all of them). Every objective builder also takes `msg` (a radio line when it starts) and, inside a parallel group, `optional = true` plus `bonus = 5000` for a cash side-goal.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Enter.title: Contract: Get In Vehicle Objective
Ess.Contract.Enter.desc: Build a 'get in that vehicle' objective. It either points at a vehicle already placed in the level or spawns one for you, marks it so the player can find it, and completes the moment a player character sits down in the chosen seat. Worth knowing: this is the one objective type the framework has deliberately never live-tested (it needs a real player physically boarding a vehicle), so test it in-game before you build a mission around it.

t.default: { desc = 'Get in the chopper', spawn = { 'Ka29b (Full)', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, seat = 'd' }
t.desc: The objective spec. Either `target = 'name'` for a vehicle already in the level, or `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` to create one. `seat` picks which seat counts - 'd' is the driver's seat and is the default.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Escort.title: Contract: Escort Objective
Ess.Contract.Escort.desc: Build an escort objective. It spawns the thing to be escorted, marks it as a friendly to protect, and completes when THAT thing reaches the destination point. If it is destroyed on the way, the mission fails. One important catch: this objective only spawns and watches - it never gives the escortee movement orders, so in practice it should be a vehicle the player actually drives to the destination, or something ordered around by the contract's own units and waypoints.

t.default: { desc = 'Get the truck to the safehouse', spawn = { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, to = { -440, -2.1, 2620 }, radius = 15 }
t.desc: The objective spec. `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` creates the escortee. `to = {x, y, z}` is the destination and `radius` is how close it has to get (defaults to 15). The destination is marked with a ground ring for the player.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Extract.title: Contract: Extraction Objective
Ess.Contract.Extract.desc: Build the exfil - the objective that ends a mission. It marks the landing zone and completes once the player gets out. With a board time of 0 the LZ itself is the finish line; give it a board time and the player must hold the LZ that many seconds while the pick-up comes in (stepping out resets the count), optionally with a chopper spawning on the pad. Add a victory lap and instead of just cutting to complete, the player is seated as a PASSENGER in that chopper and flown a couple of orbits over the wreckage with a free camera - no cutscene takeover, they can look around at what they did.

t.default: { desc = 'Fall back to the LZ and extract', at = { -522.10, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 12, boardTime = 2, heli = 'Mi26 (CH) (Driver)', victoryLap = { orbits = 2, radius = 110, height = 55, line = "Rig's ours. Let's take her home." } }
t.desc: The objective spec. `at = {x, y, z}` and `radius` (default 15) are the LZ. `boardTime` is seconds to hold it (0 = instant extract, no chopper needed). `heli` names a chopper template to spawn on the pad - for a victory lap it must be a CREWED template (one with a driver, like 'Mi26 (CH) (Driver)'), or nobody flies it. `victoryLap = {orbits, radius, height, line}` flies the exit lap; `line` is a radio send-off.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Group.title: Contract: Objective Group (Phase)
Ess.Contract.Group.desc: Bundle several objectives into ONE - a mission phase. To the mission this counts as a single objective, but inside it you can run its children one after another ('sequential', the default) or all at the same time ('parallel'). A parallel group finishes when every non-optional child is done, and fails the moment a required child fails. This is how you say 'do these three things in any order, then move on', or how you build a mission in acts. Groups can be nested inside groups.

t.default: { desc = 'Secure the compound', mode = 'parallel', objectives = { Ess.Contract.Destroy{ desc = 'Wreck the AA gun', spawns = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 } } }, Ess.Contract.Reach{ desc = 'Tag the fuel depot', at = { -500, -2.1, 2680 }, radius = 10 }, Ess.Contract.Hold{ desc = 'Bonus: hold the roof', at = { -510, -2.1, 2690 }, radius = 12, time = 20, optional = true, bonus = 2500 } } }
t.desc: The objective spec. `objectives` is the list of child objective nodes. `mode` is 'sequential' (default, one after another) or 'parallel' (all at once). In parallel mode a child marked `optional = true` never blocks the group, and if it also has `bonus = 2500` the player is paid that cash for finishing it.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Hold.title: Contract: Hold Position Objective
Ess.Contract.Hold.desc: Build a 'hold this ground' objective. The zone is marked with a ground ring, and a timer counts up only while the player is standing inside it. Reach the required number of seconds and it completes. Time inside ADDS UP - stepping out of the ring pauses the count rather than wiping it, so a player who ducks out for cover does not lose all their progress. Pair it with reinforcement waves from the contract's `support` list for a classic capture-the-point fight.

t.default: { desc = 'Hold the landing zone for 30 seconds', at = { -524.02, -2.1, 2714.44 }, radius = 20, time = 30 }
t.desc: The objective spec. `at = {x, y, z}` and `radius` (defaults to 15) define the ring the player must stand in; `time` is how many seconds of standing there it takes (defaults to 15).

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Interact.title: Contract: Interact Objective
Ess.Contract.Interact.desc: Build a 'go and use this' objective - plant a charge, hack a terminal, talk to a contact, sabotage a generator, cut a prisoner loose. The action itself is imaginary: the flavour lives entirely in the wording you give it. The player has to get close to the target (or the bare spot) and STAY there while a short hold timer runs; walking away resets the hold to zero, so they have to commit. A hold time of 0 completes the moment they arrive.

t.default: { desc = 'Plant the charge on the refinery core', at = { -526.89, -2.10, 2737.72 }, radius = 6, time = 2 }
t.desc: The objective spec. Point it at a place with `at = {x, y, z}` (a ground ring is drawn there), at an object already in the level with `target = 'name'`, or at something to create with `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}`. `radius` is how close counts (defaults to 4) and `time` is how many seconds they must stand there (defaults to 0 = instant).

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.List.title: Contract: List Registered Missions
Ess.Contract.List.desc: Gives you every mission definition registered so far, in the order they were registered - the raw material for a mission-select board or a debug menu. The list is rebuilt from scratch on every level load, because nothing about a contract is ever written into the save.

returns.name: missions
returns.desc: An array of the registered definition tables (each with its `id`, `title`, `briefing`, `reward`, and so on).

Ess.Contract.Protect.title: Contract: Protect (Fail Condition)
Ess.Contract.Protect.desc: A background FAIL CONDITION, not a goal - it belongs in the contract's `fail` list, never in `objectives`. It watches one unit for the entire mission, marks it as a friendly, and instantly fails the whole mission the moment it dies. It can never complete on its own; it just sits there in the background the whole time. Use it for 'the convoy must survive' or 'do not let the hostage die' rules that apply across every objective.

t.default: { desc = 'Keep the hostage alive', spawn = { 'Allied Officer', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 } }
t.desc: The spec. Either `target = 'name'` for something already placed in the level, or `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` to create it. `desc` is just documentation here - a fail condition never draws its own HUD line.

returns.name: condition
returns.desc: Put this in the contract's `fail` list (not `objectives`).

Ess.Contract.Race.title: Contract: Race Objective
Ess.Contract.Race.desc: Build a checkpoint run. Only the NEXT checkpoint is marked at any time, so the player is always chasing one ring; hit it and the marker jumps to the following one. It completes when they have gone through all of them in order, and the finishing time is logged. Set a par time and blowing it fails the mission - that is your street-race or timed-delivery objective.

t.desc: The objective spec. `checkpoints` is a list of `{x, y, z}` points in the order they must be crossed. `radius` is how wide each gate is, in metres (defaults to 12 - keep it generous for vehicles). `time` is an optional par time in seconds; run out and the mission fails.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Reach.title: Contract: Reach Objective
Ess.Contract.Reach.desc: Build a 'get to this place' objective - the simplest one there is. It draws a ground ring and a destination blip at the point so the player can see where to go, and completes the instant a player walks or drives inside the radius. Nothing to kill, nothing to spawn.

t.default: { desc = 'Reach the extraction point', at = { -522.1, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 12 }
t.desc: The objective spec. `desc` is the HUD line, `at = {x, y, z}` is the spot (replace these coordinates with your own - stand there and read them with Ess.Player.pose(0)), and `radius` is how close counts, in metres (defaults to 15). Anything under about 8 gets fiddly in a vehicle.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Register.title: Contract: Register Mission
Ess.Contract.Register.desc: Files a whole mission definition under an id so it can be started later. This is the heavyweight of the three mission tools: a full engine with 16 objective types, rewards, spawned units, triggers and support call-ins. A contract is EPHEMERAL - it is built only from safe primitives and never writes anything into your game save, so it can never corrupt one; the trade-off is that it does not survive a save/reload, it is simply re-offered next time the level loads. Registering does not start anything: follow it with Accept.

def.default: { id = 'my_first_mission', title = 'Clear the Yard', briefing = 'Wreck the two cars, then reach the extraction point.', reward = { cash = 5000, fuel = 50 }, objectives = { Ess.Contract.Destroy{ desc = 'Destroy the 2 cars', spawns = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -510, -2.1, 2700, 0 } } }, Ess.Contract.Reach{ desc = 'Reach the extraction point', at = { -522.1, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 12 } }, onComplete = function() Ess.Log('mission complete, reward paid') end }
def.desc: The mission definition. Only `id` is truly required (and it should have `objectives` or nothing will happen). Common keys: `title`/`briefing` (text), `reward = {cash=, fuel=}`, `objectives = { ...objective nodes... }`, `mode = 'parallel'` to run them all at once instead of in order, `start = {x,y,z,yaw}` to place the heroes when it begins, `timeLimit` in seconds, `fail = { Protect/StayInArea nodes }`, `intro` (an opening radio line), `onComplete`/`onFail` functions. Bigger missions add `units`, `waypoints`, `support`, `triggers`, `relations`, `cinematic` and `sandbox = true`.

Ess.Contract.Status.title: Contract: Mission Status
Ess.Contract.Status.desc: Reads how the current mission is going - which objectives are ticked off, overall progress, and how much time is left on a time limit. Returns nothing at all when no mission is running. After a mission ends the last result stays readable (until the next Accept) so you can check whether it was completed or failed.

returns.name: status
returns.desc: A table: `objectives` (a list of `{done = true/false}`, one per objective), `progress` (0 to 1), `timeLeft` (seconds, only with a time limit), and `finished` ('complete' or 'failed') once it is over. Nil if no mission has run.

Ess.Contract.StayInArea.title: Contract: Stay In Area (Fail Condition)
Ess.Contract.StayInArea.desc: A background FAIL CONDITION, not a goal - it belongs in the contract's `fail` list, never in `objectives`. It fails the mission the instant the player leaves a circle around the given point: the classic 'do not leave the mission area' leash, running quietly under every objective. Note it draws NO marker or boundary of any kind, so say where the edge is in the mission briefing or the player will just get failed with no warning.

t.default: { desc = 'Do not leave the refinery grounds', at = { -522.10, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 250 }
t.desc: The spec. `at = {x, y, z}` is the centre of the allowed area and `radius` is how far the player may stray, in metres. The default radius if you omit it is only 100, which is very tight for anything with a vehicle in it - a few hundred is usually fairer.

returns.name: condition
returns.desc: Put this in the contract's `fail` list (not `objectives`).

Ess.Contract.Survive.title: Contract: Survive Objective
Ess.Contract.Survive.desc: Build a 'stay alive until the clock runs out' objective. This one draws its OWN countdown on the HUD ('Hold out (23s)') so the player watches the seconds tick down, and completes when it hits zero. You can also name something that must survive alongside them - if it dies first the mission fails. Almost always paired with enemy waves fired from the contract's `support` list, otherwise the player just stands around for a minute.

t.default: { desc = 'Hold out until evac arrives', time = 45 }
t.desc: The objective spec. `time` is the countdown in seconds (defaults to 60). `target` is optional and names something that must not die - either a group name from the contract's own `units` list, or the name of an object placed in the level.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract.Verify.title: Contract: HVT Bounty Objective
Ess.Contract.Verify.desc: Build a bounty on one named individual - a high-value target. It marks them and completes when they are killed. Turn on capture and there is a second way to finish it: get right up next to them while they are badly wounded and they count as taken alive instead, which is how you build a 'bring them in' contract without needing a real subdue animation.

t.default: { desc = 'Take out the Allied boss', spawn = { 'Allied Boss', -535.11, -2.15, 2706.61, 21.84 }, capture = true, captureHealth = 25, radius = 3 }
t.desc: The objective spec. Either `target = 'name'` for someone already placed in the level, or `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` to create them. `capture = true` also allows taking them alive: standing within `radius` metres (default 3) while their health is at or below `captureHealth` (default 25) counts as verified.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

Ess.Contract._CleanupAll.skip_reason: Internal teardown of a running mission's spawns, events and markers - happens automatically when a contract ends.

Ess.Contract._applyRelations.skip_reason: Internal - faction stances are declared with the mission's `relations` list, not applied by hand.

Ess.Contract._finish.skip_reason: Internal end-of-mission routine (payout, fanfare, cleanup); use Cancel Mission, or let the objectives resolve.

Ess.Contract._newTask.skip_reason: Internal bookkeeping bucket the engine uses to track and clean up one objective's spawns and events.

Ess.Contract._restoreRelations.skip_reason: Internal counterpart to the relations setup - runs automatically when the mission ends.

Ess.Contract._run.skip_reason: Internal single-objective runner; it needs a live mission instance no mod author ever holds.

Ess.Contract._runList.skip_reason: Internal objective-list runner - the mission's `objectives` list and the Objective Group node express this already.

Ess.Contract._spawnUnits.skip_reason: Internal - mission units are declared with the definition's `units` list, which this spawns for you.

Ess.Contract._startBackground.skip_reason: Internal - started automatically from the definition's `timeLimit` and `fail` entries.

Ess.Contract._startSupport.skip_reason: Internal - started automatically from the definition's `support`, `triggers` and `waypoints` entries.

Ess.Easy.AIOrders.attack.title: Easy AI Orders: Attack
Ess.Easy.AIOrders.attack.desc: Point a group of units at something and turn them loose - they hunt it down and open fire. Works on any units you hold guids for; they don't have to be your followers.

guids.desc: The units to command, as a Lua list of guids - normally the list a spawn node handed you. The default spawns three soldiers ahead of you (without setting them on you yet) so this node does something on its own.

target.desc: Who they go after. Ess.Player.character(0) is you, for a guaranteed instant firefight. Wire in any character or vehicle guid instead.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out.

Ess.Easy.AIOrders.guard.title: Easy AI Orders: Guard
Ess.Easy.AIOrders.guard.desc: They plant themselves on a spot and fight anything that comes inside it. This is the friendlier name for the engine's defend behaviour. Guarding has no natural finish - they hold that ground until you give them a different order.

guids.desc: The units to command, as a Lua list of guids - normally the list a spawn node handed you.

at.desc: The spot to hold, as {x, y, z}. The default { Ess.Player.pose(0) } means right where you're standing - Ess.Player.pose gives back your x, y, z (plus a yaw that's ignored here).

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out.

Ess.Easy.AIOrders.patrol.title: Easy AI Orders: Patrol
Ess.Easy.AIOrders.patrol.desc: They walk a beat between the points you list, over and over - a moving picket instead of a static guard. The route loops forever unless you drop down to Ess.AIOrders.command and pass loop = false.

guids.desc: The units to command, as a Lua list of guids - normally the list a spawn node handed you.

points.desc: The route, as a list of {x, y, z} waypoints. Switch on Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read your own coordinates off the screen and paste real ones in here.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out.

Ess.Easy.Airstrike.at.title: Easy Airstrike: On a Spot
Ess.Easy.Airstrike.at.desc: A gunship screams over the spot and four artillery shells rain down on it a fraction of a second apart. This is real, lethal ordnance - don't call it on ground you're standing on.

x.desc: World X of the target spot. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read coordinates off the screen.

y.desc: World Y (height/ground level) of the target spot.

z.desc: World Z of the target spot.

Ess.Easy.Airstrike.onMe.title: Easy Airstrike: On Me
Ess.Easy.Airstrike.onMe.desc: Calls the jet pass and the shell barrage down on your own head. For the brave, or for a cinematic - these are real explosives and they will kill you.

i.desc: Player slot: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

Ess.Easy.Airstrike.onTarget.title: Easy Airstrike: On My Target
Ess.Easy.Airstrike.onTarget.desc: Whatever your crosshair is resting on takes the full treatment - a jet pass plus four shells on its position. Aim first, then fire this node. If your reticle isn't on anything, nothing happens at all.

i.desc: Player slot whose reticle to read: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

Ess.Easy.Camera.fadeIn.title: Easy Camera: Fade In
Ess.Easy.Camera.fadeIn.desc: Fades the screen back up from black. The other half of Fade Out - always pair them, or you leave the player staring at a black screen.

Ess.Easy.Camera.fadeOut.title: Easy Camera: Fade Out
Ess.Easy.Camera.fadeOut.desc: Slams the screen to black. Nothing else stops - the world keeps running behind it, and the player keeps their controls. Call Easy Camera: Fade In to bring the picture back.

Ess.Easy.Camera.orbit.title: Easy Camera: Orbit a Target
Ess.Easy.Camera.orbit.desc: Takes over the camera and glides it in a slow circle around whatever you point it at - the money shot for showing off something you just spawned. WARNING: this steals the camera from the player until you call the stop function it hands back (or Ess.Camera.endCinematic), so always wire up a way out.

uGuid.desc: The thing to circle. Ess.Player.character(0) orbits you; wire in a vehicle or character guid from a spawn node instead.

opts.desc: Optional dials: radius (how far out, default 12), height (above the target, 4), speed (degrees per second, 40), startAngle (0), look (a different guid to point the lens at), bone, i. The motion is damped by default so a fast target doesn't make the shot jitter - add smooth = false for the old exact snap, or smoothFactor from 0 to 1 (higher = snappier, lower = glassier).

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to end the shot and hand the camera back to the player.

Ess.Easy.Camera.shake.title: Easy Camera: Shake
Ess.Easy.Camera.shake.desc: Kicks the screen around for a moment - the impact punch you want right after an explosion. Zero configuration: a medium shake centred on your character.

i.desc: Player slot to shake: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

Ess.Easy.Camera.watch.title: Easy Camera: Watch a Target
Ess.Easy.Camera.watch.desc: Locks a cinematic camera onto something and keeps it framed as it moves - perfect for watching the helicopter you just spawned fly in. By default the camera sits still at a fixed vantage and pans to follow; set chase = true and it flies along behind instead. WARNING: this steals the camera from the player until you call the stop function it hands back.

uGuid.desc: The thing to keep in frame. Wire in the guid a spawn node handed you.

opts.desc: Optional dials: at = {x,y,z} (where the camera parks; default just above you), height (6), chase = true (fly along behind instead of panning), angle (chase viewpoint in degrees, 200), dist (chase distance, 16), chaseHeight (6), look (a different guid to frame), bone, i. GOTCHA: aiming at a moving VEHICLE doesn't track - point at whoever is riding it instead, e.g. { look = Ess.Vehicle.driver(heli), bone = "Bone_Chest" }.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to end the shot and hand the camera back to the player.

Ess.Easy.Cinematic.play.title: Easy Cinematic: Play a Cutscene
Ess.Easy.Cinematic.play.desc: Plays a cutscene. Your steps fire in order, each held for its own few seconds, with the camera taken over and ESC letting the player skip. Control is ALWAYS handed back - on the last step, on a skip, or on a stop - so a cutscene can never strand the player. A skip still fires every remaining step (so actors a scene spawns end up in place), just with no waiting.

steps.desc: The storyboard: a Lua list of step tables in play order. Ess.Easy.Cinematic.shot(...) builds the simplest one (a static camera shot). Steps can also be waits, spawns, AI orders, on-screen narration, fades, shakes, music and teleports - see Ess.Cinematic for the full set.

onDone.desc: Runs the moment the cutscene ends, whether it played out or the player skipped it. This is where you start the mission the scene was introducing.

returns.name: seq
returns.desc: The running sequence - hand it to Ess.Cinematic.stop to cut it short.

Ess.Easy.Cinematic.shot.title: Easy Cinematic: Build One Shot
Ess.Easy.Cinematic.shot.desc: Builds ONE static camera shot - lens parked at one point, aimed at another, held for a few seconds - ready to drop into a Play a Cutscene list. It doesn't play anything by itself; it just describes the shot, so a hand-written scene reads like a storyboard.

at.desc: Where the camera sits, as {x, y, z}.

lookAt.desc: The world point it aims at, as {x, y, z}.

seconds.desc: How long this shot is held before the scene cuts on. Default 3.

returns.name: step
returns.desc: One step table. Collect several into a list and hand them to Easy Cinematic: Play a Cutscene.

Ess.Easy.Confirm.title: Easy UI: Yes/No Dialog
Ess.Easy.Confirm.desc: Pops a yes/no dialog in front of the player and runs one of your two callbacks depending on which they pick.

text.desc: The question shown in the dialog.

onYes.desc: What happens when they choose yes.

onNo.desc: What happens when they choose no. Optional - leave it out and a no simply does nothing.

Ess.Easy.Console.close.title: Easy Console: Close
Ess.Easy.Console.close.desc: Shuts the in-game Ess reference board, the playground and the search prompt - whichever of them is open.

Ess.Easy.Console.open.title: Easy Console: Open Reference
Ess.Easy.Console.open.desc: Opens the in-game reference board: every Ess.Easy call in the framework, grouped by namespace, browsable with the D-pad and with a description for each. The node to reach for when you want to see what else is available without leaving the game.

Ess.Easy.Console.play.title: Easy Console: Open Playground
Ess.Easy.Console.play.desc: Opens the PLAYGROUND - a drill-down menu where you actually RUN framework calls live and cycle through their parameter values to watch what each one does. The fastest way to learn what a call looks like in game. Calling it a second time closes it again.

Ess.Easy.Console.search.title: Easy Console: Search Reference
Ess.Easy.Console.search.desc: Opens a text prompt and filters the whole reference down to whatever you type, matching names, usage lines and descriptions (case doesn't matter). Submitting an empty search brings everything back.

Ess.Easy.Contract.destroy.title: Easy Contract: Destroy Mission
Ess.Easy.Contract.destroy.desc: Registers a full kill-these-guys contract AND accepts it, in one node. The enemies spawn where you placed them, the mission shows up in the player's contract UI with its reward, and it completes when the last one is dead. Without this you'd have to learn Register, def.id and Accept just to get one mission running.

sTitle.desc: The mission name the player sees in the contract UI.

tSpawns.desc: Who to spawn and where, as a list of {template, x, y, z} entries (an optional fifth number sets their facing). Killing all of them completes the contract.

tOpts.desc: Extras: desc (the objective line the player reads; defaults to the title) and reward = { cash = , fuel = }.

returns.name: id
returns.desc: The auto-generated contract id (easy1, easy2, ...) - keep it if you want to look this contract up later.

Ess.Easy.Contract.reach.title: Easy Contract: Go-Here Mission
Ess.Easy.Contract.reach.desc: Registers and accepts a go-here contract in one node: a real mission, in the player's contract UI, with a marked destination that completes the moment they arrive.

sTitle.desc: The mission name the player sees in the contract UI.

at.desc: The destination, as {x, y, z}. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read real coordinates off the screen.

radius.desc: How close the player has to get, in world units. Default 15.

tOpts.desc: Extras: desc (the objective line the player reads; defaults to the title) and reward = { cash = , fuel = }.

returns.name: id
returns.desc: The auto-generated contract id (easy1, easy2, ...) - keep it if you want to look this contract up later.

Ess.Easy.Debug.hide.title: Easy Debug: Hide Overlay
Ess.Easy.Debug.hide.desc: Forces the dev overlay off whether or not it's currently showing - unlike the overlay node itself, which toggles.

Ess.Easy.Debug.isOn.title: Easy Debug: Is Overlay On?
Ess.Easy.Debug.isOn.desc: Reports whether the dev overlay panel is currently up. A pure read - it changes nothing.

returns.name: on
returns.desc: True while the overlay panel is showing.

Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay.title: Easy Debug: Dev Overlay
Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay.desc: Toggles a live panel that follows you around showing the things you constantly need while building a mod: your exact world position and yaw (the number you keep needing to paste into spawn and teleport calls), what your crosshair is on with its name, faction and distance, whether you're on foot or in a vehicle, your health, and how many people and vehicles are nearby. Call it again to hide it. There's deliberately no FPS readout - this refreshes on a timer, so any framerate it printed would be a confidently wrong number.

opts.desc: All optional: x and y (where the panel sits on screen, default 20 and 40), interval (how often it refreshes in seconds, 0.2), radius (how far the nearby-count scan reaches, 40), i (player slot).

returns.name: panel
returns.desc: The panel widget - or nothing at all when the call toggled it back off.

Ess.Easy.Followers.hideMarkers.title: Easy Followers: Hide Markers
Ess.Easy.Followers.hideMarkers.desc: Clears the floating coloured icons from over your followers' heads, along with any ground ring showing where you last sent them. It only removes markers this system placed, never anyone else's.

Ess.Easy.Followers.orderAttack.title: Easy Followers: Attack
Ess.Easy.Followers.orderAttack.desc: Every follower on your roster breaks off and goes after one target. The moment it dies they automatically fall back in behind you - no second order needed.

target.desc: Who they attack. The default is whatever your crosshair is resting on right now - aim, then fire this node. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out to the roster.

Ess.Easy.Followers.orderEnter.title: Easy Followers: Board a Vehicle
Ess.Easy.Followers.orderEnter.desc: Your followers pile into a vehicle. The role defaults to driver rather than passenger on purpose: a follower in the driver's seat keeps taking every later order you give (move, attack, guard) and drives the vehicle there, through the same guid you already hold. Confirmed live - when that order finishes they climb back out and go back to following on foot, exactly like any other order.

vehicleGuid.desc: The vehicle to board. The default is whatever you're sitting in right now; wire in the guid a summon or spawn node handed you instead.

role.desc: driver, passenger or gunner. Keep driver if you want to keep steering the vehicle by ordering the follower. A passenger or gunner is still yours to command - they just aren't the vehicle.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out to the roster.

Ess.Easy.Followers.orderGuard.title: Easy Followers: Guard a Spot
Ess.Easy.Followers.orderGuard.desc: The whole roster digs in around a spot and fights anything that enters it. Guarding has no natural end - they stay there until you order something else.

at.desc: The ground to hold, as {x, y, z}. The default { Ess.Player.pose(0) } means right where you're standing.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out to the roster.

Ess.Easy.Followers.orderPatrol.title: Easy Followers: Patrol
Ess.Easy.Followers.orderPatrol.desc: The whole roster walks a repeating beat between the points you list, instead of trailing behind you.

points.desc: The route, as a list of {x, y, z} waypoints. Switch on Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read real coordinates off the screen.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out to the roster.

Ess.Easy.Followers.recruit.title: Easy Followers: Recruit
Ess.Easy.Followers.recruit.desc: Turns any character in the world into your follower - they fall in behind you and tag along, climbing into vehicles with you on their own, using the game's real recruit mechanic. Once recruited they answer to every Easy Followers order, and they take themselves off the roster automatically when they die.

guid.desc: Who to recruit. The default is whoever your crosshair is resting on - aim at someone and fire this node. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if they were recruited onto the roster.

Ess.Easy.Followers.showMarkers.title: Easy Followers: Show Markers
Ess.Easy.Followers.showMarkers.desc: Puts a floating icon over every follower's head, each one a different colour, and drops a white ground ring wherever you last ordered them - so you can see at a glance who is yours and where you just sent them. Anyone you recruit later gets a marker too.

Ess.Easy.Fun.dance.title: Easy Fun: Technoviking Dance
Ess.Easy.Fun.dance.desc: Your character breaks into the technoviking dance on the spot. Pure easter egg - nothing to configure, nothing to undo.

Ess.Easy.Fun.fanfare.title: Easy Fun: Victory Fanfare
Ess.Easy.Fun.fanfare.desc: Plays the game's own mission-complete music sting - or the mission-failed one. The right way to punctuate the end of something you built.

bWin.desc: true plays the victory sting, false plays the failure sting.

Ess.Easy.Human.giveWeapon.title: Easy Human: Give a Weapon
Ess.Easy.Human.giveWeapon.desc: Puts a weapon straight into someone's hands by name - nothing spawns, nothing has to be walked over. Confirmed to genuinely ADD a weapon to their inventory rather than just re-equip something they already carry. (For a pickup lying on the ground instead, use Easy Spawn: Weapon Pickup.)

uChar.desc: Who gets the weapon. Ess.Player.character(0) is you; wire in any character guid instead.

sTemplateName.desc: The weapon's in-game name, e.g. Grenade Launcher, RPG, Sniper Rifle, Assault Rifle, Minigun, Shotgun, C4, Anti-Material Rifle, Pistol. A name the game doesn't know is refused safely and written to the log.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if that weapon name was found and equipped.

Ess.Easy.Impulse.knockback.title: Easy Impulse: Knockback
Ess.Easy.Impulse.knockback.desc: Blasts something directly away from a source with a little upward lift - the sent-them-flying feel of an explosion. Mass-scaled, so it looks right on a person or a truck. GOTCHA: unlike Launch and Speed Boost this one has no fallback - with no target guid the call is refused and nothing moves at all.

uGuid.desc: Who gets thrown. Required - there's no fallback. The default is whatever your crosshair is on. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

fromGuid.desc: What they get thrown away FROM. Defaults to you, so they fly straight backwards from where you're standing. Point it at an explosion's location instead for a proper blast-wave shove.

strength.desc: How hard the shove is. Default 10 - a few units is a stumble, well past 10 is a full ragdoll launch.

Ess.Easy.Impulse.launch.title: Easy Impulse: Launch Upward
Ess.Easy.Impulse.launch.desc: Pops something straight up into the air - a little hop or a car-flipping launch, depending on the strength you give it.

uGuid.desc: What to launch. The default is you. (In hand-written Lua, leaving this out entirely picks the vehicle you're driving, or you on foot.)

strength.desc: The upward kick. Default 12 - try 4 for a hop, 30 for something ridiculous.

Ess.Easy.Impulse.speedBoost.title: Easy Impulse: Speed Boost
Ess.Easy.Impulse.speedBoost.desc: Slams whatever it is forward - the Spy Hunter effect. Mass-scaled, so it feels the same in a bike or a tank.

uGuid.desc: What to boost. The default is the vehicle you're driving; if you're on foot it quietly falls back to boosting you.

strength.desc: How hard. Default 8 - the original Spy Hunter script used 6 to 8.

Ess.Easy.Mark.enemy.title: Easy Mark: Enemy
Ess.Easy.Mark.enemy.desc: Tags a hostile so they show up on your radar and in your PDA - deliberately with NO floating world icon, matching how the game's own wave-defense script marks enemies (an icon over every enemy clutters the whole screen).

uGuid.desc: Who to mark. The default is whatever your crosshair is on. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The marker handle - hand it to Ess.Mark.clear to take the mark off again.

Ess.Easy.Mark.objective.title: Easy Mark: Objective
Ess.Easy.Mark.objective.desc: Marks something as a real mission objective on all three surfaces at once - radar, PDA, and a floating icon in the world - the same way the game's own contracts mark their targets.

uGuid.desc: What to mark as the objective. The default is whatever your crosshair is on. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The marker handle - hand it to Ess.Mark.clear to take the mark off again.

Ess.Easy.Mark.zone.title: Easy Mark: Zone Ring
Ess.Easy.Mark.zone.desc: Draws a glowing ring on the ground at a spot - the go-here disc, with no radar or PDA clutter added.

x.desc: World X of the ring's centre. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read coordinates off the screen.

y.desc: World Y (ground level) of the ring's centre.

z.desc: World Z of the ring's centre.

r.desc: The ring's radius in world units. About 8 is a comfortable you-are-here size; go bigger to circle a whole compound.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The marker handle - hand it to Ess.Mark.clear to remove the ring.

Ess.Easy.Menu.title: Easy UI: Menu
Ess.Easy.Menu.desc: Opens a menu on screen right now - one flat list of labelled actions, nothing to configure. Picking an entry runs your function.

title.desc: The heading across the top of the menu.

entries.default: { {"Summon a car", function() Ess.Easy.Vehicle.summon("Veyron") end}, {"Big boom", function() Ess.Easy.Spawn.explosion() end} }
entries.desc: The choices, as {label, action} pairs in the order you want them listed. One flat level only - for nested sub-menus use Ess.UI.Menu directly instead.

returns.name: menu
returns.desc: The open menu object.

Ess.Easy.Objective.title: Easy Objective: Counted Goal
Ess.Easy.Objective.desc: Puts a counted goal on the HUD objective line - Collect the intel 0/5 - that ticks up each time you advance it and fires your callback the moment it's met. This is the MANUAL kind: nothing moves it but your own script. For goals that watch the world themselves, use the reach, destroy, clear or survive variants.

label.desc: The text shown on the HUD objective line.

target.desc: How many times it has to be advanced before it counts as done. This is a COUNT, not a thing in the world. 1 makes it a plain do-this-once goal; anything above 1 shows a running counter on the HUD.

onComplete.desc: Runs the moment the count is reached.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: The live objective - call advance on it to tick it up, or complete / cancel to end it early.

Ess.Easy.Objective.clear.title: Easy Objective: Clear the Area
Ess.Easy.Objective.clear.desc: The eliminate-everyone-here goal. It rings the area on the ground, counts the enemies inside it, and updates the HUD line as they drop (Clear the area   4 left), completing when the last one falls. It works by counting the area's population once a second - the engine has no clean per-kill event, so this is the honest way to detect area cleared, bundled up for you.

x.desc: World X of the area's centre. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read coordinates off the screen.

y.desc: World Y (ground level) of the area's centre.

z.desc: World Z of the area's centre.

r.desc: How wide the area is, in world units. Default 40 - roughly a compound.

faction.desc: Which side to count, e.g. VZ, Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate. Leave it out to count every human inside the radius no matter whose side they're on.

label.desc: The HUD text. The live count is appended to it automatically.

onDone.desc: Runs when the last one inside the ring is dead.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: The live objective - cancel it if the mission moves on before the area is cleared.

Ess.Easy.Objective.destroy.title: Easy Objective: Destroy Target
Ess.Easy.Objective.destroy.desc: A destroy-this goal wired to one specific object you already hold: it marks the target on radar, PDA and in the world, and completes the instant that object dies - cleaning its own marker up afterwards.

guid.desc: The object that has to die. The default is whatever your crosshair is on; normally you wire in the guid a spawn node handed you. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

label.desc: The text shown on the HUD objective line.

onDone.desc: Runs the moment the target is destroyed.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: The live objective - cancel it if the mission moves on first.

Ess.Easy.Objective.reach.title: Easy Objective: Reach a Point
Ess.Easy.Objective.reach.desc: A go-here goal in one node: it drops a glowing ring on the ground so the player can see where, puts the label on the HUD, and completes the moment they walk inside it - then clears its own marker. One node instead of hand-wiring an area trigger, a marker, a goal and its teardown.

x.desc: World X of the destination. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read coordinates off the screen.

y.desc: World Y (ground level) of the destination.

z.desc: World Z of the destination.

r.desc: How close counts as arrived, in world units. Default 8 - a comfortable you're-here radius.

label.desc: The text shown on the HUD objective line.

onDone.desc: Runs the moment the player steps inside the ring.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: The live objective - cancel it if the mission moves on first.

Ess.Easy.Objective.survive.title: Easy Objective: Survive N Seconds
Ess.Easy.Objective.survive.desc: A live countdown on the HUD objective line (Survive   12s) that completes when it runs out - and FAILS if the local player dies before it does. The player watches the clock without you building any extra HUD.

seconds.desc: How long they have to last, in seconds. Default 30; anything under 1 is clamped up to 1.

label.desc: The HUD text. The remaining seconds are appended to it automatically.

onDone.desc: Runs when the timer runs out with the player still alive.

onFail.desc: Runs instead if the player dies before the clock does.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: The live objective - cancel it to stop the clock early.

Ess.Easy.Player.freeSupport.title: Easy Player: Free Support
Ess.Easy.Player.freeSupport.desc: Switches off every stock count and unlock requirement on the airstrike and support menu, so you can call anything in, as often as you like, for nothing. This is the game's own cheat-menu function.

bOn.desc: true makes support free, false puts the normal stock and unlock rules back.

Ess.Easy.Player.ghost.title: Easy Player: Ghost Mode
Ess.Easy.Player.ghost.desc: Stealth mode - drops your AI detectability to the engine's own floor so enemy perception mostly stops noticing you, and toasts on screen to confirm. Calling it again (or passing false) restores your original value EXACTLY, because it remembers the number it replaced. Honest limit: flooring detectability is confirmed reversible in game, but whether it makes AI genuinely blind or merely very short-sighted hasn't been measured yet.

bOn.desc: true to go dark, false to restore your original detectability exactly. (In hand-written Lua, calling it with no argument at all toggles.)

i.desc: Player slot: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

returns.name: on
returns.desc: Whether ghost mode is on after this call.

Ess.Easy.Player.giveAllRewards.title: Easy Player: Give All Rewards
Ess.Easy.Player.giveAllRewards.desc: Dispenses every unlock reward in the game at once - the same cheat-menu function the game itself uses.

Ess.Easy.Player.giveGrapplingHook.title: Easy Player: Give Grappling Hook
Ess.Easy.Player.giveGrapplingHook.desc: Unlocks the grappling hook and puts it on your character right now.

Ess.Easy.Player.skin.title: Easy Player: Change Skin
