Ess.Easy.Player.skin.desc: Swaps your character's entire look for another figure in the game - be Fiona, a VZ soldier, a beach civilian, a police officer. GOTCHAS: it's whole-figure only (individual body parts don't work), a level reload puts your normal look back, and a freshly skinned model's bones aren't ready for about a third of a second, so wait a beat before gluing bone effects onto a just-skinned character.

sCode.desc: The model code. Confirmed ones include pmc_hum_fiona, pmc_hum_eva, pmc_hum_diablo, vz_hum_solano, al_hum_boss, ch_hum_boss, gr_hum_boss, civ_hum_beachfemale_a and police_hum_officer_b - around thirty more exist.

i.desc: Player slot to re-skin: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

Ess.Easy.Player.unlockAllHQs.title: Easy Player: Unlock All HQs
Ess.Easy.Player.unlockAllHQs.desc: Unlocks every HQ and outpost on the map at once.

Ess.Easy.Player.unlockFastTravel.title: Easy Player: Unlock Fast Travel
Ess.Easy.Player.unlockFastTravel.desc: Unlocks every landing zone, so you can fast-travel anywhere on the map immediately.

Ess.Easy.Quest.title: Easy Quest: Linear Mission
Ess.Easy.Quest.desc: A whole linear mission in one node: an ordered list of goals, shown one at a time on the HUD objective line. Steps can wire themselves to the world (arrive somewhere, blow something up, clear an area) or be manual ones you finish yourself. Lighter than a full contract, far more than a bare HUD line.

steps.desc: The mission, in order. Each step is either { reach = {x,y,z,radius}, label = ... }, { destroy = someGuid, label = ... } or { clear = {x,y,z,radius,"VZ"}, label = ... } to complete itself off a world event, or just a plain string for a manual step you finish by calling advance on the quest.

onComplete.desc: Runs when the last step is done. The default plays the victory sting.

returns.name: quest
returns.desc: The running quest - advance, skip or cancel it, or ask which step it's on.

Ess.Easy.Relations.makeAllies.title: Easy Relations: Make Allies
Ess.Easy.Relations.makeAllies.desc: Every faction in your list becomes allied with every other one in it - they stop shooting each other and fight side by side. GUARDRAIL: this Easy tier keeps exactly ONE relation set alive at a time, so calling any Easy Relations node again first puts the previous one back. It can't leak or stack. Use Ess.Relations directly if you need several sets at once.

factionList.desc: The factions to pair up, as a list of names. Valid names: Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ and PMC (PMC is you).

Ess.Easy.Relations.makeHostile.title: Easy Relations: Make Hostile to You
Ess.Easy.Relations.makeHostile.desc: Every faction you list turns on YOU - on PMC - and the change is registered properly so the HUD's attitude display reflects it. One node and half the map wants you dead. GUARDRAIL: only one Easy relation set is alive at a time; calling another Easy Relations node first restores this one.

factionList.desc: Who turns on you, as a list of faction names. Valid names: Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ.

Ess.Easy.Relations.restore.title: Easy Relations: Restore
Ess.Easy.Relations.restore.desc: Puts faction relations back exactly as they were before your last Easy Relations call. Safe to fire at any time - if no Easy relation set is active it simply does nothing.

Ess.Easy.Relations.sideWith.title: Easy Relations: Side With
Ess.Easy.Relations.sideWith.desc: Picks your side in one node: you ally with one faction, go hostile to the other, and set those two at war with each other. The whole stance for I'm helping this lot crush that lot - e.g. side with China against the Allies and back their assault on the Allied refinery.

friend.desc: The faction you're backing. One of Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ.

foe.desc: The faction you're both turning on. One of Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ.

Ess.Easy.Relations.war.title: Easy Relations: Start a War
Ess.Easy.Relations.war.desc: Sets two factions at each other's throats with you left out of it entirely - a firefight you can stand back and watch. This is the case Make Hostile can't express, because Make Hostile always means hostile to you.

a.desc: One side of the war. One of Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ.

b.desc: The other side. One of Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ.

Ess.Easy.Sandbox.arena.title: Easy Sandbox: Begin Arena
Ess.Easy.Sandbox.arena.desc: Walls off a temporary playground with every protection on at once: your cash is banked away and restored exactly afterwards, the support menu is isolated, faction relations are snapshotted, world layers are managed - and SAVING IS BLOCKED for the whole duration, so a crash mid-arena just leaves your normal game untouched. Everything is guaranteed restored by Easy Sandbox: Done.

id.desc: A name for this sandbox - pass the same one to Easy Sandbox: Done to end it. Beginning an id that's already running does nothing.

opts.desc: Optional: startCash (what your wallet holds inside the arena - your real balance is restored on finish either way) and relations (a list of {factionA, factionB, stance} to apply only for the arena).

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: False if that id was already running, or if nothing could actually be isolated (a typo'd provider name).

Ess.Easy.Sandbox.done.title: Easy Sandbox: Done
Ess.Easy.Sandbox.done.desc: Ends the arena and restores everything it touched - your cash, the support menu, faction relations, layers - and lets the game save again.

id.desc: The same name you gave Easy Sandbox: Begin Arena.

Ess.Easy.Sound.play.title: Easy Sound: Play a Cue
Ess.Easy.Sound.play.desc: Fires a one-shot sound effect straight at the player with no world position - the UI beep, alert or sting case. (For a sound coming out of an object in the world, use Ess.Sound.cue with its guid.)

sCueName.desc: The game's internal name for the sound cue. The framework confirms no cue names of its own, so you need a real one from the game's sound bank - see the string catalog at wiki.mercs2.tools/reference.html. An empty or unknown name is ignored safely and written to the log.

Ess.Easy.Spawn.airstrike.title: Easy Spawn: Shell On My Head
Ess.Easy.Spawn.airstrike.desc: Drops a live artillery shell out of the sky onto your own position from 250 units up - the classic sandbox gag. It's real, impact-fused, lethal ordnance and it is aimed squarely at you.

sRound.desc: Which round falls. Confirmed: Artillery Shell (default), Gunship Shell, Cluster Bomb Projectile, Cruise Missile Projectile, Bomb.

Ess.Easy.Spawn.crate.title: Easy Spawn: Supply Crate
Ess.Easy.Spawn.crate.desc: A supply crate parachutes down just in front of you - spawned high on purpose so it drifts in under its chute exactly the way the game's own bounty crates do.

sType.desc: Which crate falls. Confirmed types: Supply Drop (Light MG) (default), Supply Drop (Blueprints), Supply Drop (Treasure).

returns.name: crate
returns.desc: The crate that appeared - wire it into other nodes. Nothing comes back if the template name was wrong.

Ess.Easy.Spawn.enemies.title: Easy Spawn: Enemy Squad
Ess.Easy.Spawn.enemies.desc: A squad of hostiles drops in a short way ahead of you and immediately comes at you - an instant firefight in one node. It hands back their guids so you can keep ordering or tracking them afterwards.

nCount.desc: How many spawn. They're laid out three to a row, so 3 is a line abreast and 6 is two ranks. Default 3.

opts.desc: Optional: template (who spawns - VZ Soldier is the confirmed one), dist (how far ahead of you, 14), spread (how far apart, 3), attack (set false and they just stand there instead of charging you), target (who they go for; you by default).

returns.name: guids
returns.desc: A Lua list of the units that spawned - wire it into an AI Orders node to command them further.

Ess.Easy.Spawn.explosion.title: Easy Spawn: Explosion
Ess.Easy.Spawn.explosion.desc: A real explosion goes off about ten units in front of you - placed ahead rather than in your face so it's dramatic without instantly killing you. These are genuine, damaging blasts; don't stand in them.

sType.desc: How big a bang. Confirmed types: Explosion (Grenade) (default), Explosion (C4), Explosion (MOAB), Explosion (Rocket Artillery), fx_Explosion_Huge.

returns.name: guid
returns.desc: The spawned explosion object. Nothing comes back if the template name was wrong.

Ess.Easy.Spawn.fx.title: Easy Spawn: Effect at a Point
Ess.Easy.Spawn.fx.desc: Puts a particle effect at a world position. One-shot effects clean themselves up when they finish; ambient ones like a smoke plume keep going until you remove them yourself with Ess.Object.remove.

sTemplate.desc: Which effect. Confirmed names: fx_Explosion_Huge, global_particle_explosion_c4, global_particle_env_smokeplume_distance_tall, plus the whole Explosion (...) family.

x.desc: World X to put it. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read coordinates off the screen.

y.desc: World Y (height) to put it.

z.desc: World Z to put it.

returns.name: guid
returns.desc: The spawned effect. Nothing comes back if the template name was wrong.

Ess.Easy.Spawn.fxOn.title: Easy Spawn: Effect on an Object
Ess.Easy.Spawn.fxOn.desc: Sticks an effect on an object. Give it a bone name and the effect is GLUED there and travels with them - smoke pouring off a running man. Leave the bone out and it's a one-shot fired at wherever they happen to be standing, which will NOT follow them. You have to supply the bone name yourself, since only you know your model's bones: a character's real bones work, vehicle hardpoints don't bind at all.

sTemplate.desc: Which effect. Confirmed names: fx_Explosion_Huge, global_particle_explosion_c4, global_particle_env_smokeplume_distance_tall, plus the whole Explosion (...) family.

uGuid.desc: What to put the effect on. Ess.Player.character(0) is you.

sBone.desc: The bone to glue it to, e.g. Bone_Chest on a character - the effect then follows them around. Leave it out entirely for a one-shot at their current position that stays behind. Remove a glued one with Ess.Bones.detachFX.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The effect handle - pass a glued one to Ess.Bones.detachFX to take it off again.

Ess.Easy.Spawn.weapon.title: Easy Spawn: Weapon Pickup
Ess.Easy.Spawn.weapon.desc: Drops a weapon pickup on the ground just in front of you - walk over it to grab it. (To put one straight into someone's hands instead, use Easy Human: Give a Weapon.)

sName.desc: Which weapon. Confirmed names: RPG (default), Sniper Rifle, Assault Rifle, Minigun, Shotgun, Grenade Launcher, C4, Anti-Material Rifle, Pistol.

returns.name: pickup
returns.desc: The pickup lying on the ground. Nothing comes back if the template name was wrong.

Ess.Easy.Squad.assignRole.title: Easy Squad: Assign Role
Ess.Easy.Squad.assignRole.desc: Tags one squad member with a role. Roles are just labels and nothing enforces them - but Mount Up reads them: whoever you tag as driver claims the driver's seat before anyone else can take it.

guid.desc: Which member to tag. The default is whoever your crosshair is on. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

roleType.desc: A free-form label. driver is the one the framework actually acts on; anything else (heavy, medic, gunner) is purely yours to read back later.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the role was recorded.

Ess.Easy.Squad.cancelQueue.title: Easy Squad: Cancel Queue
Ess.Easy.Squad.cancelQueue.desc: Aborts a team's running step sequence part-way through and drops them straight back to following you - the safe fallback.

teamName.desc: The team whose plan you're calling off - the same name you gave Create Team.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if a queue was found and cancelled.

Ess.Easy.Squad.clearFormation.title: Easy Squad: Clear Formation
Ess.Easy.Squad.clearFormation.desc: Stops holding a formation. The squad simply stays wherever they were standing when you called it - nothing marches them back.

teamName.desc: The team to release - the same name you gave Create Team.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the formation was stopped.

Ess.Easy.Squad.createTeam.title: Easy Squad: Create Team
Ess.Easy.Squad.createTeam.desc: Carves a named team out of your followers so you can order that group on its own instead of the whole roster. GOTCHA: only units already recruited as followers make it in - anyone else in your list is silently dropped. Teams look after themselves: a member who dies or is dismissed falls out of the team automatically.

teamName.desc: What to call this team. You use this name in every other Easy Squad node. (The name __all__ is reserved and will be refused.)

guids.desc: The members, as a Lua list of guids. Ess.Followers.list() is everyone you currently have; wire in a subset to split your roster into two teams.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the team was defined.

Ess.Easy.Squad.dismountAndSecure.title: Easy Squad: Dismount and Secure
Ess.Easy.Squad.dismountAndSecure.desc: The team piles out of whatever they're riding and sets up a defensive perimeter on the spot. A gotcha the framework already handles for you: the engine's own deploy only ejects PASSENGERS - the driver stays glued to the wheel - so this explicitly kicks the driver out too, then waits two seconds for everyone to actually get clear before the defend order lands.

teamName.desc: The team to disgorge - the same name you gave Create Team.

atPos.desc: Where the perimeter goes, as {x, y, z}. The default { Ess.Player.pose(0) } means right where you're standing.

radius.desc: How wide a perimeter they hold, in world units. Default 15.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the team had anyone to dismount.

Ess.Easy.Squad.mountUp.title: Easy Squad: Mount Up
Ess.Easy.Squad.mountUp.desc: The whole team boards one vehicle, in the right order: anyone you tagged with the driver role gets in first so nobody else steals the wheel, and everyone else piles in as passengers. If the vehicle is full or the way is blocked it quietly gives up after about 20 seconds - a real, expected outcome here, not an error.

vehGuid.desc: The vehicle they board. The default is whatever you're sitting in; wire in the guid a summon or spawn node handed you instead.

teamName.desc: The team to load - the same name you gave Create Team. (A raw Lua list of guids works here too.)

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the boarding orders went out.

Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamAttack.title: Easy Squad: Team Attack
Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamAttack.desc: Just this team peels off to attack a target - your other teams carry on doing whatever they were already doing. When the target dies, this team falls back in behind you on its own.

teamName.desc: Which team goes in - the same name you gave Create Team.

target.desc: Who they attack. The default is whatever your crosshair is on - aim, then fire this node. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out. False if the team is empty or unknown.

Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamFollow.title: Easy Squad: Team Follow
Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamFollow.desc: Sends one team back to following you. Vehicle-aware, and that matters: a member who's currently DRIVING gets an escort route instead of being told to climb out and follow on foot, and passengers and gunners are left completely alone. This is the fix for the gunner jumps out the instant an order finishes problem.

teamName.desc: Which team comes back to you - the same name you gave Create Team.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out. False if the team is empty or unknown.

Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamGuard.title: Easy Squad: Team Guard
Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamGuard.desc: This team digs in at a spot and fights anything that enters it, while your other teams keep their own orders. Guarding never finishes on its own - they hold until you order something else.

teamName.desc: Which team holds the ground - the same name you gave Create Team.

at.desc: The ground to hold, as {x, y, z}. The default { Ess.Player.pose(0) } means right where you're standing.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out. False if the team is empty or unknown.

Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamPatrol.title: Easy Squad: Team Patrol
Ess.Easy.Squad.orderTeamPatrol.desc: This team walks a repeating route between your waypoints while the rest of your followers get on with their own orders.

teamName.desc: Which team walks the beat - the same name you gave Create Team.

points.desc: The route, as a list of {x, y, z} waypoints. Switch on Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read real coordinates off the screen.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out. False if the team is empty or unknown.

Ess.Easy.Squad.queue.title: Easy Squad: Queue a Plan
Ess.Easy.Squad.queue.desc: Runs a team through a multi-step plan, waiting for each step to genuinely finish before starting the next: board the truck, wait until everyone's seated, drive to the LZ, wait for arrival, pile out. Every step also carries a watchdog (30 seconds unless you say otherwise) so one stuck unit or blocked path can never freeze the sequence forever. HONEST LIMIT: only move, non-looping patrol, attack and enter have real completion signals - a guard or hold step just runs out its timeout before the plan moves on.

teamName.desc: Which team runs the plan - the same name you gave Create Team. (A raw Lua list of guids works here too.)

steps.default: { { behavior = "move", opts = { at = { Ess.Player.pose(0) } } }, { behavior = "defend", opts = { at = { Ess.Player.pose(0) }, radius = 15 } } }
steps.desc: The plan in order, as a list of { behavior = ..., opts = { ... }, timeout = seconds }. Behaviors are the AI order names: move, attack, patrol, defend, hold, enter, deploy, follow, face, flee, animate. The default is come to me, then hold this ground.

onComplete.desc: Runs once the last step is done. (For an onCancel handler or per-step timeouts, drop to Ess.Squad.queue directly.)

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the plan started.

Ess.Easy.Squad.setFormation.title: Easy Squad: Set Formation
Ess.Easy.Squad.setFormation.desc: The team spreads into a shape around you and holds it as you move - a wedge fanned out ahead, single file in a column, a flat line, or a diamond ringing you completely. It's visual sugar rather than a precision tactical system: underneath, it's units walking to waypoints that get recomputed every tick as you move.

teamName.desc: Which team forms up - the same name you gave Create Team.

formationType.desc: wedge (a V opening forward, the default), column (single file behind you), line (a flat wall abreast) or diamond (a full 360-degree ring around you).

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the formation took hold.

Ess.Easy.Time.slowmo.title: Easy Time: Slow Motion
Ess.Easy.Time.slowmo.desc: Drops the game into bullet time and puts it back by itself a few seconds later - the finisher-moment beat you want right on an explosion. The countdown to the restore runs in REAL seconds, deliberately not slowed itself, so it always comes back exactly when you expect.

n.desc: How slow, as a multiplier of normal speed. Default 0.2 (one fifth speed); 0.5 is a gentle sag, 0.05 is nearly frozen.

seconds.desc: How long the slow motion lasts, in real seconds. Default 2.

Ess.Easy.Toast.title: Easy UI: Toast
Ess.Easy.Toast.desc: Flashes a short notification on screen and forgets about it. The simplest possible way to prove your script actually ran.

msg.desc: The line of text to flash up. Anything you pass is turned into text for you.

Ess.Easy.Triggers.after.title: Easy Triggers: After N Seconds
Ess.Easy.Triggers.after.desc: Waits, then runs your code once. The whole do-this-in-a-moment thought in one node - a delayed explosion, a reinforcement wave, a line of dialogue after a beat.

seconds.desc: How long to wait before firing, in seconds.

fn.desc: The code that runs when the time is up. It fires once and the trigger is done.

returns.name: cancel
returns.desc: Call it to disarm the timer before it ever fires.

Ess.Easy.Triggers.onDeath.title: Easy Triggers: On Death
Ess.Easy.Triggers.onDeath.desc: Watches one object and runs your code the moment it's destroyed - the enemy commander drops and the gates open. Fires once.

uGuid.desc: What to watch. The default is whatever your crosshair is on; normally you wire in the guid a spawn node handed you. (The wrapping parentheses matter: they trim the extra values that call returns.)

fn.desc: The code that runs the instant it dies.

returns.name: cancel
returns.desc: Call it to disarm the trigger before it ever fires.

Ess.Easy.Triggers.onPlayerNear.title: Easy Triggers: On Player Near
Ess.Easy.Triggers.onPlayerNear.desc: Arms an invisible tripwire at a spot: the moment the player comes within the radius, your code runs. The ambush-when-they-arrive node.

x.desc: World X of the tripwire's centre. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read coordinates off the screen.

y.desc: World Y (ground level) of the tripwire's centre.

z.desc: World Z of the tripwire's centre.

r.desc: How close the player has to get before it fires, in world units. Nothing is drawn on screen - add Easy Mark: Zone Ring if you want them to see it.

fn.desc: The code that runs when they walk in. The default drops an ambush squad on them.

returns.name: cancel
returns.desc: Call it to disarm the tripwire before it ever fires.

Ess.Easy.Vehicle.summon.title: Easy Vehicle: Summon
Ess.Easy.Vehicle.summon.desc: The one-liner this whole namespace exists for: a vehicle appears a short way in front of you and you're already in the driver's seat. It spawns slightly airborne on purpose, so a helicopter is hovering the instant you have the controls and a ground vehicle just drops and settles. A template name the game doesn't know spawns nothing and logs which name failed.

sTemplate.desc: The vehicle's in-game name, e.g. UH1 Transport (a helicopter you're flying immediately), AH1Z (Full) (a fully armed attack helicopter) or Veyron (a supercar).

opts.desc: Optional: dist (how far ahead it appears, default 18), height (how high above the ground, 10), useView = true to put it where you're LOOKING rather than where your body is turned.

returns.name: vehicle
returns.desc: The vehicle that appeared - wire it into other nodes. Nothing comes back if the template name was wrong.

Ess.Easy.World.brightness.title: Easy World: Brightness
Ess.Easy.World.brightness.desc: Turns the world's light level up or down. It STICKS: crossing into a new zone would normally reset the lighting, so a small keeper watches for that and snaps your setting straight back - it survives driving right across the map until you call Reset Atmosphere. REGION-GATED: it only shows while you're standing in a real map region, not inside the HQ.

n.desc: The light level. 1 is normal daylight, 0.05 is near-black, above 1 blows the picture out. Try 0.15 for a blackout.

Ess.Easy.World.clearWanted.title: Easy World: Clear Wanted Level
Ess.Easy.World.clearWanted.desc: Every police and faction pursuit on you drops instantly - you go from hunted to cold in one node. This is a one-shot clear, though: fresh heat can start building again straight away. Use Easy World: No Pursuit if you want to stay cold.

Ess.Easy.World.hellscape.title: Easy World: Hellscape
Ess.Easy.World.hellscape.desc: The world goes dark and blood-red in one node - the ready-made preset. It sticks across zone changes, and Easy World: Reset Atmosphere puts it back. REGION-GATED: it only shows while you're standing in a real map region, not inside the HQ.

Ess.Easy.World.noPursuit.title: Easy World: No Pursuit
Ess.Easy.World.noPursuit.desc: Kills the chase you're in AND keeps new heat from building, so you stay cold - the whole thought in one node. Pass false to hand normal pursuit behaviour back. Note it only blocks heat the world generates on its own; a pursuit a script starts deliberately was never blocked either way.

bOn.desc: true stops the current chase and keeps new heat off, false restores normal pursuit behaviour.

Ess.Easy.World.removeMapBoundary.title: Easy World: Remove Map Boundary
Ess.Easy.World.removeMapBoundary.desc: Tears down the invisible wall that fences you into the story-unlocked part of the map, along with Fiona's warning and the screen static. Drive anywhere. GOTCHAS: there's no clean way to put it back, and it's host-authoritative - it works in single-player and for a co-op HOST but does nothing at all on a co-op CLIENT (use Ess.Player.removeBoundaries there instead).

Ess.Easy.World.resetAtmosphere.title: Easy World: Reset Atmosphere
Ess.Easy.World.resetAtmosphere.desc: Stops the keeper and lets the world's own natural lighting and colour come back, undoing any tint, brightness change or hellscape you applied.

Ess.Easy.World.tint.title: Easy World: Tint
Ess.Easy.World.tint.desc: Washes the whole world in a colour. It STICKS across zone changes - a keeper re-applies it the instant a new zone tries to overwrite it - until you call Reset Atmosphere. REGION-GATED: it only shows while you're standing in a real map region, not inside the HQ.

b.desc: Blue, from 0 to 255. Default 30 - the three defaults together give the deep red used by the hellscape preset.

Ess.Event.off.title: Event: Unhook
Ess.Event.off.desc: Deletes a hook made by Event: Hook Engine Event. Engine hooks are never cleaned up for you, so every hook a feature makes needs one of these when the feature ends - or a tracker doing it for you.

handle.desc: The handle the hook node handed back. Wire it in; an empty one just does nothing.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if a hook was actually deleted. False means the handle was empty or already gone - harmless, but a sign you are unhooking twice.

Ess.Event.on.title: Event: Hook Engine Event
Ess.Event.on.desc:
Wires an action to a raw engine event, for the cases the On: nodes do not cover. This is the low-level door, so it is easy to get wrong.

THE TRAP: if the arguments do not match the shape that event expects, nothing errors and nothing is logged - the hook simply never fires. When a handler seems dead, it is almost always this, not your action.

eventType.desc: The engine's event constant, typed as code and NOT in quotes - Event.ObjectDeath, Event.TimerRelative, and so on. Quoting it gives you a hook that never fires.

args.desc: The arguments that event expects, as a Lua list. Every event wants its own shape and getting it wrong fails silently - check the event's wiki page rather than guessing.

cb.desc: What to run when it fires. What it is handed depends on the event.

tracker.desc: Optional. Wire in a tracker from Track: New and this hook is torn down with everything else in that bin, instead of you having to remember it separately.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The hook's handle, or nothing if it could not be created (that failure IS logged). Keep it and pass it to Event: Unhook, or you have no way to turn this off.

Ess.Followers._emit.skip_reason: Internal event-bus trigger the framework uses to fire follower events; it takes open-ended extra arguments, and beginners subscribe with the On Event node instead.

Ess.Followers._followLoopAnchorOf.title: Followers: Current Waypoint (debug)
Ess.Followers._followLoopAnchorOf.desc: A live-map diagnostic. When a follower is escorting you as a vehicle driver, or catching back up to you on foot after an order, the system walks them toward an invisible marker post that it repositions every second. This hands you that post, so you can watch where a unit is ACTUALLY being sent right now - which is what makes a stuck escort obvious instead of a unit standing still with no visible explanation. Empty when this follower is not in one of those loops.

returns.name: anchor
returns.desc: The invisible waypoint object this follower is currently being walked toward, or nothing if they are not escorting or catching up right now.

Ess.Followers._issue.skip_reason: Internal raw order primitive with no markers and no automatic return to following - the Order Everyone and Order Team nodes are the ones to use.

Ess.Followers._orderScoped.skip_reason: Internal core shared by Order Everyone and Order Team; exposed only so ordering one team cannot clash with another team's order.

Ess.Followers.count.title: Followers: Count
Ess.Followers.count.desc: How many followers you have right now. It reads the same live, self-cleaning roster, so units that have been killed are never counted.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: The number of followers currently on your roster. 0 if you have none.

Ess.Followers.dismiss.title: Followers: Dismiss
Ess.Followers.dismiss.desc: Releases one follower. They stop following, get their ordinary background life back, lose their marker, and drop off your roster - any escort or catch-up loop running for them is stopped too. Dismissing somebody who was never recruited is a safe no-op. This same thing runs automatically when a follower is killed, which is why dead units never linger on your roster.

guid.desc: The follower to release. The default picks the first person you recruited.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if they were on the roster and have now been released. False if they were not a follower in the first place.

Ess.Followers.dismissAll.title: Followers: Dismiss Everyone
Ess.Followers.dismissAll.desc: Releases every follower at once. Your whole roster goes back to being ordinary game characters and the roster is left empty. Good as a reset while you are testing, or at the end of a mission.

Ess.Followers.isFollower.title: Followers: Is One Of Mine
Ess.Followers.isFollower.desc: Asks whether a particular character is on your roster right now. Useful as a gate before ordering somebody about, or to check a unit is still with you. Anyone who has died or been dismissed reads false.

returns.name: bool
returns.desc: True if they are currently one of your followers.

Ess.Followers.list.title: Followers: Roster
Ess.Followers.list.desc: Hands you your current roster: everybody following you right now, oldest recruit first. It is self-cleaning - anyone who died or was dismissed is pruned as this is read, so what you get back is always live. Feed it straight into Create Team to turn your whole roster into a named team.

returns.name: guids
returns.desc: A list of your follower handles, in recruit order. Empty if you have nobody.

Ess.Followers.markersEnabled.title: Followers: Markers Showing?
Ess.Followers.markersEnabled.desc: Tells you whether the follower markers are currently showing. They start ON, so this reads true until you turn them off.

returns.name: bool
returns.desc: True if follower markers are on.

Ess.Followers.on.title: Followers: On Event
Ess.Followers.on.desc: Runs your own code whenever something happens to your followers - no checking every frame, it just fires. Events today: "onRecruit" (their handle) when somebody joins, "onDismiss" (their handle, and true if they were killed) when somebody leaves for any reason, and "onFollowerDown" (their handle) when one is killed. Squad's own events travel on this same bus, so the Squad On Event node is the identical mechanism. An event name nobody ever fires is harmless - your code simply never runs.

eventName.desc: Which event to listen for: "onRecruit", "onDismiss" or "onFollowerDown".

fn.desc: Your code, run each time that event fires. It receives whatever that event sends - onRecruit and onFollowerDown send the character; onDismiss sends the character plus true/false for whether they were killed.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to stop listening. Keep hold of it if you might ever want to unsubscribe.

Ess.Followers.order.title: Followers: Order Everyone
Ess.Followers.order.desc: Gives one command to your WHOLE roster at once - the real payoff of having followers. Pick from 11 behaviours: follow, move, face, hold, defend, attack, patrol, flee, enter, deploy, animate. They keep doing it until you say otherwise, with three exceptions that finish by themselves and hand control back: an attack ends when its target dies, and a move or a one-shot patrol ends once everyone arrives - after which they automatically go back to following you. Guard, hold and a looping patrol have no natural finish, so order 'follow' yourself when you want them back. Confirmed live: a follower who is DRIVING a vehicle is still commanded through their OWN character handle, never the vehicle's - order 'move' and the car drives there. While markers are on, the spot you just ordered them to also gets a white ring on the ground.

opts.desc: The details for that order: { at = {x,y,z} for move/face/defend, points = { {x,y,z}, ... } for patrol, loop = false to make a patrol run once instead of forever, target = <enemy handle> for attack or <vehicle handle> for enter, radius for defend, role = "driver" / "passenger" / "gunner" for enter, action = "Cower" for animate, speed, priority }. "follow", "hold" and "deploy" need nothing at all.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the order has been handed over. It is optimistic - the command actually fires about 1.5 seconds later, which is the settle time confirmed necessary for a follower to accept a new order.

Ess.Followers.recruit.title: Followers: Recruit
Ess.Followers.recruit.desc: Makes a character join you. From that moment they are one of YOUR units: they follow you around, ride along in vehicles, and answer to every order you give the roster. A follower is a real game character who keeps doing whatever you last told them until you tell them something else. Recruiting the same person twice is harmless. If they are already sitting in a vehicle that is handled properly - a driver keeps the wheel and escorts you instead of climbing out. If they die they drop off your roster on their own, no cleanup needed. Markers are ON by default, so a new follower gets their own coloured icon floating over their head.

guid.desc: The character to recruit. Wire in someone you spawned or picked out of the world - pointing this at yourself does nothing useful.

opts.desc: Optional settings: { target = <who they follow, defaults to you>, minDistance = 2, maxDistance = 30, moveDistance = 4, speed = <number>, escortMinDistance / escortMaxDistance = <how close they trail you while DRIVING a vehicle> }. Leave it empty for the confirmed-good defaults.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if they are now on your roster - also true if they already were. False if no character was given, or the game refused the join sequence.

Ess.Followers.setMarkersEnabled.title: Followers: Show Markers
Ess.Followers.setMarkersEnabled.desc: Turns the floating follower markers on or off. They are ON by default: every current AND future follower wears their own coloured icon above their head, each a distinctly different colour, and the place you last ordered them to gets a white ground ring that clears when a new order replaces it. Turning them on also marks everybody you already have; turning them off clears only the markers this system placed, never anyone else's.

bOn.desc: True to show markers, false to hide them. Setting it to what it already is does nothing.

Ess.Gfx.call.title: Gfx: Call Movie Function
Ess.Gfx.call.desc: Reach into a Flash widget from Lua and run one of the movie's own functions -- this is how text and numbers get into a custom UI, e.g. calling its SetTitle to change the header text on screen. The function name and its arguments must match what your .gfx movie actually defines; a wrong name quietly does nothing rather than crashing.

widget.desc: The widget handle from Gfx: Create Widget.

fn.desc: Name of the function inside the movie to run.

args.desc: The values to hand that movie function, in order. Leave it as {} for a movie function that takes none -- if you skip this entirely an empty list is used.

returns.desc: True if the call reached the movie.
returns.name: ok

Ess.Gfx.menuNav.title: Gfx: Drive Menu With Arrow Keys
Ess.Gfx.menuNav.desc: A HUD Flash widget receives no keyboard input of its own, so this watches the keys on its behalf: Up and Down tell the movie to move its highlight, Enter tells it to pick the highlighted row. The movie owns the selection and all the visuals -- Lua only ever says "up", "down" or "choose". Your movie must define Move and Choose functions or nothing happens. Keep the returned stop function and call it when you're done, or it keeps polling forever.

widget.desc: The widget handle from Gfx: Create Widget.

keys.desc: Which key codes count as up / down / enter. Defaults to the arrow keys and Enter.

returns.desc: Call it with no arguments to stop watching the keys.
returns.name: stop

Ess.Gfx.onEvent.title: Gfx: On Movie Event
Ess.Gfx.onEvent.desc: Listen for something the Flash movie sends back to Lua -- typically the player clicking or picking something inside your custom UI. Your handler simply receives the value the movie sent; this node hides the awkward native shape (a mandatory two-argument callback plus a mandatory trailing empty table) that is very easy to get subtly wrong by hand. The event name has to match exactly what your .gfx movie broadcasts.

widget.desc: The widget handle from Gfx: Create Widget.

name.desc: The event name your movie broadcasts, e.g. "choose" or "close".

cb.desc: What to run when the movie fires that event. It receives the value the movie sent.

returns.desc: True if the listener was registered.
returns.name: ok

Ess.Gfx.setVisible.title: Gfx: Show Or Hide Widget
Ess.Gfx.setVisible.desc: Turn a Flash widget on or off on screen. TRAP THIS FIXES: there is no IsVisible() on these widgets -- the real getter is GetVisible(), and calling the wrong name fails silently so a hand-written toggle just never flips. Worse, GetVisible() answers with 1 or 0 rather than true/false, and 0 is not falsy in Lua, so even the correct name breaks a naive toggle. Never read the engine back: this node records the state on the handle itself as widget.shown, so check that instead.

widget.desc: The widget handle from Gfx: Create Widget.

bOn.desc: True to show it, false to hide it.

Ess.Gfx.warmupRerender.title: Gfx: Repaint After Load
Ess.Gfx.warmupRerender.desc: Loading a .gfx movie is asynchronous, so text you push into a widget in the same instant you build it can silently vanish -- the movie had not finished loading yet, and you are left staring at an empty box wondering why. This re-runs your repaint step several more times over the next fraction of a second (8 times, one every 0.05s, by default) so at least one of them lands after the movie is genuinely ready. Put whatever re-sends your widget's text inside the repaint step.

rt.desc: Your repaint step: a no-argument function that re-sends everything the widget needs to display. Swap the placeholder for your own Gfx: Call Movie Function calls.

ticks.desc: How many extra repaints to fire, one every 0.05 seconds. Defaults to 8.

Ess.Gfx.widget.title: Gfx: Create Widget
Ess.Gfx.widget.desc: Put a Flash (.gfx) movie on screen at a position and size, and hand back a handle the other Graphics nodes use. Nothing appears unless that .gfx file is actually deployed with your mod -- the stock game does not ship the Ess UI movies. Positions are on a fixed 640x480 virtual canvas that the game stretches to whatever resolution the player runs. TRAP THIS FIXES: the raw engine call wants CORNER coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2), NOT width and height. You pass plain x/y/width/height here and the corner maths is done for you -- getting it wrong renders the widget slightly too small instead of erroring, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed.

file.desc: Name of the deployed .gfx movie file to show.

x.desc: Left edge, on the 640-wide virtual screen.

y.desc: Top edge, on the 480-tall virtual screen.

w.desc: Width in virtual pixels (this node converts it to a corner for you).

h.desc: Height in virtual pixels (this node converts it to a corner for you).

returns.desc: The widget handle ({ raw = <FlashWidget>, shown = false }) -- feed it into the other Graphics nodes. Nothing comes back if the movie could not be built.
returns.name: result

Ess.Guid.title: Find By Name
Ess.Guid.desc: Looks something up in the level by name and hands back the live handle that every other node wants. Names come from the level's own placed objects, and faction names like China, Allied or PMC work too. A typo just gives you nothing back in silence - that is one of the most common beginner dead ends, and turning debug on (a Lua line reading Ess.DEBUG = true) makes it say so.

name.desc: The exact name to look up. Spelling and capitals matter.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The live handle for that name, or nothing at all if no such name exists in this level.

Ess.Hud.banner.title: HUD: Banner
Ess.Hud.banner.desc: Flash big plain text across the middle of the screen, like a mission announcement -- no icon, no gold header, just your words. It rides the game's own event-fanfare animation, so it plays once and clears itself; there is no hide call and nothing to clean up. Live-confirmed working.

sMsg.desc: The text to flash across the screen.

Ess.Hud.hideHint.title: HUD: Hide Hint
Ess.Hud.hideHint.desc: Take down a popup put up by HUD: Hint Popup. TRAP: the id must MATCH the one you showed it with -- a wrong or missing id leaves the hint sitting on screen, confirmed by live testing. That is deliberate, so two scripts showing messages at the same time can't wipe each other's.

sId.desc: The same id you passed to HUD: Hint Popup.

bBroadcast.desc: Leave false for your own screen only. True also hides it for other players in co-op (untested).

Ess.Hud.hint.title: HUD: Hint Popup
Ess.Hud.hint.desc: Show the game's own tutorial-style hint popup -- the little box with an icon and a notification sound that normally says things like "you're swimming" or "low on fuel" -- with any text you want. Confirmed reusable and live-tested with a screenshot. TRAP: it has no timer at all. It stays on screen forever until you take it down with HUD: Hide Hint using the SAME id, so always give it an id you can hide it by.

sMsg.desc: The text to show in the popup.

sId.desc: A name for this hint. HUD: Hide Hint must be given the exact same one to clear it.

bBroadcast.desc: Leave false to show it only on your own screen. True opts into the game's co-op broadcast (its real network behaviour is untested).

Ess.Hud.objective.title: HUD: Set Objective Line
Ess.Hud.objective.desc: Write a line into the objective tray -- the mission-goal text that sits on the HUD and STAYS there until you change or clear it. Line 1 is the "current objective" line most missions use. Pass no text at all to wipe that line. Careful with line 3: that is the radio-chatter line, and HUD: Radio Line will overwrite anything you leave there.

sText.desc: The objective text. Leave it empty (nil) to clear that line instead.

nSlot.desc: Which tray line to write. 1 (the default) is the current objective; 3 is the radio line.

Ess.Hud.radio.title: HUD: Radio Line
Ess.Hud.radio.desc: Drop a one-off radio-chatter subtitle on the HUD (objective-tray line 3) -- the game's own mission-chatter line, and the natural home for cutscene dialogue and subtitles. It wipes ITSELF after the hold time, 5 seconds if you don't say otherwise, so never clear it by hand. Firing a newer line won't get cut short early by an older line's pending timer.

sText.default: Bravo Six, we have eyes on the target.

nHold.desc: Seconds it stays up before clearing itself. Defaults to 5.

Ess.Human.allWeapons.title: Human: All Weapons
Ess.Human.allWeapons.desc: Lists every weapon a character is carrying, so you can loop over them to refill ammo, count a loadout, or check what changed after giving them something.

uChar.desc: The person whose kit you want.

returns.name: tWeapons
returns.desc: A list of weapon handles. Always a real list, empty rather than nil when they carry nothing or cannot be read.

Ess.Human.ammo.title: Human: Weapon Ammo
Ess.Human.ammo.desc: Reads how much SPARE ammo a weapon has left in reserve - not the rounds in the magazine it is currently firing.

uWeapon.desc: A weapon handle, normally wired in from the Primary Weapon or All Weapons node - this takes the WEAPON, not the person holding it.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: Reserve rounds remaining. Comes back as 0 rather than nil if the weapon cannot be read, so a 0 does not always mean empty.

Ess.Human.disableWeapons.title: Human: Disable Weapons
Ess.Human.disableWeapons.desc: Stops a character being able to use their guns without taking them away - for a cutscene, a truce, or a non-combat stretch.

uChar.desc: The person to disarm. Pair every use with Enable Weapons or they stay unable to shoot.

Ess.Human.doAction.title: Human: Do Action
Ess.Human.doAction.desc: Plays a named animation or behaviour on a character - how you make a civilian cower, stand back up, or react.

uChar.desc: The person who should perform it.

sActionName.desc: The action name, spelled the way the game spells it - known-good examples are "Cower", "Stand" and "Proximity". A blank name is quietly ignored rather than erroring, so a typo just means nothing visibly happens.

Ess.Human.dropWeapon.title: Human: Drop Weapon
Ess.Human.dropWeapon.desc: Makes a character throw a weapon on the ground - disarming an enemy, or leaving a gun for the player to pick up.

uWeapon.desc: Which of their weapons to drop - usually wired in from the Primary Weapon or All Weapons node.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Human.enableWeapons.title: Human: Enable Weapons
Ess.Human.enableWeapons.desc: Gives a character the use of their weapons back after they were disabled.

Ess.Human.equipWeapon.title: Human: Equip Weapon
Ess.Human.equipWeapon.desc: Puts a weapon in a character's hands - either switching them to one they already carry, or genuinely adding a brand-new gun if you hand it a weapon looked up by template name.

uWeapon.desc: The weapon handle. Looking a weapon TEMPLATE up by name and passing that was live-confirmed to actually ADD a new weapon (their weapon count went 2 to 3), not just re-select one they already had.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Human.knockdown.title: Human: Knock Down
Ess.Human.knockdown.desc: Knocks a character off their feet for a moment - a stun, a shockwave reaction, or a scripted takedown.

nDuration.desc: How long they stay down, in seconds. Leave blank for the built-in 0.5.

Ess.Human.maxAmmo.title: Human: Weapon Max Ammo
Ess.Human.maxAmmo.desc: Reads the biggest reserve a weapon can hold, which is what you compare against to show an ammo bar or decide whether a resupply is worth it.

uWeapon.desc: The weapon handle to ask about.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: The maximum reserve rounds. Comes back as 0 rather than nil if it cannot be read.

Ess.Human.primaryWeapon.title: Human: Primary Weapon
Ess.Human.primaryWeapon.desc: Gets the handle of a character's main gun, which is what the ammo and refill nodes need as their input.

returns.name: uWeapon
returns.desc: The weapon handle, or nil if they have no primary.

Ess.Human.refillAmmo.title: Human: Refill Weapon Ammo
Ess.Human.refillAmmo.desc: Fills a single weapon's spare ammo right back up to its maximum - the same one-liner the shipped game's own contract scripts use for a resupply.

uWeapon.desc: The weapon to top up. This fills the SPARE pool - follow it with Reload All if you also want the loaded magazine full right now.

Ess.Human.reloadAll.title: Human: Reload All Weapons
Ess.Human.reloadAll.desc: Tops up the loaded magazines on every weapon a character carries, from their spare ammo.

Ess.Human.secondaryWeapon.title: Human: Secondary Weapon
Ess.Human.secondaryWeapon.desc: Gets the handle of a character's sidearm or second weapon slot.

returns.name: uWeapon
returns.desc: The weapon handle, or nil if that slot is empty.

Ess.Human.setAllWeapons.title: Human: Set All Weapons
Ess.Human.setAllWeapons.desc: Replaces a character's entire weapon loadout in one call, instead of equipping guns one at a time.

uChar.desc: The person whose loadout is being replaced.

tWeaponGuids.desc: The full list of weapon handles they should end up with. This REPLACES what they carry, so anything missing from the list is gone - the default here just hands back their current list, which changes nothing and is a safe starting point to edit.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Human.setAmmo.title: Human: Set Weapon Ammo
Ess.Human.setAmmo.desc: Sets a weapon's spare ammo to an exact number - for a low-ammo challenge, a scripted resupply, or emptying a reserve.

uWeapon.desc: The weapon handle to change - the WEAPON, not the person.

n.desc: The new reserve count. This is the spare pool only; the magazine already loaded is untouched.

Ess.Human.setInfiniteAmmo.title: Human: Infinite Ammo
Ess.Human.setInfiniteAmmo.desc: Switches endless ammo on or off for a character, so their spare ammo never runs down.

uChar.desc: The person to give endless ammo to. Note this one takes the PERSON, unlike the other ammo nodes which take a weapon.

bOn.desc: True to switch it on, false to switch it back off. Live-tested behaviour: it keeps the RESERVE topped up forever, but the magazine being fired still empties and still needs a reload - and grenades still get thrown one at a time.

Ess.Impulse.mass.title: Impulse: Mass
Ess.Impulse.mass.desc: Reads how heavy something is - useful for telling a car from a tank, and it is the same number the push nodes scale their force by.

uGuid.desc: The thing to weigh.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: The mass, or nil when it cannot be read. The push nodes fall back to 1000 in that case so a shove still does something.

Ess.Impulse.push.title: Impulse: Push
Ess.Impulse.push.desc: Shoves an object with a physics kick, handling the mass maths and axis order for you so a boost feels the same on a light bike as on a heavy tank.

uGuid.desc: The thing to shove - a vehicle, a prop, a person.

opts.desc: How to shove it. Either the object-relative form - forward (the way it is facing), up, side, any of which you can leave out - or dir = {x,y,z} for a WORLD direction instead, with strength to scale it (default 1). scaleByMass defaults to true and is what makes the same numbers feel the same on any weight; set it false only if you want to supply the raw force yourself. A forward of about 8 is a strong speed boost.

Ess.Impulse.spin.title: Impulse: Spin
Ess.Impulse.spin.desc: Shoves an object OFF-CENTRE so it rolls or flips instead of just moving - this is how the barrel-roll style stunt is done.

uGuid.desc: The thing to spin.

opts.desc: forward / up / side are the kick itself, relative to the object. at = {x,y,z} is where on the object the kick lands, measured from its centre - that offset is the lever arm, so further out means more spin. scaleByMass works as it does on Push.

Ess.Input.VkToChar.title: Input: Key To Character
Ess.Input.VkToChar.desc: Turns a key code into the character that key types on a US keyboard, which is what a text box needs to build up what the player is typing. Letters, digits, space and the usual punctuation are covered.

vk.desc: The Windows key code, usually one taken straight from Input: Poll Keyboard's pressed list. 65 is A.

bShift.desc: Was Shift held - the difference between a and A, and between 1 and !. Read the live Shift state with Input: Key Held rather than guessing.

returns.name: char
returns.desc: The character, or nothing at all for keys that do not type anything (F5, arrows, Enter). Always allow for nothing before adding it to a buffer.

Ess.Input.clear.title: Input: Clear Pending Keys
Ess.Input.clear.desc:
Throws away every key press waiting in the buffer.

The classic use: a script that was LAUNCHED by a key press flushes the buffer as it starts, so its own trigger key - and anything the player mashed while it was loading - does not immediately fire an action on the very first tick. If your menu opens and instantly selects something, this is the fix.

Ess.Input.held.title: Input: Key Held
Ess.Input.held.desc:
Is this key down at this exact moment.

Safe to call from as many loops as you like: it only reads the keyboard's current state and never touches the press buffer, so it cannot steal presses from a menu or another script. This is the right node for 'hold Shift to boost'; for a one-shot press use Keys: On Key Press instead, or it will fire on every single tick the key is down.

vk.desc: The Windows key code. 16 is Shift, 17 is Ctrl, 32 is Space. Rather than memorise numbers, use the Keys: Key Code node to turn a name like 'F5' into one.

returns.name: held
returns.desc: True while the key is physically down. It stays true tick after tick, which is exactly what you want for a hold and exactly what you do not want for a press.

Ess.Input.hijackController.title: Input: Hijack Controller
Ess.Input.hijackController.desc:
NICHE, AND UNVERIFIED IN THIS BUILD - most mods never need it, and it is put together from documentation rather than a confirmed live test.

What it is for: while the world is paused there is no per-frame callback at all on this engine, so a PDA-style pause menu cannot animate or read a stick. Controller input is the one thing that still comes through, so this hides the PDA widget and takes over its controller callback to ride it.

Two catches. The PDA underneath still claims the arrow keys, Enter and Escape, so any keyboard interface you layer on top must use letter keys. And an idle stick sends NOTHING - not even a final zero - so if 'the stick just went back to centre' matters, you have to decide that yourself.

ALWAYS call the release it hands back, or the PDA stays hidden.

onInput.desc: Runs on every scrap of controller activity while hijacked. It does not run at all when the player is not touching the controller.

returns.name: release
returns.desc: Keep this and call it (or feed it to an Ess.stop node) to give the PDA back. Nothing else will do it for you. You still get one back even if the hijack failed - calling it is then harmless.

Ess.Input.poll.title: Input: Poll Keyboard
Ess.Input.poll.desc:
The one correct way to read the keyboard: call it ONCE per tick and read both halves off the result - which keys were just pressed, and which are held right now.

IT DRAINS THE PRESS BUFFER. The presses it hands you are gone for everyone else, so if a menu is also reading keys this will eat the presses that menu needed. When you only care whether a key is held, use Input: Key Held instead and leave the presses alone.

Never check keys one at a time in a loop - that is where every framerate bug in this project's menus came from.

returns.name: input
returns.desc: Read it in a Lua field. input.pressed is the list of key codes that went down since your last poll (usually empty). input.down(vk) answers whether a key is held right now. Use pressed for one-shot actions and down for hold-to-do-something.

Ess.Input.usingController.title: Input: Using Controller
Ess.Input.usingController.desc:
Is the player on a controller right now. The everyday use is wording a hint correctly - 'Press A' against 'Press E' - without keeping a setting of your own.

Carefully written: not every build of the game exposes this, and the engine sometimes answers with a 1 or a 0 rather than a real yes/no, so this checks properly instead of being fooled by a 0 (which Lua would otherwise treat as true).

returns.name: usingController
returns.desc: True if a controller is in use. Comes back false when the game cannot tell, so keyboard wording is the safe fallback.

Ess.Keys.clear.title: Keys: Unbind All
Ess.Keys.clear.desc: Drops every key binding at once. A good first action in a script that re-runs and rebinds its keys, so old bindings from a previous run cannot linger with stale actions attached.

Ess.Keys.isBound.title: Keys: Is Key Bound
Ess.Keys.isBound.desc: Is anything currently handling this key. Useful before binding, so you do not silently replace another part of your own mod's hotkey.

key.desc: A key name like 'F5', or a raw key code number.

returns.name: bound
returns.desc: True if something is bound to that key right now. It only knows about keys bound through Keys nodes, not the game's own controls.

Ess.Keys.off.title: Keys: Unbind Key
Ess.Keys.off.desc: Stops handling one key. If it was the last binding, the shared poll loop notices on its next check and shuts itself down, so nothing keeps running in the background.

key.desc: The same key name or code you bound. Unbinding a key that was never bound is harmless.

Ess.Keys.on.title: Keys: On Key Press
Ess.Keys.on.desc:
Binds a key to an action, so ONE script can own a whole panel of hotkeys - the game's own loader only gives a script a single key.

Edge-triggered: holding the key down fires your action ONCE, not every tick. Binding the same key again REPLACES the old action rather than stacking a second one, so a script that re-runs cannot end up firing twice per press.

It quietly runs one shared poll loop behind the scenes, which shuts itself off when nothing is bound. Careful: it reads the same key presses that a focused Ess.UI menu reads, so do not run both on the same keys.

key.desc: A key name - 'F5', 'space', 'a', '1', 'up', 'escape' - or a raw key code number. An unrecognised name is not an error: it is logged and simply not bound, so nothing at all happens when you press it.

fn.desc: What to run on each press. It is told whether Shift was held, so one key can do two things. Errors inside it are swallowed, so it cannot take the poll loop down with it.

Ess.Keys.vk.title: Keys: Key Code
Ess.Keys.vk.desc: Turns a friendly key name into the Windows key code number, for nodes that want the number rather than the name - Input: Key Held, for one. Numbers pass straight through unchanged, so it is safe to send anything through it.

key.desc: The name: 'f1' to 'f12', 'a' to 'z', '0' to '9', 'space', 'enter', 'escape', 'tab', 'backspace', 'up', 'down', 'left', 'right', 'shift', 'ctrl', 'insert', 'delete', 'home', 'end', 'pageup', 'pagedown'. Capitals do not matter.

returns.name: vk
returns.desc: The key code, or nothing at all if the name is not in that list - which is the usual reason a binding silently does nothing.

Ess.Layers.add.title: Layers: Add
Ess.Layers.add.desc: Streams extra layer(s) into the level. The single most common reason this appears to do nothing: it is ignored outright unless a mode is already open, so put a Layers: Begin node before it. Layers already loaded are skipped, and STATIC layers - terrain and geometry - are refused and logged, because pulling those around mid-session is not survivable.

vLayers.desc: The layer name(s) to load, as a Lua list (a single name on its own also works). Names are the vz_state_* pieces of the level; 'vz_state_mer_oilrig_pristine' is one confirmed working example. Capitalisation does not matter.

fCb.desc: Optional. Runs once the loading finishes. It still runs immediately if every name you gave was skipped or refused.

Ess.Layers.begin.title: Layers: Begin Mode
Ess.Layers.begin.desc: Opens a layer mode. Layers are the chunks of the level the game streams in and out - an alternate, undamaged version of a building, an extra set of props - and this node writes down exactly which ones are loaded right now so the Layers: Finish node can put the world back precisely. Saving is switched off for the duration, so a crash mid-mode leaves the player's ordinary save on disk. Nothing else in this group does anything until a mode is open.

sId.desc: A name for this mode, used in the log to tell modes apart.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the mode opened. False if a mode is already open - only one layer mode runs at a time, and the second call is ignored rather than nesting.

Ess.Layers.composite.title: Layers: Force Recomposite
Ess.Layers.composite.desc: Optional extra step that forces the engine to visibly rebuild the scene after layers were added or removed. Many modes never need it - one that teleports or fast-travels the player recomposites for free - but a change made while the player stands still may not appear until you call this. Run it AFTER the add/remove work has finished. If the engine's state manager is unavailable it is skipped with a log line rather than failing.

fCb.desc: Optional. Runs once the rebuild is done.

Ess.Layers.current.title: Layers: Currently Loaded
Ess.Layers.current.desc: Lists the layers loaded in the level right now. Compare it against the baseline snapshot to see exactly what your mode has changed so far. Only streamed layers appear here; static terrain and geometry are not part of this list.

returns.name: layers
returns.desc: A list of the layer names currently loaded.

Ess.Layers.expect.title: Layers: Expect State
Ess.Layers.expect.desc: Declares what the world should look like and makes it so, issuing only the missing loads and unloads. This is the fix for drift: instead of tracking what you changed, you state what must be present and what must be gone, and anything already correct is left alone. Ignored unless a mode is open.

spec.desc: present = the layers that must be loaded, absent = the layers that must not be, cb = optional code to run once the world has converged. Static terrain layers named in either list are refused and logged.

Ess.Layers.finish.title: Layers: Finish Mode
Ess.Layers.finish.desc: Closes the layer mode and puts the world back. It compares what is loaded now against the picture taken at Begin and issues exactly the loads and unloads needed to match it, whatever happened in between - so it still restores correctly even if something else changed layers behind your back. Saving is allowed again afterwards (once no sandbox is still holding it). Static terrain layers are never unloaded on the way back.

fCb.desc: Optional. Runs once the world is back to its pre-mode state. It still runs if there was no mode open or if the restore could not be issued, so it is a safe place to continue from.

Ess.Layers.isActive.title: Layers: Is Mode Open
Ess.Layers.isActive.desc: Checks whether a layer mode is currently open. Worth testing before Add or Remove, since those quietly do nothing when no mode is running.

returns.name: active
returns.desc: True while a mode is open.

Ess.Layers.isLoaded.title: Layers: Is Layer Loaded
Ess.Layers.isLoaded.desc: Checks whether one named layer is loaded in the level right now. This is the honest way to confirm a layer change actually took effect, rather than assuming it did because nothing errored.

name.desc: The layer name to check. Capitalisation does not matter.

returns.name: loaded
returns.desc: True if that layer is currently loaded.

Ess.Layers.remove.title: Layers: Remove
Ess.Layers.remove.desc: Unloads layer(s) from the level - how you make a set of props or an alternate version of a building disappear for your encounter. Like Add, it is ignored entirely unless a mode is open, and it flatly refuses to unload STATIC terrain and geometry layers.

vLayers.desc: The layer name(s) to unload, as a Lua list (a single name on its own also works).

fCb.desc: Optional. Runs once the unloading finishes.

Ess.Layers.snapshot.title: Layers: Baseline Snapshot
Ess.Layers.snapshot.desc: Lists the layers that were loaded at the moment the mode opened - the state Finish will restore the world to. Useful for checking what you started from while a mode is running.

returns.name: layers
returns.desc: A list of layer names. Empty when no mode is open, since there is no baseline to report.

Ess.Layers.swap.title: Layers: Swap
Ess.Layers.swap.desc: Unloads one set of layers and then loads another, properly sequenced - the everyday 'switch this area over to its arena version' move. Doing it with separate Remove and Add nodes lets the two overlap; this one waits for the removal to finish first. Ignored unless a mode is open.

vRemove.desc: The layer name(s) to unload first.

vAdd.desc: The layer name(s) to load once the removal is done.

fCb.desc: Optional. Runs once both halves have finished.

Ess.Log.title: Log Message
Ess.Log.desc: Writes one line into the game's log file (scripts/lua_loader_printf.log), tagged [Ess] so it is easy to find among everything else. This is the simplest 'did my mod get this far' check there is: drop it between two nodes and see whether the line shows up.

msg.desc: The line to write. Wire a value in if you want to print something the graph produced.

Ess.Loop.isRunning.title: Loop: Is Running
Ess.Loop.isRunning.desc: Is a loop with this name alive right now. The usual use is a toggle: if it is running, stop it; if not, start it - so one key turns your feature on and off.

id.desc: The name used when the loop was started.

returns.name: running
returns.desc: True while that loop exists. It becomes false the moment a tick returns false or Loop: Stop is called.

Ess.Loop.list.title: Loop: List All
Ess.Loop.list.desc: Every loop running right now, sorted by name. The first thing to look at when the game starts slowing down: a name you do not recognise, or several near-identical names, is what a leaked loop looks like.

returns.name: loops
returns.desc: A list of entries, each with .id plus the same fields as Loop: Stats. Walk it in a Lua field to print or draw a monitor.

Ess.Loop.start.title: Loop: Start
Ess.Loop.start.desc: Run something over and over on the one shared heartbeat - a HUD that redraws, a watcher that keeps checking, anything that must not be a one-shot. It runs until the tick returns false or until Loop: Stop is called with the same name; nothing stops it on its own.

id.desc: A name for this loop. Starting again with the SAME name REPLACES the old one instead of adding a second, so a script that re-runs on every key press cannot leak a duplicate loop. Two different names means two loops both running.

interval.desc: Seconds between ticks. 0.2 is five times a second, fine for a HUD or a watcher. Smaller is smoother and more expensive; there is no per-frame option on this engine.

tickFn.desc: What to do each tick. It MUST return true to keep going - returning false, or forgetting to return anything at all, stops the loop after that one tick. That is the number one reason a loop 'only runs once'.

Ess.Loop.stats.title: Loop: Stats
Ess.Loop.stats.desc: A snapshot of how one loop is behaving. This is how you answer 'is my loop what is making the game chug' - compare how long a tick takes against the interval it runs at.

id.desc: The name of the loop to inspect.

returns.name: stats
returns.desc: Nothing if that loop is not running. Otherwise a frozen copy (it will not change under you) with .interval, .ticks, .lastDuration, .avgDuration and .lastError. If lastDuration is anywhere near interval, that tick is doing too much work for how often it runs. lastError holds the message from the last tick that errored.

Ess.Loop.stop.title: Loop: Stop
Ess.Loop.stop.desc: Cancels a running loop by name. The tick already scheduled just notices the loop is gone and quietly does not book another one, so there is no error and nothing left dangling. Stopping a name that was never running is harmless.

id.desc: The exact same name you gave Loop: Start. A typo here silently stops nothing and leaves the real loop running.

Ess.Mark.clear.title: Mark: Clear
Ess.Mark.clear.desc:
Removes a marker: every surface that handle actually used, plus the invisible anchor prop if it came from Mark: Zone. This is the ONLY thing that takes a marker off the screen.

Safe on a half-built handle and safe to call on one you already cleared - anything missing is simply skipped.

handle.desc: The handle from Mark: Object or Mark: Zone, wired in. An empty one does nothing at all - which is what 'my marker will not go away' usually turns out to be.

Ess.Mark.object.title: Mark: Object
Ess.Mark.object.desc:
Puts a marker on a thing: a round-radar blip, a PDA map blip and a floating in-world icon, each one an independent switch, plus an optional ring on the ground around it.

Keep the handle it gives back. Markers do NOT clean themselves up - not even when the thing they are stuck to dies - so a marker you drop the handle for is stuck on screen for the rest of the session.

uGuid.desc: The thing to mark, wired in from whatever spawned or found it.

opts.default: { radar = true, pda = true, world = true }
opts.desc: Which surfaces to use. radar, pda and world (the floating icon) are all ON unless you set one to false. Extras: disc = true adds a ring on the ground (radius = 15 by default, discAlpha sets its fill), kind picks the icon set out of 'destroy', 'verify', 'defend', 'action' or 'destination' (default 'action'), rgb = { 255, 0, 0 } colours it, size and dist tune the floating icon's size and how far off it stays visible.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: Keep this. It is the only way to remove the marker later - feed it to Mark: Clear, an Ess.stop node, or a tracker.

Ess.Mark.zone.title: Mark: Zone
Ess.Mark.zone.desc:
Marks a PLACE rather than a thing: a ring drawn on the ground plus radar and PDA blips, for a delivery point or an area objective.

There is nothing at a bare position to hang a blip on, so this quietly spawns an invisible anchor prop and marks that. The zone OWNS that prop, so Mark: Clear removes it for you - which is exactly why you must not throw the handle away.

x.desc: East/west centre of the zone.

y.desc: Height of the centre. Put it near ground level or the ring hangs in the air.

z.desc: North/south centre of the zone.

radius.desc: How wide the ground ring is drawn, in world units.

opts.default: { world = true, radar = true, pda = true }
opts.desc: Which surfaces to use. world (the ground ring), radar and pda are all ON unless you set one to false. Extras: icon = true ALSO drops a floating icon on the anchor (off by default), kind picks the icon set (default 'destination'), rgb = { 0, 255, 0 } colours it, discAlpha sets the ring's fill, size and dist tune the floating icon.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: Keep this for Mark: Clear. It comes back empty if the anchor prop could not be spawned, so a zone that never appears means the spawn failed, not the marking.

Ess.Math.angleTo.title: Math: Angle Toward Point
Ess.Math.angleTo.desc: Which way to point something so it faces a spot: gives the yaw, in degrees, that looks from one place toward another. Feed it into Ess.Object.setYaw to turn a thing to face a target. It uses the engine's own yaw convention (forward is +sin, +cos) and is the exact opposite of Math: Point Ahead. If the two points are identical you get 0.

fromX.desc: X of the thing doing the facing.

fromZ.desc: Z of the thing doing the facing.

toX.desc: X of the spot to face.

toZ.desc: Z of the spot to face.

returns.name: yawDegrees
returns.desc: The facing angle in degrees, in the engine's yaw convention.

Ess.Math.approach.title: Math: Approach
Ess.Math.approach.desc: Moves a number toward a target by a limited step and never overshoots it. Run it every frame with maxStep = speed * deltaTime and you get smooth easing that behaves the same whatever the frame rate.

cur.desc: Where the value is right now.

target.desc: Where you want it to end up.

maxStep.desc: The biggest jump allowed this call.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The new value, one step closer to the target (or exactly the target if it was within reach).

Ess.Math.clamp.title: Math: Clamp
Ess.Math.clamp.desc: Keeps a number inside a low/high range. Anything below lo comes back as lo, anything above hi comes back as hi. Use it so health, ammo or a speed can never go out of bounds.

v.desc: The number to keep in range.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The number, pulled back inside lo..hi.

Ess.Math.clamp01.title: Math: Clamp 0 to 1
Ess.Math.clamp01.desc: Squashes a number into the 0..1 range. The usual tidy-up before feeding a blend or ease amount into Math: Blend Numbers.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The number, never below 0 and never above 1.

Ess.Math.dist2D.title: Math: Distance 2D
Ess.Math.dist2D.desc: How far apart two points are on the ground, ignoring height. This is the one you normally want, so something on a rooftop right above you doesn't read as far away just because it is high up.

returns.name: distance
returns.desc: Ground distance in world units.

Ess.Math.dist2DSq.title: Math: Distance 2D (Squared)
Ess.Math.dist2DSq.desc: Ground distance with the expensive square root skipped, so it is cheaper to run a lot. Only use it to COMPARE distances ("which one is closer") - the number itself is the distance multiplied by itself, not the distance.

returns.name: distanceSq
returns.desc: Ground distance squared. Comparable, but not a real distance.

Ess.Math.dist3D.title: Math: Distance 3D
Ess.Math.dist3D.desc: True straight-line distance between two points, height included. Use Distance 2D instead when a difference in height shouldn't count.

returns.name: distance
returns.desc: Straight-line distance in world units.

Ess.Math.dist3DSq.title: Math: Distance 3D (Squared)
Ess.Math.dist3DSq.desc: Straight-line distance including height, with the square root skipped for speed. Good for sorting or comparing only - the number is not a real distance.

returns.name: distanceSq
returns.desc: 3D distance squared. Comparable, but not a real distance.

Ess.Math.lerp.title: Math: Blend Numbers
Ess.Math.lerp.desc: Blends smoothly between two numbers. t = 0 gives a, t = 1 gives b, 0.5 gives the halfway point. The workhorse behind fades, growing bars and easing a value over time.

t.desc: How far along, usually 0 to 1.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The blended number.

Ess.Math.lerpAngle.title: Math: Blend Angles
Ess.Math.lerpAngle.desc: Blends between two facing angles the SHORT way round, so going from 350 to 10 eases forward 20 degrees through zero instead of spinning 340 the wrong way. This is the right blend for a turning yaw - plain number blending gets it wrong.

t.desc: How far through the turn, 0 to 1.

returns.name: degrees
returns.desc: The in-between angle, between -180 and 180.

Ess.Math.normDeg.title: Math: Normalize Angle
Ess.Math.normDeg.desc: Folds any angle into the -180 to 180 range, so the gap between two facings reads as the SHORTEST turn: 350 and 10 come out 20 apart, not 340. Use it before asking "am I roughly facing this?" or easing a turn.

returns.name: degrees
returns.desc: The same angle, expressed between -180 and 180.

Ess.Math.pointAhead.title: Math: Point Ahead
Ess.Math.pointAhead.desc: Finds the spot a set distance directly in front of something, given where it is and which way it faces. This is the "put it 10 units ahead of me" maths behind spawnAhead, so you never re-derive the sin/cos. Two things to know: it uses the engine's yaw convention (forward is +sin, +cos), and a character's yaw is its BODY facing, not where the player is looking - so this lands in front of the chest, not the crosshair. Height (Y) is left to you.

x.desc: Starting X.

z.desc: Starting Z.

yawDeg.desc: The facing angle in degrees. 0 means facing +Z.

dist.desc: How far ahead, in world units.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: X of the spot ahead.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Z of the spot ahead.

Ess.Math.remap.title: Math: Remap Range
Ess.Math.remap.desc: Rescales a number from one range onto another - turn 0..maxHealth into 0..1 for a bar, or a distance into a fade amount. If the input range has no width you get outLo back instead of a divide-by-zero error.

inLo.desc: Bottom of the range it's currently in.

inHi.desc: Top of the range it's currently in.

outLo.desc: Bottom of the range you want.

outHi.desc: Top of the range you want.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The rescaled number.

Ess.Math.rotateOffset.title: Math: Rotate Offset To World
Ess.Math.rotateOffset.desc: Turns a "5 to my right and 10 ahead of me" offset into real world coordinates for something facing yawDeg. Use it for squad formations, grids and side-by-side placement instead of writing your own rotation maths - a hand-rolled one is exactly where this project got the signs wrong before. Point Ahead is just this with no sideways part.

x.desc: X of the thing you're offsetting from.

z.desc: Z of the thing you're offsetting from.

yawDeg.desc: Which way that thing faces, in degrees.

localX.desc: Sideways offset - positive is to its right.

localZ.desc: Forward offset - positive is ahead of it.

returns.name: worldX
returns.desc: World X of the offset spot.

returns.name: worldZ
returns.desc: World Z of the offset spot.

Ess.Math.round.title: Math: Round
Ess.Math.round.desc: Rounds a number to the nearest whole number, or to however many decimal places you ask for. Use it so a HUD shows 13 or 12.99 instead of 12.9999997.

decimals.desc: How many decimal places to keep. Leave at 0 for the nearest whole number.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The rounded number.

Ess.Math.sign.title: Math: Sign
Ess.Math.sign.desc: Tells you which way a number points: 1 if it is positive, -1 if negative, 0 if exactly zero. Handy for turning a difference into a simple left/right or up/down decision.

Ess.Math.smoothstep.title: Math: Smooth Ease
Ess.Math.smoothstep.desc: Turns straight-line 0..1 progress into eased 0..1 progress that starts and ends gently. Feed the result into Math: Blend Numbers for smooth ease-in-out movement instead of something that snaps into motion. t is clamped for you.

t.desc: Raw progress, 0 to 1.

returns.name: eased
returns.desc: Eased progress, 0 to 1.

Ess.Math.within2D.title: Math: Within Range 2D
Ess.Math.within2D.desc: Is the second point within r units of the first, measured on the ground? This is the proximity check every "has the player reached the zone yet" poll needs, already written correctly so you can't fumble the maths.

returns.name: inRange
returns.desc: True if the second point is inside the circle.

Ess.Math.within3D.title: Math: Within Range 3D
Ess.Math.within3D.desc: Is the second point within r units of the first, height included? The sphere version of Within Range 2D - use this when something being far above or below should push it out of range.

returns.name: inRange
returns.desc: True if the second point is inside the sphere.

Ess.Math.wrap.title: Math: Wrap Into Range
Ess.Math.wrap.desc: Wraps a number back around whenever it runs off the end of a range - keeps a menu index, an angle or a scrolling cursor in bounds. The top end is excluded, so wrapping into 0..360 gives 0 up to 359.99, and 370 comes back as 10.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The number wrapped into lo..hi.

Ess.Name.title: Name Of
Ess.Name.desc: The other direction: give it a live handle and it gives back that object's name as text - useful for printing what you just picked up, spawned or aimed at. Safe on anything: the raw engine call behind it is confirmed to throw outright on at least one real object, and this one absorbs that instead of crashing your mod.

uGuid.desc: The thing whose name you want. Wire one in, or leave it as the player.

returns.name: name
returns.desc: The object's name text, or nothing at all if it could not be read.

Ess.Net.Get.title: Co-op: Get Shared Value
Ess.Net.Get.desc: Reads back a value that either machine put into the shared store under that name. In single-player it simply reads back whatever you set locally, so the same graph works solo and in co-op.

key.desc: The same name that was used to set it.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: Whatever was stored under that name, or nothing at all if nobody has set it yet.

Ess.Net.IsAuthority.title: Co-op: Am I In Charge?
Ess.Net.IsAuthority.desc: True when playing alone, and true on the host in co-op.
