This is the check to put in front of anything that must happen exactly once no matter how many players there are: spawning a wave, paying out money, deciding the boss is dead. Almost always the one you want, because Am I The Host is false in single-player and would skip your logic entirely.

returns.name: isAuthority
returns.desc: True if this machine should be the one running the logic.

Ess.Net.IsCoop.title: Co-op: In A Co-op Game?
Ess.Net.IsCoop.desc: True when you are actually in a live two-player session, false when you are playing alone. Check it before doing anything co-op-specific.

returns.name: isCoop
returns.desc: True only in a live co-op session.

Ess.Net.IsHost.title: Co-op: Am I The Host?
Ess.Net.IsHost.desc: True only on the machine hosting a live co-op session. It is FALSE in single-player, which catches people out - if what you really mean is 'should this machine be the one running the logic', use Am I In Charge instead.

returns.name: isHost
returns.desc: True only on the co-op host. False when playing alone.

Ess.Net.Me.title: Co-op: My Player Id
Ess.Net.Me.desc: Which player this machine is, 0 or 1. Use it to tell the two sides apart - a different colour, a different spawn point, a different half of the job.

returns.name: id
returns.desc: This machine's player id, 0 or 1.

Ess.Net.On.title: Co-op: On Message
Ess.Net.On.desc: Listens on a named channel and runs your code whenever the other player sends on it. Pair it with a Co-op: Send Message node using exactly the same channel name. One name has one listener - registering the same name again replaces the previous one rather than adding a second.

name.desc: The channel to listen on. Must match the sender's name character for character.

fn.desc: Runs when a message arrives. It is handed the sender's player id (0 or 1) and the value that was sent.

Ess.Net.OnRaw.skip_reason: the expert raw-numbers channel; Co-op: On Message receives the same traffic as ordinary Lua values instead of hand-packed numbers.

Ess.Net.Send.title: Co-op: Send Message
Ess.Net.Send.desc: Fires a one-off message to the other player on a named channel - 'the boss spawned', 'I picked up the case'. Use this for events; use Set Shared Value for state that should stay true. The other machine needs a Co-op: On Message node listening on the exact same channel name. Same honest limit as the rest of the co-op layer: two-machine delivery has not been re-verified since the port.

name.desc: The channel name. It must match the listener's name character for character.

value.desc: The payload: text in quotes, a number, true/false, or a small table. Keep it small.

reliable.desc: Leave this on so the message is guaranteed to arrive. Turn it off only for chatter you can afford to lose.

Ess.Net.SendRaw.skip_reason: sends a hand-packed array of raw numbers on the expert channel; Co-op: Send Message covers the same wire with ordinary values.

Ess.Net.Set.title: Co-op: Set Shared Value
Ess.Net.Set.desc: Stores a value under a name and pushes it to the other player, so both machines agree on it - a score, a wave number, whether the boss is down. The most recent write wins. Honest limit: this wire is a faithful port of co-op code that was working in real sessions, but full two-machine delivery has not been re-verified (it needs a second machine), so co-op sync is the one part of Ess that has not been proven again. In single-player it still stores locally, so a mod built on these works either way.

key.desc: The name to store it under. Both machines use this same name to find it.

value.desc: What to store: a number, text in quotes, true/false, or a small table. Keep it small - this is a channel for state, not for moving files. Numbers stay exact up to about 16 million.

Ess.Net.Shared.skip_reason: returns a magic proxy table whose whole point is `S.field = x` assignment syntax, which a graph cannot express; Co-op Set/Get reach the same store.

Ess.Net.Track.skip_reason: needs a hand-written closure that re-reads a live variable on every heartbeat; Co-op: Set Shared Value covers pushing a value you already have.

Ess.Net.getv.skip_reason: the namespaced form of Co-op: Get Shared Value; a second near-identical node only invites picking the wrong one.

Ess.Net.hijackCallback.skip_reason: replaces a live engine callback and takes two hand-written functions plus a module table that must be import()ed in the same file first.

Ess.Net.setv.skip_reason: the namespaced form of Co-op: Set Shared Value; a second near-identical node only invites picking the wrong one.

Ess.Object.addLabel.title: Object: Add Label
Ess.Object.addLabel.desc: Sticks a text tag onto an object so you (or the game) can find and identify it later - the simplest way to mark the things your script created.

uGuid.desc: The thing to tag.

sLabel.desc: The tag text. Make up your own for your own bookkeeping; be careful reusing the game's own tags like 'PMC' or 'Disposable', as other systems act on those.

Ess.Object.alive.title: Object: Is Alive
Ess.Object.alive.desc: Checks whether something is still alive and in the world - this is the reliable 'is it gone yet' test, unlike Is Valid.

uGuid.desc: The thing to check. Remember both Kill and Remove are deferred - this still reports true for roughly half a second afterwards, so give it a tick or two before you trust a false.

returns.name: alive
returns.desc: True if it is still alive. Safe to use in a plain if - the engine's 1/0 answers are converted to real true/false for you.

Ess.Object.damage.title: Object: Damage
Ess.Object.damage.desc: Takes a chunk of health off something, and finishes it off properly if that would drop it to zero or below.

uGuid.desc: The thing to hurt. Leaving this as the player will damage YOU - normally you wire in an enemy or a vehicle.

nAmount.desc: How much health to take off. There is no real 'damage' call in this engine, so this reads health, subtracts your amount and writes it back - and if the result would be zero or less it kills the object outright, because writing 0 health doesn't reliably count as death here.

returns.name: newHealth
returns.desc: The health it has left - 0 if this blow killed it, or nothing at all if its health couldn't be read.

Ess.Object.disablePhysics.title: Object: Disable Physics
Ess.Object.disablePhysics.desc: Freezes an object's physics so it stops falling and reacting to collisions - useful for pinning a prop in mid-air or stopping a wreck sliding around.

uGuid.desc: The object to freeze physics on.

Ess.Object.displayName.title: Object: Display Name
Ess.Object.displayName.desc: Gets the readable, translated name of something so you can print it on the HUD or in a message - 'Veyron' rather than an internal code.

uGuid.desc: The thing to name.

returns.name: name
returns.desc: The human-readable name. This is a completely different thing from the object's ID string - use this one for anything a player will read.

Ess.Object.distance.title: Object: Distance
Ess.Object.distance.desc: Measures how far apart two things are, or how far an object is from a fixed map point - one node instead of two different engine calls.

uGuidBOrX.desc: The other object to measure to. To measure to a fixed map point instead, type the X coordinate number here and fill in the next two slots as Y and Z.

yOrIgnoreY.desc: Object-to-object: leave as false, or set true to ignore height (a flat, map-view distance). Point mode: this is the Y (height) coordinate instead.

z.desc: Only used in point mode - the north/south coordinate. Leave alone when measuring to another object.

bIgnoreY.desc: Only used in point mode - true measures flat along the ground and ignores the height difference.

returns.name: distance
returns.desc: Distance in world units, or nothing at all if either object couldn't be read.

Ess.Object.enablePhysics.title: Object: Enable Physics
Ess.Object.enablePhysics.desc: Turns physics back on for an object so it falls, collides and can be shoved around again.

uGuid.desc: The object to re-activate physics on.

Ess.Object.faceObject.title: Object: Face Another Object
Ess.Object.faceObject.desc: Turns one object to look at another one's position right now - a one-off snap, not a follow, so re-run it if the target moves.

uGuid.desc: The thing that should turn.

uTarget.desc: The thing to look at. If this object can't be read, nothing happens.

Ess.Object.faceToward.title: Object: Face A Point
Ess.Object.faceToward.desc: Turns an object so it looks at a spot on the map - the everyday 'make this NPC or prop look over there' for a cutscene or a scripted pose.

uGuid.desc: The thing that should turn.

x.desc: East/west coordinate of the spot to look at.

y.desc: Height of the spot. Accepted so you can pass a full position straight through, but it is IGNORED - objects only turn left/right, never tilt up or down.

z.desc: North/south coordinate of the spot to look at.

Ess.Object.hasLabel.title: Object: Has Label
Ess.Object.hasLabel.desc: Checks whether an object carries a particular text tag - the way to tell 'is this one of mine' or 'is this a PMC unit' apart from a plain civilian.

uGuid.desc: The thing to check.

sLabel.desc: The tag to look for. Labels are free-form text that the game itself and other scripts read - real examples are 'PMC', 'Disposable' and 'garage'.

returns.name: hasLabel
returns.desc: True if the object carries that tag.

Ess.Object.heal.title: Object: Heal To Full
Ess.Object.heal.desc: Restores something to its maximum health in one go - the confirmed 'patch me up' move for the player, an ally or a beaten-up vehicle.

uGuid.desc: The thing to fully heal. Silently does nothing if its max health can't be read.

Ess.Object.health.title: Object: Health
Ess.Object.health.desc: Reads how much health something has left, so you can react when it drops - the read side of the health nodes.

uGuid.desc: The character, vehicle or destructible to read.

returns.name: health
returns.desc: Current health, or nothing at all if the object is dead or invalid.

Ess.Object.heightAboveGround.title: Object: Height Above Ground
Ess.Object.heightAboveGround.desc: Reads how far an object is floating above the terrain - the check behind 'is this helicopter airborne' or 'did that prop spawn buried in a hill'.

uGuid.desc: The thing to measure. A reading of exactly 0 is ambiguous - near the player it almost always means genuinely touching the ground, but far away or in a just-loaded area it can be the engine's placeholder for terrain that hasn't loaded yet.

returns.name: height
returns.desc: Distance above the terrain in world units, or nothing at all if it couldn't be read.

Ess.Object.impulse.title: Object: Apply Impulse
Ess.Object.impulse.desc: Gives an object a sudden physical shove - the raw primitive behind launching cars into the air and knocking people back.

uGuid.desc: The thing to shove.

x.desc: Sideways push strength.

y.desc: Upward push strength. Numbers here are big - real launch code uses values in the thousands, and heavier objects need a proportionally bigger push, so start around 10000 and tune.

z.desc: Forward/backward push strength.

bLocal.desc: True (the default) pushes along the object's OWN facing, so 'forward' means forward for that car. False pushes along fixed world directions.

Ess.Object.invincible.title: Object: Is Invincible
Ess.Object.invincible.desc: Checks whether something is currently immune to damage - lets you avoid stacking protection or clean it up afterwards.

uGuid.desc: The thing to check.

returns.name: invincible
returns.desc: True if it currently can't be damaged. Safe in a plain if - a 1/0 answer from the engine is converted to a real true/false.

Ess.Object.kill.title: Object: Kill
Ess.Object.kill.desc: Destroys something where it stands, leaving a corpse or a burnt-out wreck behind - one-way, there is no undo beyond Revive.

uGuid.desc: The thing to kill. Leaving this as the player kills YOU - usually you wire in an enemy or a vehicle. The kill is NOT instant: the Alive node still reports true in the same moment you call this and only flips to false a beat later, so check it a tick or two afterwards rather than immediately.

Ess.Object.localToWorld.title: Object: Local Offset To World Point
Ess.Object.localToWorld.desc: Turns an offset measured from an object ('two units to its left, one up') into an actual map position - the correct way to place something relative to a car or a person.

uGuid.desc: The object the offset is measured from.

lx.desc: Sideways offset from the object, in world units.

ly.desc: Upward offset from the object, in world units.

lz.desc: Forward offset from the object, in world units.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: Resulting east/west world coordinate.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Resulting height. This uses the engine's full 3D transform including tilt, so prefer this node over the flat maths helper whenever the object can be leaning - a car on a slope, a listing boat.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Resulting north/south world coordinate.

Ess.Object.maxHealth.title: Object: Max Health
Ess.Object.maxHealth.desc: Reads the full-health value for something, so you can work out a health percentage for a bar or a 'below half' check.

uGuid.desc: The thing to read the maximum health of.

returns.name: maxHealth
returns.desc: The object's full-health value, or nothing at all if it couldn't be read.

Ess.Object.playerControlled.title: Object: Is Player Controlled
Ess.Object.playerControlled.desc: Checks whether a person or vehicle is being driven by a real player rather than the AI - the guard you want before applying an effect meant only for NPCs.

uGuid.desc: The character or vehicle to check.

returns.name: playerControlled
returns.desc: True if a player is controlling it. Underneath, the engine actually hands back the controlling player's handle rather than a true/false, which would fool a naive check - this node converts it to a proper true/false for you.

Ess.Object.pollVehicleChange.title: Object: Watch For Vehicle Change
Ess.Object.pollVehicleChange.desc: Keeps an eye on someone and runs your code the moment they get into or out of any vehicle - the only workable way to catch this, since the game has no 'entered a vehicle' event for a vehicle you don't already know about.

onChange.default: function(uVehicle, uPrevVehicle) Ess.Log(uVehicle and "got in" or "got out") end
onChange.desc: Your code, run only when they get in or out. It receives the vehicle they're in now (nothing if they just got out) and the one they were in before. If your code errors it is caught and logged, and the watch carries on.

interval.desc: How often to check, in seconds. 0.5 is the default and is responsive enough for getting in and out of cars; smaller numbers react faster but do more work.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to end the watch early - otherwise it keeps running on the framework's normal heartbeat.

Ess.Object.pos.title: Object: Position
Ess.Object.pos.desc: Reads where something is in the world, as three numbers you can feed into teleports, distance checks or spawn points.

uGuid.desc: The thing to read the position of - a character, vehicle or prop. Wire one in, or leave it as the player.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: East/west world coordinate.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Height (up) world coordinate.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: North/south world coordinate.

Ess.Object.remove.title: Object: Remove
Ess.Object.remove.desc: Deletes an object from the world entirely - no corpse, no wreck, just gone. Use this for cleaning up things your script spawned.

uGuid.desc: The thing to delete. Removal is DEFERRED: right after this the Alive node still reports true and only reads false about half a second later, so never check for removal in the same breath - and the Valid node stays true even after that, so it is not a usable 'is it gone yet' test at all.

Ess.Object.removeLabel.title: Object: Remove Label
Ess.Object.removeLabel.desc: Takes a text tag back off an object - the undo for Add Label.

uGuid.desc: The thing to untag.

sLabel.desc: The exact tag text to remove.

Ess.Object.revive.title: Object: Revive
Ess.Object.revive.desc: Brings a killed character back, optionally after a short pause - the undo for the Kill node.

uGuid.desc: The dead thing to bring back.

nDelay.desc: Seconds to wait before it stands back up. Leave at 0 for immediate; small values like 0.5 give a beat of drama.

Ess.Object.setHealth.title: Object: Set Health
Ess.Object.setHealth.desc: Writes a health value directly onto something - use it to soften a boss or top someone up to an exact number.

uGuid.desc: The thing whose health you're setting.

n.desc: The exact health value to write. Do NOT use this to kill something - setting health to 0 does not reliably register as a death on this engine; use the Kill node or the Damage node, which kills properly.

Ess.Object.setInvincible.title: Object: Set Invincible
Ess.Object.setInvincible.desc: Makes something immune to damage (or takes that immunity away) - the usual way to protect the player during a scripted sequence or keep a mission-critical vehicle alive.

uGuid.desc: The thing to protect.

bOn.desc: True to make it invincible, false to make it vulnerable again.

sReason.desc: A short tag saying WHY, like 'Survival' or 'Hijack' or 'HQ'. This framework insists on it so another system can later work out who turned invincibility on; leave it blank and it logs a warning and files it under 'Ess'.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the engine accepted the change.

Ess.Object.setPos.title: Object: Teleport To Position
Ess.Object.setPos.desc: Instantly moves an object to a world position - solid for props, vehicles and a just-spawned object, but unreliable on freshly-spawned or AI people, who streaming and physics can snap straight back.

uGuid.desc: The thing to move. To move the PLAYER use the Player Teleport node instead - this one is unreliable on humans.

x.desc: Destination east/west coordinate. Usually wired in from an Object Position node rather than typed.

y.desc: Destination height. Too low buries it in terrain, too high drops it - add a few units if unsure.

z.desc: Destination north/south coordinate.

Ess.Object.setVisible.title: Object: Set Visible
Ess.Object.setVisible.desc: Shows or hides an object without deleting it - it stays in the world and keeps working, it just stops being drawn.

uGuid.desc: The thing to show or hide.

bOn.desc: True to show it, false to make it invisible.

Ess.Object.setYaw.title: Object: Set Facing Angle
Ess.Object.setYaw.desc: Spins an object to a given heading on the spot - handy for lining up a spawned vehicle or posing a prop.

uGuid.desc: The thing to turn.

n.desc: The new facing angle. Degrees vs radians is unconfirmed on this engine, so the safe habit is to take a value from the Facing Angle node and add to it rather than typing a raw number.

Ess.Object.size.title: Object: Size
Ess.Object.size.desc: Reads how big an object's model is in each direction - use it to space spawns out so they don't overlap, size a camera orbit, or work out where to attach something.

uGuid.desc: A LIVE object to measure - this takes a real spawned thing, not a template name, even though it's asking about a model. On an object spawned this very instant it reports zeros; wait a beat and read it again.

returns.name: ex
returns.desc: Width of the model's bounding box.

returns.name: ey
returns.desc: Height of the model's bounding box.

returns.name: ez
returns.desc: Length of the model's bounding box.

Ess.Object.snapToGround.title: Object: Snap To Ground
Ess.Object.snapToGround.desc: Drops (or lifts) an object so it sits neatly on the terrain - the tidy-up for anything you spawned that ended up floating or half-buried.

uGuid.desc: The object to place on the ground.

nOffset.desc: How far ABOVE the ground to leave it, in world units. 0 sets it right down; a small number like 1 gives a little clearance so it doesn't clip in.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if it moved. False means it was left alone - either its position couldn't be read, or its ground height read exactly 0, which is either already-grounded or unloaded terrain, and skipping is safe either way.

Ess.Object.spawn.title: Object: Spawn At Position
Ess.Object.spawn.desc: Creates a new vehicle, person or prop at an exact map position - the one node in this group that makes something out of nothing.

sTemplate.desc: The name of the thing to create, e.g. 'Veyron' for a car or 'VZ Soldier' for an enemy. Never leave this blank or all-spaces: a blank name hard-crashes the game outright, so this node refuses it and logs a warning instead.

x.desc: East/west coordinate to place it at. Usually wired from an Object Position node - if you just want it in front of the player, use the Spawn Ahead node instead and skip the coordinates.

y.desc: Height to place it at. Follow with a Snap To Ground node if you aren't sure of the terrain height.

z.desc: North/south coordinate to place it at.

yaw.desc: Which way it should face once created. Leave this out entirely to keep whatever orientation the game gives it.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The thing that was created - wire this into other nodes. You get nothing back if the name was blank or the game refused to create it.

Ess.Object.spawnAhead.title: Object: Spawn Ahead Of Player
Ess.Object.spawnAhead.desc: Creates something a set distance in front of the player, already facing the same way - saves you working out the 'in front of me' maths by hand.

sTemplate.desc: The name of the thing to create, e.g. 'Veyron' for a car or 'VZ Soldier' for an enemy. A blank name would hard-crash the game, so it is refused before anything happens.

nDist.desc: How far in front to place it, in world units. 18 is the default and leaves comfortable room for a car.

nHeight.desc: How far above the player's feet to place it, in world units. Leave at 0 for ground level; raise it for aircraft or a mid-air drop.

i.desc: Which player to spawn in front of. 0 is you; 1 is the co-op partner, which does not exist in single-player, in which case nothing is spawned and a warning is logged.

tOpts.desc: Extra settings. By default 'in front of' means in front of the character's BODY - stand still and swing the camera and your view turns but your chest doesn't, so it can appear off to one side. Set useView = true to place it where you are LOOKING instead, which is what usually feels right; that safely falls back to body facing if you're aiming at open sky.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The thing that was created - wire this into other nodes. You get nothing back if the player has no character yet or the game refused to create it.

Ess.Object.speed.title: Object: Speed
Ess.Object.speed.desc: Reads how fast something is going as a single number, ignoring direction - the easy 'is this car moving' check.

uGuid.desc: The thing to read. On an object spawned this very instant this comes back empty - wait a beat after spawning and read it again.

returns.name: speed
returns.desc: Speed in world units per second, or nothing at all if it couldn't be read.

Ess.Object.speedSq.title: Object: Speed Squared
Ess.Object.speedSq.desc: The cheaper cousin of Speed for 'is it faster than X' tests that run every frame - compare against your threshold multiplied by itself instead of the plain number.

uGuid.desc: The thing to read. On an object spawned this very instant this comes back empty - wait a beat after spawning and read it again.

returns.name: speedSq
returns.desc: Speed multiplied by itself. It skips the square root, so it's the cheapest option - but it is NOT a real speed, so only ever compare it against another squared number.

Ess.Object.valid.title: Object: Is Valid Handle
Ess.Object.valid.desc: Checks that a handle still points at something the engine recognises - a guard against passing junk into other nodes, NOT a check that the thing still exists.

uGuid.desc: The handle to sanity-check. Warning: this stays true even after an object has been removed and Is Alive has already flipped to false - the handle outlives the object, so use Is Alive to ask whether something is gone.

returns.name: valid
returns.desc: True if the engine still recognises this handle.

Ess.Object.vehicleOf.title: Object: Vehicle Of Character
Ess.Object.vehicleOf.desc: Finds the vehicle a person is currently sitting in, whether they're driving or just riding along - the reliable way to grab 'the car the player is in'.

returns.name: uVehicle
returns.desc: The vehicle they're in, counting passenger seats as well as the driver's, or nothing at all if they're on foot.

Ess.Object.velocity.title: Object: Velocity
Ess.Object.velocity.desc: Reads which way and how fast something is moving, split into three directions - the basis for chase cameras, race checks and 'has it stopped yet'.

uGuid.desc: The thing to read. On an object spawned this very instant this comes back empty - wait a beat after spawning and read it again.

returns.name: vx
returns.desc: Sideways component of the movement.

returns.name: vy
returns.desc: Upward component of the movement.

returns.name: vz
returns.desc: Forward/backward component of the movement.

Ess.Object.visible.title: Object: Is Visible
Ess.Object.visible.desc: Checks whether an object is currently drawn on screen rather than hidden.

uGuid.desc: The thing to check.

returns.name: visible
returns.desc: True if the object is being drawn. This is a genuine true/false from the engine, unlike the visibility check on UI widgets.

Ess.Object.yaw.title: Object: Facing Angle
Ess.Object.yaw.desc: Reads which way an object is turned, so you can copy that heading onto something else or nudge it by a fixed amount.

uGuid.desc: The thing whose facing you want to read.

returns.name: yaw
returns.desc: The facing angle. Whether this is degrees or radians is NOT confirmed on this engine, so read a yaw, change it, and write it back - that stays self-consistent either way.

Ess.Objective.new.title: Objective: Counted Goal
Ess.Objective.new.desc: The lightest of the three mission tools: ONE counted goal on the HUD objective line, with no mission engine behind it. It shows 'Collect intel 2/5', ticks up each time you advance it, and fires your completion callback when the count reaches the target. Use it when you want a real, stateful goal but a whole Contract would be overkill. Give it an id and it becomes reload-safe: creating another one with the same id silently cancels the old one first, so re-running your script never leaves a stale goal stuck on screen.

opts.default: { label = 'Collect intel', target = 5, id = 'collect_intel', onComplete = function() Ess.Easy.Toast('Intel secured!') end }
opts.desc: The goal spec. `label` is the text on the HUD; `target` is how many are needed (default 1 - the counter is only shown when it is above 1). `id` makes it reload-safe. `onComplete` fires when the count is reached, `onProgress(count, target)` on every step, `onFail` if you fail it. `slot` picks which HUD objective line to use (default 1) and `show = false` hides it entirely while still counting.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: The live goal. Call `:advance(n)` to add to the count, `:set(n)` to set it outright, `:progress()` for count and target, `:isDone()`, `:label(s)` to change the wording, or `:complete()` / `:fail()` / `:cancel()` to end it early. The HUD line clears itself when it ends.

Ess.On.death.title: On: Object Dies
Ess.On.death.desc: Do something when one specific thing you already have a handle for is killed or destroyed. This is a real engine event, not a poll, so it costs nothing while it waits. Something only dies once, so it fires once - call the stop if you armed it and no longer care.

guid.desc: The thing to watch, wired in from whatever spawned or found it. If this is empty the hook is NOT armed and will never fire - silently, unless Ess.DEBUG is on. A hook that never fires is the quietest failure here, so check this first when nothing happens.

fn.desc: What to do when it dies. It gets no information about who killed it - this engine has no 'who shot me' event.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this and call it (or feed it to an Ess.stop node) to release the hook early.

Ess.On.enterArea.title: On: Player Enters Area
Ess.On.enterArea.desc:
Fires the moment a player walks into a circle on the map, then stops itself - it is a ONCE hook, so it will not nag every tick. It works by checking four times a second, comparing flat map distance only, so height is ignored: a player on a rooftop directly above the spot counts as inside.

Arming it twice gives you two independent watchers, so keep the stop for each.

x.desc: East/west centre of the circle. Usually wired from an Object Position node rather than typed.

y.desc: Height of the centre. Only passed back to your callback - it is NOT used to decide who is inside.

z.desc: North/south centre of the circle.

r.desc: Radius in world units. Too small and a player can run through the gap between two checks a quarter-second apart.

fn.desc: Runs once on entry. It is handed the player's east/west and north/south position, but the MIDDLE value is the height you passed in above, not the player's own height.

i.desc: Which player: 0 is you. 1 is the co-op partner, who usually does not exist in single-player.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this and call it to cancel the watcher if the player never turns up. After it fires, it has already cleaned itself up.

Ess.On.exitArea.title: On: Player Leaves Area
Ess.On.exitArea.desc: Fires the moment a player leaves a circle, then stops itself. It only counts as leaving once they have actually BEEN inside, so arming this while the player is on the other side of the map will not fire straight away - it waits for them to come in and go out again. Flat map distance, checked four times a second.

x.desc: East/west centre of the circle.

y.desc: Height of the centre. Passed back to your callback but NOT used to decide who is inside.

z.desc: North/south centre of the circle.

fn.default: function(px, py, pz) Ess.Easy.Toast('left the area') end
fn.desc: Runs once on the way out. It is handed the player's east/west and north/south position, but the MIDDLE value is the height you passed in above, not the player's own height.

i.desc: Which player: 0 is you.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this and call it to cancel the watcher before it ever fires.

Ess.On.healthBelow.title: On: Health Drops Below
Ess.On.healthBelow.desc:
Fires once when something has lost enough health, then stops itself. Good for a scripted 'the boss is nearly down' beat.

The percentage is measured against the health it had when you ARMED this, not its maximum - arm it on an already wounded enemy and 50% means half of what was left. It checks a bit over twice a second.

pct.desc: The threshold as a percentage of its health at arm time. Leaving it empty means 50.

fn.desc: Runs once when the threshold is crossed, given the health value that tripped it.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this and call it to cancel the watch if it becomes irrelevant - otherwise it keeps polling until the threshold is crossed.

Ess.On.insideArea.title: On: While Player Inside Area
Ess.On.insideArea.desc:
Runs your action AGAIN AND AGAIN, four times a second, the whole time a player is standing in the circle - a live zone, for draining health, holding a capture point or keeping a prompt on screen.

This one NEVER stops itself. It keeps polling forever even when the player is nowhere near, so you must keep the stop and call it, or it is a leak that outlives your feature.

x.desc: East/west centre of the circle.

y.desc: Height of the centre. Passed back to your callback but NOT used to decide who is inside.

z.desc: North/south centre of the circle.

fn.desc: Runs on EVERY check while they are inside - four times a second. Keep it cheap, and do not leave a toast in the real version or you will bury the screen. The middle value it is handed is the height you passed in above, not the player's own.

i.desc: Which player: 0 is you.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: You MUST keep this - it is the only thing that ends the zone. Call it, or feed it to an Ess.stop node or a tracker.

Ess.On.labeled.title: On: Labeled Object Found
Ess.On.labeled.desc:
The way to FIND things by the label the map designers gave them - collectible boxes, scripted props - which you cannot simply ask the engine for. It fires once for each matching object as it comes near a player and streams into memory.

Each object is remembered and excluded after its first hit, so it never fires twice for the same one. Distant objects do not exist yet, so streaming, not your radius, is the real limit on what you can find. If the label is empty or that player has no character, the hook is NOT armed and nothing will ever fire.

sLabel.desc: The world label objects carry, spelled exactly. A wrong label is not an error - you just never get a single hit.

nRadius.desc: How near a player they have to come, in world units. Leaving it empty means 300.

fn.desc: Runs once per object as it is discovered, given that object's handle - mark it, count it, or hold on to it.

i.desc: Which player things have to come near: 0 is you.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this and call it to stop discovering. Without it the search stays armed for the rest of the session.

Ess.On.playerHurt.title: On: Player Takes Damage
Ess.On.playerHurt.desc:
Runs every time a player's health goes DOWN, and keeps repeating for as long as you let it - the feasible version of 'I got hit' on this engine, since there is no real damage event and no way to know who hit you.

It polls five times a second, so several quick hits can read as one bigger drop. It never stops itself: keep the stop.

fn.desc: Runs on each drop, given the new health and how much was just lost. Healing does not fire it - only drops.

i.desc: Which player: 0 is you.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this - it is the only way to end the watcher. Call it, or feed it to an Ess.stop node or a tracker.

Ess.On.tick.title: On: Every Few Seconds
Ess.On.tick.desc:
The simplest repeater: do this every so often, forever, until you stop it. It never stops itself.

WATCH OUT: unlike Loop: Start this names itself a new name every time, so arming it twice gives you TWO loops doing the same work - there is no name to replace. In a script that re-runs on a key press, use Loop: Start with a fixed name instead.

interval.desc: Seconds between runs. Leaving it empty means one second.

fn.desc: What to do each time. Unlike Loop: Start you do NOT return anything here - it always keeps going.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this. Calling it (or feeding it to an Ess.stop node, or a tracker) is the only way to end this repeater.

Ess.On.vehicle.title: On: Player Enters Or Exits Vehicle
Ess.On.vehicle.desc:
Runs whenever a player gets into or out of a vehicle, and keeps repeating. Your action is handed what they are in now and what they were in before, so you can tell the two apart: nothing now means they just got out.

If that player has no character - asking for the co-op partner in single-player does exactly this - the hook is NOT armed, and the stop it hands back does nothing.

fn.desc: Runs on each change, given the vehicle now and the one before. On foot, the first is nothing.

i.desc: Which player: 0 is you. Player 1 usually does not exist in single-player, and asking for them leaves this hook unarmed.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Keep this and call it to end the watcher. It never stops itself.

Ess.Override.mergeIntoLiveTable.skip_reason: targets an engine module table that only exists after an import() in the same file, which an emitted graph cannot do, and each table's row shape is its own recipe.

Ess.Override.wrap.skip_reason: replaces a live engine function with a hand-written wrapper that has to invoke callOriginal itself; not expressible from a graph.

Ess.Player.camera.title: Player: Camera
Ess.Player.camera.desc: Gets the camera handle belonging to a player in one step, instead of the usual two-step of fetching the player slot and then asking it for its camera.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner and has no camera in single-player.

returns.name: uCamera
returns.desc: The camera handle to hand to camera nodes, or nil if that player index has no slot.

Ess.Player.character.title: Player: Character
Ess.Player.character.desc: Gets the handle for a player's actual body in the world - the thing you feed into almost every other node that acts on a person.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, the local player. 1 is the co-op partner, and that is genuinely nil in single-player, so downstream nodes will do nothing.

returns.name: uChar
returns.desc: The character handle, or nil when there is no such player (index 1 outside co-op).

Ess.Player.giveCash.title: Player: Give Cash
Ess.Player.giveCash.desc: Adds money to the player's wallet through the route that also refreshes the HUD - the plain engine cash setters change the number without the player ever seeing it move.

n.desc: How much cash to add. Amounts are whole dollars; a negative number takes money away.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the call went through.

Ess.Player.giveFuel.title: Player: Give Fuel
Ess.Player.giveFuel.desc: Adds fuel to the player's stock through the HUD-updating route, the same reason the cash node exists.

n.desc: How much fuel to add. There is no player index here because fuel is this machine's own campaign stock, not a per-character resource - in co-op each machine already has its own.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the call went through.

Ess.Player.inVehicle.title: Player: Vehicle They Are In
Ess.Player.inVehicle.desc: Gets the vehicle the player is currently sitting in, driving or riding, so you can gate a boost, a horn or a car-only menu on actually being in one.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: uVeh
returns.desc: The vehicle handle - driver OR passenger seat both count - or nil when they are on foot.

Ess.Player.onFoot.title: Player: Is On Foot
Ess.Player.onFoot.desc: The plain yes/no complement of the vehicle check - true when the player is in no vehicle at all.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: bOnFoot
returns.desc: True when they are walking, false when they are in any vehicle.

Ess.Player.pose.title: Player: Pose
Ess.Player.pose.desc: One read that answers 'where is this player and which way are they turned', handing back the position, facing and both handles together so you do not need four separate nodes.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner and returns nils for position in single-player.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: East/west world coordinate. Nil when there is no character at all.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Height. Y is up on this engine.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: North/south world coordinate.

returns.name: yaw
returns.desc: The CHEST/BODY facing in degrees, which is NOT where the player is looking - swinging the mouse turns the view without turning the body. Use Player View Yaw if you mean 'in front of me' the way a player sees it. Falls back to 0 if unreadable.

returns.name: uChar
returns.desc: That player's character handle, passed through so you do not need a second node.

returns.name: uPlayerSlot
returns.desc: That player's slot handle, passed through the same way.

Ess.Player.removeBoundaries.title: Player: Remove Map Boundaries
Ess.Player.removeBoundaries.desc: Lifts every out-of-bounds volume that is active right now, for every connected player at once, so you can leave the mission area without the turn-back warning.

returns.name: nCleared
returns.desc: How many players had their boundaries cleared. Note this only clears what is active AT THIS MOMENT - it does not switch the boundary system off, so the game's own scripts can add a fresh one later (on a mission or area change), and it does not survive a reload.

Ess.Player.rumble.title: Player: Controller Rumble
Ess.Player.rumble.desc: Buzzes the controller for a moment - the cheap bit of 'juice' a hit, pickup or explosion moment wants.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

fLength.desc: How long to buzz, in seconds. The shipped game's own scripts use values around 0.15, so keep it short.

Ess.Player.setInputEnabled.title: Player: Freeze / Unfreeze Input
Ess.Player.setInputEnabled.desc: Freezes or restores a player's gameplay controls - the standard way to hold someone still during a scripted moment or while a menu of yours has focus.

bOn.desc: True restores control, false freezes the player. Always pair a freeze with an unfreeze or the player is stuck for good.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner. This works on the player SLOT, matching the engine call.

Ess.Player.slot.title: Player: Slot Handle
Ess.Player.slot.desc: Gets the player SLOT handle, which is a different thing from the character - camera calls and some AI calls want this one, not the body.

i.desc: Which player slot: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: uPlayerSlot
returns.desc: The player-slot handle. TRAP (confirmed live): slot 1 comes back as a real, non-nil handle even in single-player, so never use 'is slot 1 not nil' as an are-we-in-co-op test - test Player Character with index 1 instead.

Ess.Player.targetUnderReticle.title: Player: Target Under Crosshair
Ess.Player.targetUnderReticle.desc: Answers 'what am I aiming at right now', giving both the thing under the crosshair and the exact world point the aim lands on.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The thing under the crosshair, or nil when the aim lands on nothing targetable. The raw engine call hands the coordinates back first and the handle last; this node reorders it so the handle comes first like every other Ess node.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: East/west coordinate of the aim point. Can still be a real point even when the handle above is nil.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Height of the aim point.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: North/south coordinate of the aim point.

Ess.Player.teleport.title: Player: Teleport
Ess.Player.teleport.desc: Warps the player to a spot on the map using the confirmed hero-teleport route rather than a raw position set, which is unreliable on people because streaming and physics can snap them back.

x.desc: Destination east/west coordinate. Usually wired in from a Pose or Position node rather than typed.

y.desc: Destination height. WARNING: interior coordinates do not round-trip - teleporting to a height taken inside the PMC HQ drops you onto open-world terrain below it and you take fall damage instead.

z.desc: Destination north/south coordinate.

yaw.desc: Which way to face on arrival, in degrees. Leave at 0 if you do not care.

onDone.desc: Runs once the warp has actually finished. Use it to spawn or enable things only after the player has landed, instead of guessing at a delay.

Ess.Player.viewYaw.title: Player: View Yaw
Ess.Player.viewYaw.desc: Gets the direction the player is actually LOOKING, which on this engine can be up to 111 degrees away from the direction their body is turned - this is the one that matches what the player perceives as 'in front of me'.

i.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: yaw
returns.desc: The look direction in degrees. Never nil while the player has a character, so it is always safe to use.

returns.name: bFromReticle
returns.desc: True when the look direction was really measured from the crosshair. False means it fell back to the body facing because the crosshair had nothing usable - aiming at open sky, or something closer than 3 units, both give junk. Branch on this only if you care.

Ess.Points.bucket.title: Points: Sort Spawn Points By Size
Ess.Points.bucket.desc: Sorts a list of spawn points into three groups by the room recorded on each one: 5 or less is infantry-sized, up to 15 fits a vehicle, anything bigger is a helicopter landing spot. That is the same convention MissionForge exports with. If not a single point counts as infantry-sized, the infantry group falls back to the whole list rather than being empty, so whatever you draw from it you always get something. Pure list maths - it doesn't touch the world at all.

spawnList.desc: A Lua list of spawn points. Each point is four numbers: x, y, z, and the radius saying how much clear room it has. Leave the radius off and it counts as 3, i.e. infantry-sized.

returns.name: tBuckets
returns.desc: A table holding three lists: .inf for infantry points, .veh for vehicle-sized ones, .heli for the big open ones.

Ess.Points.ideal.title: Points: Pick The Best Spawn Points
Ess.Points.ideal.desc: Picks the spawn points that make sense around a place - far enough away that enemies don't appear in the player's lap, close enough that they matter - nearest first. Height is deliberately ignored: points are compared flat, as if on a map. It always gives you something usable: if fewer than four points fit the window it drops the far limit and tries again, and if that still finds nothing it hands back every point you gave it.

pts.desc: The candidate points, in the same four-number shape as the sorting node - usually wired straight out of it.

refX.desc: East/west coordinate to measure from - normally the player, or the objective the fight is about.

refZ.desc: North/south coordinate to measure from. There is deliberately no height here - distance is measured flat.

opts.desc: Tuning: minDist is how close a point is allowed to be (18 keeps spawns off the player), maxDist how far away (80), maxCount how many to hand back at most (24). These are the values confirmed working in the wave-defense mod this came from - using more points means fewer enemies appearing at each one.

returns.name: tPoints
returns.desc: The chosen points, nearest first.

Ess.Probe.allByName.title: Probe: All By Name
Ess.Probe.allByName.desc: Finds EVERY live object matching a name, where the ordinary name lookup only ever hands back one - use it when a template has many instances in the world.

sName.desc: The template or object name, spelled exactly as the game spells it. A blank name returns an empty list.

returns.name: tGuids
returns.desc: A list of every matching handle. Always a real list, empty rather than nil on no match or failure.

Ess.Probe.describeSafe.title: Probe: Describe
Ess.Probe.describeSafe.desc: Turns any handle into one readable line - name, position, health and faction - for logging and for working out what your search actually found.

uGuid.desc: The thing to describe. A nil handle is fine and just gives back "<nil>".

returns.name: sDescription
returns.desc: A line like: NAME (12.3,4.5,67.8) hp=100 VZ. Every field is guarded on its own, so an unreadable one shows as "pos?", "hp?" or "fac?" instead of blanking the whole line.

Ess.Probe.getFaction.title: Probe: Faction Of
Ess.Probe.getFaction.desc: Tells you which side something belongs to, as the short faction code - so you can tell friend from enemy before acting on it.

uGuid.desc: The thing to identify - a person, vehicle or building.

returns.name: sAbbrev
returns.desc: The short faction code, such as "VZ", "Allied", "OC", "China", "Guerilla" or "Pirate". Nil when the thing has no readable faction.

Ess.Probe.nearby.title: Probe: Find Nearby
Ess.Probe.nearby.desc: Finds everything of a chosen kind within a radius of a point - the workhorse for 'all enemies around me', 'every car on this street', 'anything in this zone'.

x.desc: East/west coordinate of the centre of the search. Usually wired in from a Player Pose node.

y.desc: Height of the centre of the search.

z.desc: North/south coordinate of the centre of the search.

radius.desc: How far out to look, in world units. Start small - a big radius over a busy area returns a lot.

kind.desc: What to look for: "humans", "vehicles", "buildings", or "any" (people plus ground vehicles plus aircraft). Narrower families: "tanks", "helicopters", "boats", "cars", "jets", "props", "usables", "groundNoTanks". TRAP: a misspelled kind is NOT an error - it silently falls back to "any", which has really caused a script to act on the wrong thing.

filter.desc: Optional label to narrow results, for example "VZ" to keep only that faction's stuff. Leave it empty to keep everything; a label nothing carries returns an empty list rather than an error.

includeSelf.desc: Leave false. The raw engine search has no idea what 'me' is, so a radius covering you returns YOUR OWN character as an ordinary result - a real incident had a mistyped search return only the player and a destructive action then killed them. Set true only when you genuinely want to count yourself, such as tallying everyone in a zone.

returns.name: tGuids
returns.desc: A list of handles, de-duplicated. Always a real list, empty rather than nil when nothing matched.

Ess.Probe.nearest.title: Probe: Find Nearest
Ess.Probe.nearest.desc: Finds the single closest match to a point instead of the whole list - 'the nearest enemy', 'the car I'm standing next to' - and tells you how far away it is.

x.desc: East/west coordinate to measure from. Usually wired in from a Player Pose node.

y.desc: Height to measure from.

z.desc: North/south coordinate to measure from.

radius.desc: How far out to look, in world units. Nothing beyond this is considered at all.

kind.desc: What to look for: "humans", "vehicles", "buildings", "any", or the narrower "tanks", "helicopters", "boats", "cars", "jets", "props", "usables", "groundNoTanks". A misspelled kind silently becomes "any" instead of erroring.

filter.desc: Optional label to narrow results, for example "VZ". Leave empty to keep everything.

includeSelf.desc: Leave false, or the answer to 'what is nearest to me' will very often be me. Set true only when you deliberately want yourself in the running.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The closest matching handle, or nil when nothing matched in range.

returns.name: nDist
returns.desc: How far away it is, in world units.

Ess.Pursuit.capLevel.title: Pursuit: Cap Max Level
Ess.Pursuit.capLevel.desc: Sets a ceiling on how hot things can ever get - genuinely useful for a mode that must never exceed heat 2, but read the warning first.

nLevel.desc: The highest heat level allowed from now on. WARNING - THIS IS ONE-WAY: nothing raises the ceiling back for the rest of the session. A bigger number, 99, the per-faction form, the duration and custom nodes were ALL tried and none of them undo it; only a save-load or a full restart does. Treat this as a commitment for the whole play session, not a setting you tweak. It logs a loud warning every time it runs.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.clear.title: Pursuit: Clear
Ess.Pursuit.clear.desc: The real off switch for a chase already in progress - it drops the heat straight to 0. None of the Restrict nodes do this, despite their names.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.clearRestrictions.title: Pursuit: Clear Restrictions
Ess.Pursuit.clearRestrictions.desc: Lifts every heat restriction you set, putting the wanted system back to behaving normally.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through. Remember this only re-allows heat to build - it neither starts nor stops any pursuit that is already running.

Ess.Pursuit.custom.title: Pursuit: Custom
Ess.Pursuit.custom.desc: Runs a pursuit with your own settings table and duration, for a chase that does not behave like the stock one.

nDur.desc: How long the custom pursuit should run, in seconds.

tSettings.desc: The custom settings table. Its shape matches the shipped game's own usage, but be warned: the effect can only be SEEN while a pursuit is actively engaged, so testing this from a cold start will look like nothing happened.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.level.title: Pursuit: Level
Ess.Pursuit.level.desc: The quick 'how hot am I right now' read, for showing heat stars or gating something on being chased.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: The current heat level. Comes back 0 both when you are clean and when the state cannot be read at all.

Ess.Pursuit.levelTimes.title: Pursuit: Level Durations
Ess.Pursuit.levelTimes.desc: Tunes how long each heat level lasts before it decays, so you can make a chase drag on or blow over quickly.

n1.desc: First level duration in seconds. 120 is the value the shipped game's own scripts use.

n2.desc: Second level duration in seconds. 300 is the shipped value.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.lock.title: Pursuit: Lock Level
Ess.Pursuit.lock.desc: Pins the heat at a level so it stops ticking down on its own - for a scripted 'you will not shake them' stretch.

faction.desc: Who is doing the chasing: "Allied", "China", "Guerilla", "OC", "Pirate" or "VZ".

nLevel.desc: The level to pin it at. Undo it with the Pursuit Clear node - that is the only thing that releases the lock.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.restrictAll.title: Pursuit: Restrict All Heat
Ess.Pursuit.restrictAll.desc: Turns the natural build-up of heat on or off for every faction, so ordinary mayhem stops attracting attention.

bOn.desc: True to block heat from building, false to let it build normally again. TRAP: this only gates heat the AI raises on its own. It does NOT end a chase already running - use Pursuit Clear for that - and it does NOT stop a script that calls Pursuit Start.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.restrictFaction.title: Pursuit: Restrict One Faction
Ess.Pursuit.restrictFaction.desc: Same as restricting all heat, but for one faction only - go loud on the cartel while the army still leaves you alone.

bOn.desc: True to block that faction's heat from building, false to allow it again. Like the all-factions version, this never ends a chase already in progress.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.seconds.title: Pursuit: Set Seconds Left
Ess.Pursuit.seconds.desc: Sets how much time is left on the current pursuit for a faction - shorten it for mercy, stretch it to keep the pressure on.

faction.desc: Whose pursuit clock to set: "Allied", "China", "Guerilla", "OC", "Pirate" or "VZ".

n.desc: Seconds remaining. Leaving it at the built-in 0 runs the clock straight out.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.start.title: Pursuit: Start
Ess.Pursuit.start.desc: Puts the player wanted by a faction at a chosen heat level, seeding a real countdown (about 400 seconds at level 3).

faction.desc: Who wants you: "Allied", "China", "Guerilla", "OC", "Pirate" or "VZ" (an already-resolved faction handle also works). A name the game does not know just logs a message and does nothing.

nLevel.desc: The heat level to start at. TRAP: starting a pursuit spawns NOTHING to chase you on its own - the state stays "Stopped" until that faction's units actually engage you, so this alone will not feel like a chase.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Pursuit.state.title: Pursuit: State
Ess.Pursuit.state.desc: Reads the whole wanted/heat situation in one go - level, whether it is running, how long is left and who is chasing you.

returns.name: tState
returns.desc: A table with Level, Active, PlayerState, Faction, Locked, SecondsLeft, SecondsLeftInLevel and Duration - or nil if it cannot be read. When nothing is happening you see Level = 0, Active = false and Faction = 0xFFFFFFFF (a placeholder meaning 'nobody', not a real faction).

Ess.Quest.new.title: Quest: Step Sequence
Ess.Quest.new.desc: The middle weight: a linear sequence of goals, shown one at a time on the HUD objective line as '(2/3) Blow the tower'. Steps can be MANUAL (a plain line of text you advance yourself) or AUTO-WIRED - a reach, destroy or clear step completes itself off what actually happens in the world AND drops its own map marker, so a whole scripted mission becomes one table with no event wiring at all. When the last step is done the line clears and your completion callback fires. Heavier than a single Objective, far lighter than a Contract (no rewards, no spawned units, no fail conditions).

opts.default: { steps = { { reach = { -522, -2.1, 2697, 10 }, label = 'Get to the docks' }, { clear = { -522, -2.1, 2697, 50, 'VZ' }, label = 'Clear them out' }, 'Escape on foot' }, onComplete = function() Ess.Easy.Toast('Mission complete!') end }
opts.desc: The sequence spec. `steps` is the ordered list; each step is either `'plain text'` (manual - you call `:advance()`), `{label = , target = }` (a manual counted step), or one of the auto-wired kinds: `{reach = {x, y, z, radius}}` completes on arrival, `{destroy = guid}` when that object dies, `{clear = {x, y, z, radius, faction}}` when every unit of that faction in the area is dead. `onStep(i, total)` fires as each one clears, `onComplete` at the end. `showCounter = false` drops the '(2/3)' prefix.

returns.name: quest
returns.desc: The live sequence. Call `:advance(n)` to push the current step along, `:skip()` to force it done and move on, `:step()` for the current index and total, `:current()` for the live Objective, `:isDone()`, or `:cancel()` to abandon it.

Ess.RNG.chance.title: Random: Chance
Ess.RNG.chance.desc: Rolls against a probability and answers true or false - "does this enemy drop loot?", "does a car spawn here?". p runs 0 to 1, so 0.25 means it happens about a quarter of the time; leave it out for a straight coin flip. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.

p.desc: Probability from 0 (never) to 1 (always). Leave at 0.5 for a coin flip.

returns.name: hit
returns.desc: True roughly p of the time.

Ess.RNG.int.title: Random: Integer
Ess.RNG.int.desc: Rolls a whole number from 1 up to n - a dice roll, or a random slot in a list of n things. Asking for less than 1 just gives you 1. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.

n.desc: The highest number you can roll (the lowest is always 1).

returns.name: value
returns.desc: A whole number between 1 and n.

Ess.RNG.new.title: Random: New Generator
Ess.RNG.new.desc: Makes a random number generator that actually works in this game. Mercenaries 2's Lua stores numbers as 32-bit floats, so the usual random generators quietly break here - one real mod had every crate and unit roll come out identical for a whole play session before anyone noticed - and the engine's own math.random is dead too. Always start from this instead. Give it a seed number to get the same sequence every run (handy while testing), or leave it blank to seed from the clock. Each generator is its own independent stream, so two mods rolling in the same tick can't disturb each other.

seed.desc: A starting number for a repeatable sequence. Leave empty for a different sequence each run.

returns.name: generator
returns.desc: The generator to feed into the other Random nodes.

Ess.RNG.next.title: Random: Fraction
Ess.RNG.next.desc: Draws the next random fraction, from 0 up to (but never quite reaching) 1 - the raw roll every other Random node is built on. Multiply it to get any range you like. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: A random fraction from 0 up to just under 1.

Ess.RNG.pick.title: Random: Pick One
Ess.RNG.pick.desc: Picks one random entry out of a list, optionally weighted so some come up more often. If an entry is a table, its "w" field (or whichever key name you give) is how heavily it's weighted; plain entries like object handles, numbers or text all weigh 1, giving an even pick. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.

list.desc: The list to pick from. Entries can be plain values, or tables carrying a weight.

weightKey.desc: Which field on a table entry holds its weight. Entries missing it weigh 1.

returns.name: picked
returns.desc: One entry from the list.

Ess.RNG.pickN.title: Random: Pick Several
Ess.RNG.pickN.desc: Picks n DIFFERENT entries from a list at random, in random order - a loot draw or a random squad selection where nothing repeats. Asking for more than the list holds just gives you all of it, shuffled; asking for none gives an empty list. Your original list is never touched. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.

list.desc: The list to draw from. Left unchanged.

n.desc: How many distinct entries you want.

returns.name: picked
returns.desc: A new list of n different entries, in random order.

Ess.RNG.shuffle.title: Random: Shuffle List
Ess.RNG.shuffle.desc: Shuffles a list into a random order. It rearranges the list you hand it (and gives that same list back), so copy it first if you need the original order kept. Use this rather than sorting with a random comparator - that trick is biased and can even crash, because an inconsistent comparator is undefined behaviour in Lua. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.

list.desc: The list to shuffle. It is rearranged in place.

returns.name: list
returns.desc: The same list, now in random order.

Ess.Raw.AIOrders.actor.skip_reason: resolves a vehicle to its driver so AI orders land; the AI Orders nodes already do this internally and Vehicle Driver reads the same thing.

Ess.Raw.AIOrders.enable.title: Raw AI: Freeze AI Control
Ess.Raw.AIOrders.enable.desc: Turns the AI's control of a character on or off. Off freezes them exactly where they stand - the standard way to hold someone still for a scripted or cutscene beat - and on hands control back. Point it at a person; for someone in a vehicle, aim it at the driver rather than the vehicle.

g.desc: The character to freeze or release.

bOn.desc: False freezes them (the AI stops driving them), true gives control back. Always pair the two - a frozen character stays frozen until something unfreezes them.

Ess.Raw.AIOrders.goal.skip_reason: the raw engine order call, whose args table (AIGuid/Goal/Target/Priority) must be hand-assembled; the AI Orders nodes assemble it correctly.

Ess.Raw.AIOrders.haste.skip_reason: sets the movement speed of an order already in flight; on its own there is nothing to speed up - it belongs to the AI Orders node's speed option.

Ess.Raw.AIOrders.pri.skip_reason: a pure string lookup that turns 'hi' into 'HiPri'; it touches nothing in the game.

Ess.Raw.AIOrders.priorityTarget.title: Raw AI: Make Enemies Focus This
Ess.Raw.AIOrders.priorityTarget.desc: Marks one thing as the priority target for hostile AI, so enemies in the area come for it. This is the standalone 'everyone attack THIS' switch behind a boss fight or an escort-and-defend scenario, without having to hand orders to each enemy yourself.

g.desc: The thing enemies should focus on - a player, an ally you want them to swarm, a vehicle.

Ess.Raw.Impulse.apply.skip_reason: the raw unscaled shove in the engine's side/up/forward axis order; Impulse Push does the same thing with the mass scaling that makes it feel the same on a bike and a tank.

Ess.Raw.Impulse.applyAtPoint.skip_reason: the raw off-centre shove behind Impulse Spin, with the lever-arm offset and mass scaling left for you to work out.

Ess.Raw.Impulse.mass.skip_reason: reads an object's mass, which the tier above already exposes as Impulse Mass.

Ess.Raw.Mark.haltPulse.title: Raw Mark: Stop Flashing
Ess.Raw.Mark.haltPulse.desc: Stops the flashing that Raw Mark: Flash Marker started, leaving the marker itself in place. Like its partner it takes the object, not a marker handle.

uGuid.desc: The object that is currently flashing.

Ess.Raw.Mark.pda.skip_reason: places only the PDA blip and hands back a name you must store yourself; Mark Object covers it as one opt-out of a single marker.

Ess.Raw.Mark.pulse.title: Raw Mark: Flash Marker
Ess.Raw.Mark.pulse.desc: Makes an object's EXISTING marker flash in a colour - a 'look at this' pulse, not a new marker. If the thing has no marker yet nothing will show, so place one with a Mark node first. Unlike the other marker calls, this one takes the object itself rather than a marker handle.

uGuid.desc: The object whose marker should flash.

rgb.desc: Flash colour as { red, green, blue }, each 0 to 255. Left alone it is the game's own amber objective colour.

Ess.Raw.Mark.radar.skip_reason: places one of three marker surfaces and hands back a name you must store and remove yourself; Mark Object places every surface in one node and Stop tears them all down.

Ess.Raw.Mark.removePda.skip_reason: undoes one surface of a hand-assembled raw marker by name; Mark Clear or Stop takes the whole marker handle.

Ess.Raw.Mark.removeRadar.skip_reason: undoes one surface of a hand-assembled raw marker by name; Mark Clear or Stop takes the whole marker handle.

Ess.Raw.Mark.removeWorld.skip_reason: undoes one surface of a hand-assembled raw marker by handle; Mark Clear or Stop takes the whole marker handle.

Ess.Raw.Mark.showPlayerMarkers.title: Raw Mark: Show Player Markers
Ess.Raw.Mark.showPlayerMarkers.desc: One global switch for whether the other players' HUD markers draw at all. The confirmed use is quieting the HUD for a scripted moment: turn it off as your cutscene starts, back on when it ends. Unlike every other marker call this is not tied to a single object - it affects all of them at once, so always turn it back on.

bOn.desc: True draws player markers, false hides them.

Ess.Raw.Mark.world.skip_reason: places only the floating in-world icon and hands back a bare handle to keep track of; Mark Object covers it, and its size/distance options, in one node.

Ess.Raw.Mark.worldDisc.skip_reason: the bare ground-ring call; Mark Zone draws a ring at a map point and owns its anchor prop, and Mark Object can add one around an object.

Ess.Raw.Relations.restore.skip_reason: needs the exact snapshot table produced by the raw snapshot call; Relations Restore or Stop undoes a whole applied set instead.

Ess.Raw.Relations.set.skip_reason: a one-way raw stance write between two handles with nothing recorded to undo it; Relations Apply takes faction names, sets both directions and remembers the originals.

Ess.Raw.Relations.snapshot.skip_reason: records one direction's stance into a table you would have to hold and hand back later; Relations Apply snapshots for you.

Ess.Raw.Sandbox.gateSaves.skip_reason: documented as existing only for a raw-tier provider author holding the save gate by hand; the Save Gate node is the real surface and is keyed per holder so two users cannot clobber each other.

Ess.Raw.Sandbox.register.skip_reason: registers a provider table of your own snapshot/apply/restore functions - that is writing a Lua module, not wiring a graph.

Ess.Raw.Sandbox.ungateSaves.skip_reason: the release half of the same raw-author-only save gate; the Save Ungate node is the real surface.

Ess.Raw.Triggers.arm.skip_reason: the condition is a hand-built spec table plus a callback; the On... hooks and the Easy Triggers nodes cover the same conditions ready-made.

Ess.Relations.apply.title: Relations: Apply Faction Stances
Ess.Relations.apply.desc: Sets how whole factions feel about each other - who shoots at whom - and hands back a handle that undoes it. This is how you make a normally peaceful faction turn on the player for your fight. Both directions are set at once, so making China hate PMC also makes PMC hate China. TRAP: this is a real change to the world and it does not wear off on its own. If you never restore the handle, those factions stay at each other for the rest of the session.

pairsList.desc: The stances to set, as a list of {faction, faction, stance} entries. Faction names the game knows: Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ, PMC. Stance is 'friend', 'ally', 'allied', 'neutral', 'enemy' or 'hostile' (any capitalisation), or a raw number from -100 for hatred to 100 for friendship. A faction name this level does not know is written to the log and skipped, so a typo changes nothing at all. A pair involving PMC also updates the other faction's attitude on the HUD so the player can see the change.

label.desc: A name for this set of changes. Only used to make the log readable when several sets are live at once.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: Keep this. Feed it to the Relations: Restore node (or an Ess.stop node) when the fight is over, or your stance change stays live for the whole session. Each apply mints its own handle carrying its own before-picture, so several sets can be live at the same time without overwriting each other.

Ess.Relations.getFeeling.title: Relations: Get Personal Feeling
Ess.Relations.getFeeling.desc: Reads how one specific character feels about one other specific character. This is a personal grudge between two individuals, which is a completely different thing from the faction-wide stances the Relations: Apply node sets - you can make one guard friendly without touching his whole army.

uGuidA.desc: The character whose opinion you are reading.

uGuidB.desc: The character they have an opinion about.

returns.name: feeling
returns.desc: Roughly -100 for wants-you-dead up to 100 for friendly; below zero is hostile. Two catches: a failed read also comes back as 0, so 0 means 'neutral, or could not tell', and a character you spawned this very instant reads back a stale 0 - wait a tick before asking about anything freshly spawned.

Ess.Relations.getPerceivability.title: Relations: Get Detectability
Ess.Relations.getPerceivability.desc: Reads how visible a character is to enemy AI - the stealth stat behind sneaking past people. Live readings taken from the running game: 90 with a floor of 5 on a person on foot, 90 with a floor of 2.5 on a helicopter pilot.

uGuid.desc: The character to measure. Anything spawned this instant needs a tick to settle before it reads back correctly.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: How detectable this character currently is. Nothing comes back at all if the read failed.

returns.name: floor
returns.desc: The engine's lower limit for this character - the most hidden it will let them get.

Ess.Relations.isActive.title: Relations: Is Set Still Applied
Ess.Relations.isActive.desc: Checks whether a set of faction stance changes is still in force, so you can avoid restoring twice or show the player that a truce is still running.

h.desc: The handle the Relations: Apply node gave you.

returns.name: active
returns.desc: True while this handle's stances are still applied, false once it has been restored.

Ess.Relations.restore.title: Relations: Restore Faction Stances
Ess.Relations.restore.desc: Puts back exactly the faction stances that one apply changed, and nothing else. This is the other half of Relations: Apply and the thing beginners forget - skip it and your world stays rewritten. Safe to run twice: a second go, or a blank handle, quietly does nothing.

h.desc: The handle the Relations: Apply node gave you. If the original stance could not be read back when it was applied, there is genuinely nothing to restore it to, so that one direction is left as-is and written to the log rather than being silently skipped.

Ess.Relations.setFeeling.title: Relations: Set Personal Feeling
Ess.Relations.setFeeling.desc: Changes how one character feels about one other character, without touching either one's faction. The game's own recruit script does exactly this - writing 100 to clear a guard's hostility toward the player - immediately before giving that guard a follow order, because a hostile character refuses to follow anyone.

uGuidA.desc: The character whose opinion is being changed.

uGuidB.desc: The character they will now feel differently about. This is one-way only: A's opinion of B. Set the other direction too if you want it mutual.

n.desc: The new feeling, roughly -100 for hatred up to 100 for friendship. 100 is the value the game's own scripts use to wipe out hostility before a follow order.

Ess.Relations.setPerceivability.title: Relations: Set Detectability
Ess.Relations.setPerceivability.desc: Turns a character's visibility to enemy AI up or down - the knob behind a ghost or stealth mode. It is fully reversible: the value was driven from 90 down to 30 and back to 90 in a live session with clean reads in between. Honest caveat: the number provably moves, but whether AI genuinely stop noticing someone at a low value has not yet been proven in actual gameplay, so test your stealth mode rather than trusting the number.

uGuid.desc: The character to make more or less noticeable.

n.desc: The new detectability. Typical starting value is 90, and the engine has its own floor per character (around 5 for a person on foot) that it will not go below. Remember the old value if you want to put it back.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the engine accepted the change.

Ess.Safe.call.skip_reason: wraps a function you pass it in a pcall; the editor already guards emitted calls.

Ess.Safe.named.skip_reason: same pcall wrapper with a label for a hand-written closure; there is no closure to label in a graph.

Ess.Safe.quiet.skip_reason: same pcall wrapper as Safe.call, only quieter; the editor already guards emitted calls.

Ess.Safe.reject.skip_reason: records a guard rejection from inside a wrapper you wrote yourself - it is for authors extending Ess, not for wiring a graph.

Ess.Safe.reset.title: Reset Failure Stats
Ess.Safe.reset.desc: Wipes the failure tally, the running total and the last error, so whatever shows up afterwards came only from the thing you are about to do. The habit that makes the diagnostics readable: reset, reproduce your problem once, then read Last Error or Failure Stats.

Ess.Safe.stats.title: Failure Stats
Ess.Safe.stats.desc: The worst-offenders list: which calls have been failing, and how often, sorted worst first. It only tallies failures that happened while debug was on (a Lua line reading Ess.DEBUG = true), while the running total counts them either way - so an empty list next to a big total means plenty failed, just before you started watching.

returns.name: byCall
returns.desc: A list of records with .label and .count, worst first. Empty unless debug was on when things failed.

returns.name: total
returns.desc: Every failure Ess has quietly swallowed this session, counted whether or not debug was on.

Ess.Safe.string.skip_reason: a type guard meant to be wrapped around Safe.call's own (ok, value) pair, which nothing in a graph produces.

Ess.Safe.template.skip_reason: a true/false check on a spawn-template string that the spawn nodes already run internally before calling the engine.

Ess.Sandbox.begin.title: Sandbox: Begin
Ess.Sandbox.begin.desc: Opens a temporary, guaranteed-cleanup mode for a fight: several parts of the world are photographed, changed for the duration, and put back by the matching Sandbox: Finish node. Saving is deliberately switched off the whole time, so if the game crashes in the middle of your encounter the save on disk is still the untouched pre-encounter one. TRAP: if you never finish this id, the player cannot save for the rest of the session.

id.desc: A name for this sandbox. Pass the exact same name to Sandbox: Finish to close it. Two sandboxes can run at once as long as they have different names.

providerNames.desc: Which parts of the world to isolate, as a list of names. 'relations' applies the faction stances in opts.relations and puts them back at the end. 'economy' banks the player's cash to zero for the duration (or to opts.startCash) and pays back the exact amount afterwards. 'supports' empties the HUD support quick-select menu and restores the old items. 'layers' opens a layer mode under this same name. A misspelled provider name is logged and skipped rather than guessed at.

opts.desc: Settings the providers read: relations = the {faction, faction, stance} list for the relations provider, startCash = the wallet to hand the player for the duration for the economy provider.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the sandbox opened. False if a sandbox with this name is already open, or if every provider name was unknown or failed - in that case nothing was isolated and there is nothing to finish, so check your spelling rather than carrying on.

Ess.Sandbox.finish.title: Sandbox: Finish
Ess.Sandbox.finish.desc: Closes the sandbox with this name: every part of the world it isolated is restored in order, and this sandbox's hold on saving is released. Saving only truly comes back once every OTHER sandbox and every layer mode has also finished, so if the player still cannot save afterwards, something else is still open. Finishing a name that is not open does nothing.

id.desc: The same name you passed to Sandbox: Begin.

Ess.Sandbox.isActive.title: Sandbox: Is Active
Ess.Sandbox.isActive.desc: Checks whether a sandbox with this name is currently open, so you can avoid opening it twice or show the player that the mode is running.

returns.name: active
returns.desc: True while that sandbox is open.

Ess.Save.gate.title: Save: Block Saving
Ess.Save.gate.desc:
Stops the game writing a savegame or autosave while something temporary is going on, so the player cannot save mid-cutscene or mid-sandbox and be stuck with it forever.

It works by holders: saving stays blocked while at least ONE holder is active, and resumes only when the last one is gone. Blocking twice under the same name is still a single holder, so one unblock clears it. A world reload clears every holder, so a script that dies halfway cannot leave the player unable to save forever.

sHolderKey.desc: A name only YOUR feature uses. If two features share a name they share one holder, so the first to unblock lets saving through while the other still believes it is blocked. Leaving it empty falls back to the shared name 'default', which is exactly the collision to avoid.

Ess.Save.holders.title: Save: Who Is Blocking
Ess.Save.holders.desc: The names of everything currently blocking saves. This is the diagnostic to reach for when the game has stopped saving and you want to know which feature forgot to clean up after itself.

returns.name: holders
returns.desc: A plain list of holder names, empty when saving is allowed. Print it in a Lua field to see who is at fault.

Ess.Save.isGated.title: Save: Is Blocked
Ess.Save.isGated.desc: Is saving currently suppressed by anyone. Worth checking before telling the player something was saved.

returns.name: gated
returns.desc: True while at least one holder is blocking saves.

Ess.Save.ungate.title: Save: Allow Saving
Ess.Save.ungate.desc: Removes your holder. Saving only actually resumes once the LAST holder is gone, so if something else is still blocking, this correctly leaves it blocked. Pair one of these with every Save: Block Saving.

sHolderKey.desc: The exact name you blocked with. A different name here removes nothing and leaves saving blocked - the usual cause of 'the game will not save any more'.
