Ess.SaveVar.flag.title: SaveVar: Get Saved Flag
Ess.SaveVar.flag.desc:
Reads a saved yes/no that answers NO the first time, before it has ever been set - exactly the shape of 'has the player unlocked this yet', with the fresh-install answer already built in.

It is strict: only a real saved true reads as yes. That matters here, because in Lua a 0 counts as true and would otherwise fool a plain check.

key.desc: The name of the flag in your drawer. Same prefix, same key, or you are reading a different flag entirely.

returns.name: on
returns.desc: True only if a real true was saved under that key. Anything else, including never having been set, reads as false.

Ess.SaveVar.get.title: SaveVar: Get Saved Value
Ess.SaveVar.get.desc:
Reads a value back out of your mod's drawer in the game's saved-variable file. This is the storage that survives QUITTING the game, so it is where totals, unlocks and settings belong.

The prefix on the drawer is the whole point: it is what keeps your 'xp' separate from every other mod's 'xp'. Read with a different prefix and you are looking in somebody else's drawer, which is why the prefix must match everywhere you use it. Building a fresh drawer inline is otherwise harmless - two drawers with the same prefix are the same drawer.

key.desc: The name of the value inside your drawer. Stored as prefix_key behind the scenes, so it can never collide with another mod's key of the same name.

default.desc: What to hand back the very first time, before anything has ever been saved - 0, 'none', false. Without one you get nothing back on a fresh install and any sum you feed it breaks.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The stored value, or your fallback if that key has never been written. Only numbers, text and yes/no values can live here - tables and object handles cannot be saved.

Ess.SaveVar.ns.title: SaveVar: Namespace
Ess.SaveVar.ns.desc:
Opens your mod's own private drawer in the game's saved-variable file - the only storage here that survives QUITTING the game, not just a re-run or a reload.

That file is one flat space shared by every mod, so this stamps your prefix onto every key and two mods can never tread on each other. Only numbers, text and yes/no values can be stored: no tables, no object handles.

Use it for unlocks, totals and settings. For 'my toggle keeps resetting' within a session, you want an Ess.State table instead - this one hits the disk.

prefix.desc: Your mod's name. Every key is stored as prefix_key, so pick something distinctive - two mods sharing a prefix will overwrite each other's saved values.

returns.name: sv
returns.desc: The drawer. Reading and writing are methods, so they have no nodes of their own - type them into any Lua field: sv:get('xp', 0) with a fallback for the first ever run, sv:set('xp', 5), sv:flag('unlocked') for a yes/no that defaults to no, and sv:setFlag('unlocked', true).

Ess.SaveVar.set.title: SaveVar: Set Saved Value
Ess.SaveVar.set.desc:
Writes a value into your mod's drawer, on disk. It is still there after the player quits the game entirely - that is the difference between this and an Ess.State table, which only survives your script re-running and is gone when the game closes.

Writing the same key again simply overwrites it. Keep writes sensible: this hits a file, so do not call it on every tick of a loop - save when something actually changes.

key.desc: The name to store it under, inside your prefixed drawer. Read it back with the same key and the same prefix.

value.desc: The value: a number, a piece of text in quotes, or true/false. Nothing else survives - a table or an object handle cannot be stored and will not come back.

Ess.SaveVar.setFlag.title: SaveVar: Set Saved Flag
Ess.SaveVar.setFlag.desc:
Stores a yes/no on disk, so it is still set after the player quits and comes back - the write half of 'this is unlocked now'.

It forces whatever you give it into a strict true or false before saving, so the value always reads back cleanly through SaveVar: Get Saved Flag.

key.desc: The name of the flag in your drawer.

bOn.desc: On or off. Anything truthy is stored as a plain true and anything else as a plain false, so it can never come back as a surprising value.

Ess.ScrollLog.new.title: Scroll Log: Create
Ess.ScrollLog.new.desc: Build a scrolling text box -- the translucent dark chat-style panel -- needing no .gfx asset at all. TRAP: it starts HIDDEN and only appears once you add your first message to the returned handle (handle:add("text", seconds)). Second trap: messages QUEUE. Each one holds the box for its whole display time before the next can appear, which is why the per-message default is a deliberately short 1 second -- a long duration on a burst of lines can block the box for literally minutes. Calling this again with the same name hands back the SAME box instead of stacking a second one on top.

name.desc: A name for this box. Reusing the name reuses the same box rather than making another.

x.desc: Left edge. Defaults to 20.

y.desc: Top edge. Defaults to 150.

returns.desc: The scroll-log handle -- call :add(msg, seconds), :setVisible(true/false) and :clearAll() on it. Nothing comes back if the box could not be built.
returns.name: result

Ess.Sound.ambience.title: Sound: Start Ambience Loop
Ess.Sound.ambience.desc: Start a looping background ambience bed -- distant gunfire, jungle, city hum. Unlike a sound effect it keeps playing indefinitely, until you shut it off with Sound: Stop Ambience using the same stream name.

sStreamName.desc: The ambience stream name, e.g. "emt_distant_battle_01" (the game's own distant-battle bed) or "amb_jungle".

Ess.Sound.cue.title: Sound: Play Sound
Ess.Sound.cue.desc: Play a one-shot sound effect the player hears immediately. Leave the object empty for a plain UI/HUD beep with no position in the world -- the convention the game's own menu code uses. Give it a real object handle instead and the sound plays FROM that object, so it gets quieter as you walk away: an alarm on a building, an engine on a vehicle.

uGuidOrNil.desc: Optional object for the sound to come from. Leave it empty for a plain UI sound with no world position.

sCueName.desc: The sound cue name, e.g. "ui_HUD_Objective_Complete" (objective chime), "ui_signal_ding_up" or "ui_HUD_Timer_Alert".

Ess.Sound.stop.title: Sound: Stop Sound
Ess.Sound.stop.desc: Stop a sound started with Sound: Play Sound. TRAP: you must pass the SAME object and the SAME cue name you started it with, or nothing stops. Mostly useful for looping cues -- a one-shot effect ends on its own anyway.

uGuidOrNil.desc: The same object you played it from. Leave empty if you played it as a plain UI sound.

sCueName.desc: The same cue name you played, e.g. "sfx_survival_lp".

Ess.Sound.stopAmbience.title: Sound: Stop Ambience Loop
Ess.Sound.stopAmbience.desc: Silence a looping ambience bed. Use the exact stream name you started it with, or it keeps playing.

sStreamName.desc: The same stream name you started, e.g. "emt_distant_battle_01".

Ess.Sound.volume.title: Sound: Master Volume
Ess.Sound.volume.desc: Set the game's master volume, optionally fading to it over a few seconds -- handy for ducking everything before a scripted line and bringing it back after. Real shipped scripts only ever use 0 (silent) and 1 (normal); values in between are not confirmed to work.

nFadeTime.desc: Seconds to fade over. 0 (the default) snaps to it instantly.

Ess.Squad.Tactics.dismountAndSecure.title: Squad: Dismount And Secure
Ess.Squad.Tactics.dismountAndSecure.desc: Gets a group out of whatever vehicles they are riding and sets them up defending a spot once they are out. Passengers are ejected by the vehicle itself, but a driver has to be pulled out explicitly - confirmed live that the game leaves the driver sitting there otherwise - and this does that for you. Two seconds later, once everyone is really on the ground, the whole group is given a defend order around your point: they hold that area and fight anything that comes inside it. Units already on foot just take the defend order.

targetGroup.desc: Who dismounts: a team name from Create Team, or a raw list of follower handles.

atPos.desc: The spot to hold, as {x, y, z}. The default is wherever you are standing when this runs.

radius.desc: How big the defended area is, in world units. Bigger lets them chase further from the point before coming back to it.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the dismount and defend went out. False if the group is empty or you gave no position.

Ess.Squad.Tactics.mountUp.title: Squad: Mount Up
Ess.Squad.Tactics.mountUp.desc: Loads a whole group into one vehicle in the right order: anyone tagged "driver" with Assign Role climbs in first and takes the wheel before a passenger can claim that seat, then everybody else boards as passengers. It watches until every unit is genuinely seated and then fires the "onVehicleMounted" event; if the vehicle fills up or the way in is blocked it gives up quietly after the timeout, which is a normal outcome here, not an error. Confirmed live: the driver stays commandable through their OWN character handle afterwards - order that follower to move and the vehicle drives there.

vehGuid.desc: The vehicle to load them into. The default is whatever you are sitting in right now; wire in a spawned vehicle instead if you have one.

targetGroup.desc: Who boards: a team name from Create Team, or a raw list of follower handles.

opts.desc: Optional: { passengerRole = "gunner" to put the non-drivers into turret seats instead of ordinary passenger seats, timeout = <seconds to wait for everyone to be seated, default 20> }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the boarding orders went out - not a promise everybody fits. False if no vehicle was given or the group is empty.

Ess.Squad._formationAnchorOf.title: Squad: Formation Slot Waypoint (debug)
Ess.Squad._formationAnchorOf.desc: A live-map diagnostic. While a unit is in formation it is continuously walked toward an invisible marker post that sits at its slot and moves with the leader. This hands you that post, so you can watch a unit's target position travel rather than just watching the unit - the quickest way to see why a formation is not settling into shape. Empty when this unit is not in formation right now.

returns.name: anchor
returns.desc: The invisible waypoint object marking this unit's formation slot, or nothing if it is not in a formation.

Ess.Squad._resolveGuids.skip_reason: Internal helper that turns a team name into a list of units; the Team Members node already does this for you.

Ess.Squad.assignRole.title: Squad: Assign Role
Ess.Squad.assignRole.desc: Tags one follower with a job, like "driver" or "heavy". The tag is just a label you pick - nothing about the unit changes by itself. Other nodes read it: Mount Up puts whoever is tagged "driver" into the driver's seat first, before anybody else can claim it, and everyone else boards as passengers.

roleType.desc: Any word you like - "heavy", "medic", "pointman". "driver" is the one with built-in meaning, because Mount Up looks for it.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the tag was stored. False only if no unit was given.

Ess.Squad.cancelQueue.title: Squad: Cancel Order Sequence
Ess.Squad.cancelQueue.desc: Stops a running order sequence part-way through and puts the group straight back to following you, which is the safe fallback. Your onCancel code runs if you gave any. A no-op if that group has no sequence running.

targetGroup.desc: Whose sequence to stop: the same team name (or the same list of units) you started it with.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if a sequence was running and has now been cancelled. False if there was nothing to cancel.

Ess.Squad.clearFormation.title: Squad: Clear Formation
Ess.Squad.clearFormation.desc: Stops holding formation. Everybody stays exactly where they are standing - they do NOT go back to following you on their own, because a formation is usually cleared in order to hand the group a different order next. If you want them back at your side, follow this with Order Team set to "follow".

targetGroup.desc: Whose formation to stop: the same team name (or list of units) you set it on.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the group was found and its formation slots were stopped. False if the group is empty.

Ess.Squad.createTeam.title: Squad: Create Team
Ess.Squad.createTeam.desc: Names a group of your followers so you can command them separately - 'alpha' takes the hill while the rest of your roster keeps guarding the truck. Only real followers can be on a team: anyone in the list who is not on your roster is quietly dropped. Calling it again with the same name replaces that team's membership rather than adding to it. The name "__all__" is reserved by the system and refused.

teamName.desc: What to call this team. You use this same name in every other Squad node.

guids.desc: The members, as a list of follower handles. The default puts your entire roster on the team; for a smaller team build a list like { unitA, unitB }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the team was defined. False only if you gave no name, or used the reserved name "__all__".

Ess.Squad.on.title: Squad: On Event
Ess.Squad.on.desc: Runs your own code when something happens to a squad. It is the very same event system as the Followers On Event node - Squad shares one bus rather than keeping a second. On top of "onRecruit" / "onDismiss" / "onFollowerDown", squad work fires "onStepComplete" (the units, which step number, which behaviour) each time an order sequence advances, "onQueueComplete" (the units) when a whole sequence finishes, and "onVehicleMounted" (the vehicle, the units) once everybody is seated after Mount Up.

eventName.desc: Which event to listen for: "onStepComplete", "onQueueComplete", "onVehicleMounted", "onRecruit", "onDismiss" or "onFollowerDown".

fn.default: function(guids) Ess.Log("squad event for " .. tostring(#guids) .. " units") end
fn.desc: Your code, run each time that event fires. It receives whatever that event sends - see the event list above for what each one passes.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to stop listening.

Ess.Squad.orderTeam.title: Squad: Order Team
Ess.Squad.orderTeam.desc: Gives one command to a single team and leaves the REST of your roster completely alone - your other followers carry on doing exactly what they were already doing. Two teams can be running different orders at the same time without clearing each other's destination markers or yanking each other back to following. Same 11 behaviours and same options as Order Everyone, and the same hand-back: an attack ends when its target dies, a move or one-shot patrol ends on arrival, and only that team then returns to following you. An empty or unknown team is a safe no-op.

teamName.desc: Which team to command, by the name you gave Create Team.

opts.desc: The details for that order: { at = {x,y,z} for move/face/defend, points = { {x,y,z}, ... } for patrol, loop = false for a one-shot patrol, target = <enemy handle> for attack or <vehicle handle> for enter, radius for defend, role = "driver" / "passenger" / "gunner" for enter, action for animate, speed, priority }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out. False if that team currently has nobody alive on it.

Ess.Squad.queue.title: Squad: Run Order Sequence
Ess.Squad.queue.desc: Runs a list of orders one after another, waiting for each one to actually finish before starting the next: board the truck, drive to the drop point, get out and defend. Unlike a single order, the group does NOT peel off back to following you between steps. A step is finished when a move or one-shot patrol arrives, when an attack's target dies, or when an "enter" step has every unit seated in some vehicle. Anything else (hold, defend, guard, a looping patrol) has no natural finish, so that step simply runs until its time is up and the queue moves on. Every step gets a timeout regardless - 30 seconds unless you set one - so a single stuck unit or blocked path can never freeze the sequence forever. Starting a new sequence for the same group replaces the one already running.

targetGroup.desc: Who runs the sequence: a team name from Create Team. A raw list of follower handles also works here if you would rather not name a team.

steps.default: { { behavior = "move", opts = { at = { Ess.Object.pos(Ess.Player.character(0)) } }, timeout = 30 }, { behavior = "hold", timeout = 10 } }
steps.desc: The steps, in order. Each one is { behavior = <an order name>, opts = { <that order's details> }, timeout = <seconds before giving up on this step, default 30> }. The example walks the group to where you are standing, then has them stand their ground for 10 seconds.

queueOpts.desc: Optional: { onComplete = function() ... end, onCancel = function() ... end } - your own code for when the whole sequence finishes, or when it gets cancelled.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the sequence started. False if you gave no steps, or the group has nobody in it.

Ess.Squad.roleOf.title: Squad: Role Of Unit
Ess.Squad.roleOf.desc: Reads back the job tag you gave a unit with Assign Role. Handy for branching your script on who is the driver, or for showing roles in your own UI.

returns.name: roleType
returns.desc: The role string you assigned, or nothing if this unit was never given one.

Ess.Squad.setFormation.title: Squad: Set Formation
Ess.Squad.setFormation.desc: Makes a group walk in a shape around a leader and keep holding it as the leader moves - each unit is steered to its own slot, recomputed twice a second. This is visual flavour rather than precision tactics, and it looks great behind you. Being in formation takes the units off ordinary following, so anything else that was steering them is stopped first to stop the two fighting over the same unit. They hold the shape until you clear it or give them a different order.

targetGroup.desc: Who forms up: a team name from Create Team, or a raw list of follower handles.

formationType.desc: "wedge" (a V opening forward, the default), "column" (single file directly behind the leader), "line" (a flat wall just behind them) or "diamond" (a ring all the way around the leader).

opts.desc: Optional: { leader = <who they form up on, defaults to you>, spacing = <how far apart the slots sit, default 3> }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the formation started. False if the group is empty, or no leader could be found.

Ess.Squad.team.title: Squad: Team Members
Ess.Squad.team.desc: Hands you a team's members as they stand right now. It is checked live every time you read it, so anyone killed or dismissed since you built the team is filtered out - this can never give you a unit that is no longer yours. An unknown team name gives an empty list rather than an error.

teamName.desc: The team to read, by the name you gave Create Team.

returns.name: guids
returns.desc: The team's currently-alive members, in the order you listed them. Empty if the team is unknown or everyone on it is gone.

Ess.Squad.teamOf.title: Squad: Team Of Unit
Ess.Squad.teamOf.desc: Tells you which team a unit was last put on. This is a convenience lookup, not the authority: somebody who has since been dismissed still shows their old team name here. When you need the truth about who is currently on a team, read Team Members instead.

returns.name: teamName
returns.desc: The team name they were last assigned to, or nothing if they were never put on one.

Ess.Squad.teams.title: Squad: All Team Names
Ess.Squad.teams.desc: Lists every team name you have created, sorted alphabetically so the order is stable. Use it to discover what teams exist. It does not check whether a team still has anybody alive on it, so pair it with the Team Members node when that matters.

returns.name: names
returns.desc: A list of team name strings, sorted A to Z. Empty if you have not created any teams.

Ess.State.title: Remembered Values
Ess.State.desc: Gives you a table that survives your script being run again. A mod script re-runs from the top on every keypress and every level reload, so ordinary variables reset every single time - anything you put in this table does not. It also merges your defaults field by field, so adding a new default later still takes effect on a table that already exists. The obvious one-line version of this quietly drops newly added fields, which is the real bug this exists to fix.

name.desc: A name for your mod's storage. Pick one and keep using it - the same name always gives you back the same table.

defaults.desc: The starting fields, e.g. { score = 0, on = false }. Only fields that are missing get filled in, so values you already changed are never overwritten.

returns.name: state
returns.desc: Your table. Read and write fields on it (state.score = state.score + 1) and they are still there next run.

Ess.Str.capitalize.title: Text: Capitalize
Ess.Str.capitalize.desc: Upper-cases the very first letter and leaves everything else exactly as it was - for turning a raw word into the start of a sentence.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The text with its first letter in upper case.

Ess.Str.contains.title: Text: Contains
Ess.Str.contains.desc: Is this shorter piece of text found anywhere inside the longer one? The search is plain literal text, NOT a Lua pattern - so a "." really does mean a full stop, which is the mistake people usually make with Lua's own string.find.

returns.name: yes
returns.desc: True if it's in there somewhere.

Ess.Str.count.title: Text: Count Occurrences
Ess.Str.count.desc: How many times a piece of text shows up inside another. Counted as plain literal text (not a Lua pattern), and overlaps don't double-count. Looking for an empty piece of text gives 0.

returns.name: count
returns.desc: How many times it appears.

Ess.Str.endsWith.title: Text: Ends With
Ess.Str.endsWith.desc: Does this text finish with that piece of text? Useful for checking file extensions or name suffixes. Matched as plain literal text, not as a Lua pattern. An empty suffix always counts as a match.

returns.name: yes
returns.desc: True if the text ends with that suffix.

Ess.Str.join.title: Text: Join
Ess.Str.join.desc: Glues a list of pieces back into one line of text with a separator between them - the opposite of Text: Split. Handy for turning a list of names into something you can print.

list.desc: The list of pieces to glue together.

sep.desc: What to put between pieces. Empty glues them with nothing between; ", " gives a readable list.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The joined-up text.

Ess.Str.lines.title: Text: Split Into Lines
Ess.Str.lines.desc: Breaks a block of text into a list of lines, one entry per line. A stray carriage return before a newline is dropped, so text written on Windows works too, and a single trailing newline won't add a phantom empty line at the end.

s.desc: The block of text to break up.

returns.name: lines
returns.desc: A numbered list of lines, in order.

Ess.Str.padLeft.title: Text: Pad Left
Ess.Str.padLeft.desc: Adds padding to the LEFT of some text until it reaches a given width, so numbers line up in a right-aligned HUD column. Pass "0" as the padding character to zero-pad a number. Text that's already long enough comes back untouched.

width.desc: How many characters wide the result should be.

ch.desc: The character to pad with. Only the first character is used.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The padded text.

Ess.Str.padRight.title: Text: Pad Right
Ess.Str.padRight.desc: Adds padding to the RIGHT of some text until it reaches a given width, so labels line up in a left-aligned column. Text that's already long enough comes back untouched.

width.desc: How many characters wide the result should be.

ch.desc: The character to pad with. Only the first character is used.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The padded text.

Ess.Str.split.title: Text: Split
Ess.Str.split.desc: Chops text into a list of pieces at every separator - the way to read a comma-separated config line or a name like "squad_alpha_2". The separator is plain literal text, not a Lua pattern: this is the classic trap, because splitting on "." with Lua's own tools splits on EVERY character instead. An empty separator gives you one entry per character, and a separator that never appears just gives the whole text as a single piece.

sep.desc: What to split on. Leave as "," for a comma list; "" splits into single characters.

returns.name: pieces
returns.desc: A numbered list of the pieces, in order.

Ess.Str.startsWith.title: Text: Starts With
Ess.Str.startsWith.desc: Does this text begin with that piece of text? Great for spotting names by prefix, like every object whose name starts with "M2_". Matched as plain literal text, not as a Lua pattern.

returns.name: yes
returns.desc: True if the text starts with that prefix.

Ess.Str.title.title: Text: Title Case
Ess.Str.title.desc: Capitalizes The First Letter Of Every Word - for turning an internal name into a readable label on screen.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The text with every word capitalized.

Ess.Str.trim.title: Text: Trim
Ess.Str.trim.desc: Strips spaces, tabs and stray newlines off both ends of some text - tidy up a line someone typed before you compare it to anything.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The text with the outside whitespace removed.

Ess.Str.truncate.title: Text: Truncate
Ess.Str.truncate.desc: Clips text down to a maximum length and tacks "..." on the end if anything was cut off - so an over-long mission or player name can't blow out your HUD panel. Text already short enough is returned unchanged.

n.desc: The most characters allowed, including the ... .

ellipsis.desc: What to stick on the end when text was cut off.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The clipped text.

Ess.Support.airstrike.title: Support: Airstrike Flyby
Ess.Support.airstrike.desc: Sends a support aircraft screaming in over the spot on a single pass, coming in from one side and carrying on past. The pass itself is what you are staging - what the aircraft shoots on the way through is down to the vehicle template, and this node has no owner setting, so kills from it are not credited to a faction. For guaranteed explosions on the ground, fire the Artillery node at the same point alongside it, which is exactly what the game's own one-tap airstrike does.

x.desc: East/west world coordinate the aircraft passes over.

y.desc: Ground height at the spot. The altitude option is measured up from this, so getting it badly wrong can fly the aircraft underground or absurdly high.

z.desc: North/south world coordinate the aircraft passes over.

opts.desc: vehicle = which aircraft makes the pass ('Support Vehicle (Autogunship)'). altitude = height above the spot (120) - drop it for a low, loud pass. speed = how fast it travels (55).

Ess.Support.artillery.title: Support: Artillery Barrage
Ess.Support.artillery.desc: Rains a barrage of shells over an area - the workhorse 'punish this position' call-in. The rounds land scattered around the point a fraction of a second apart rather than all at once, so it walks in the way a real barrage does and gives anyone in the area a moment to react.

x.desc: East/west world coordinate of the centre of the barrage.

y.desc: Ground height at the centre. Shells are spawned high above this.

z.desc: North/south world coordinate of the centre.

opts.desc: count = how many shells (5). radius = how far from the centre they scatter (14) - widen it to threaten an area, tighten it to flatten one building. stagger = seconds between each shell (0.35). ammo and owner are passed down to every shell, so 'Artillery Shell' plus owner = 'China' gives China the credit for the whole barrage.

Ess.Support.bombingrun.title: Support: Bombing Run
Ess.Support.bombingrun.desc: A plane runs in and walks a stick of bombs across the target. The bombs are released from wherever the plane actually is at the moment each one drops, a fraction of a second apart, so they land in a LINE along its flight path rather than all on the one point - aim the run at the near end of what you want flattened, not the middle.

x.desc: East/west world coordinate the plane runs in on.

y.desc: Ground height at the target. The altitude option is measured up from this.

z.desc: North/south world coordinate the plane runs in on.

opts.desc: vehicle = the plane ('Support Vehicle (A10)'). ammo = what it drops ('Bomb'). count = how many bombs in the stick (3) - more makes a longer line, not a bigger crater. altitude = height above the target (150). speed = how fast it flies (160), which also stretches or tightens the spacing of the line. owner = a faction NAME so the kills are credited to them.

Ess.Support.gunship.title: Support: Gunship Flight
Ess.Support.gunship.desc: Sends a flight of attack helicopters over the area, fanned out and arriving one after another rather than in a single clump - the set-piece 'they called in air support' moment. Like the airstrike node this stages the flyby; what the helicopters engage on the way through is the template's own behaviour.

x.desc: East/west world coordinate the flight passes over.

y.desc: Ground height at the spot. The altitude option is measured up from this.

z.desc: North/south world coordinate the flight passes over.

opts.desc: template = which helicopter to fly ('AH1Z'). count = how many (3). stagger = seconds between each one arriving (1.6). spread = how far apart they fan out (45). altitude = height above the spot (55, much lower than the jet nodes). speed = how fast they travel (45).

Ess.Support.reinforce.title: Support: Reinforcements
Ess.Support.reinforce.desc: Brings a squad of units in to a spot, either dropped from a helicopter, parachuted in behind a plane pass, or simply appearing on the ground. They arrive as ordinary spawned units and will do nothing in particular on their own - follow this with an AI Orders: Command node to give them something to do, and file them with Set Group first if you want to command them as one.

x.desc: East/west world coordinate where they arrive. They are spaced out in rows around this point so they do not land on top of each other.

y.desc: Ground height where they arrive. Too low buries them, so use a real ground reading rather than a guess.

z.desc: North/south world coordinate where they arrive.

opts.desc: units = the list of templates to bring in; leave it out or empty and NOBODY arrives, though a paradrop plane still flies over, which is the confusing part. Confirmed real infantry templates include 'Allied Soldier', 'Allied Officer', 'Allied Heavy (Light MG)', 'Allied Heavy (AA)' and 'Allied Boss'. deliver = 'copter' for a helicopter drop, 'paradrop' for a plane pass with the units appearing a second or two later, or leave it out entirely and they simply appear on the ground. faction = who the delivery helicopter belongs to ('Allied', 'China', 'Guerilla', 'OC', 'Pirate', 'VZ'), used by the copter delivery only. A blank template name is caught for you because it would otherwise crash the game outright, but the names still have to be ones this level actually knows.

Ess.Support.shell.title: Support: Single Shell
Ess.Support.shell.desc: Drops one artillery shell onto a spot - the single round every other call-in node here is built from. It appears high above the point and falls with an impact fuse, so expect about a second between calling it and the explosion. Nothing to clean up afterwards: the round is a one-shot the engine disposes of itself.

x.desc: East/west world coordinate of the target spot. Normally wired in from a position node rather than typed.

y.desc: Ground height at the target spot. The shell is spawned well above this and falls onto it.

z.desc: North/south world coordinate of the target spot.

opts.desc: ammo = which round to drop; confirmed real ones are 'Gunship Shell', 'Artillery Shell', 'Bomb', 'Cluster Bomb Projectile' and 'Cruise Missile Projectile'. dropHeight = how far above the point it starts (220) - lower it for a shorter delay before impact. owner = a faction NAME such as 'China' or 'Allied' so the game credits the damage and kills to them; leave it out and nobody is blamed for it.

Ess.Table.compact.title: Table: Compact
Ess.Table.compact.desc: Rebuilds a list so its numbered entries run 1, 2, 3 with no gaps. Fixes a real, nasty bug: setting an entry to nil to "remove" it leaves a HOLE, and Lua's # length is undefined on a holed list, which silently drops or duplicates entries later on. This CHANGES the list you give it. In new code prefer table.remove, which never leaves a hole; this is for cleaning up one that already happened. Named keys are left alone.

t.desc: The list with gaps in it.

returns.name: t
returns.desc: The same table, now packed densely from 1 upward.

Ess.Table.contains.title: Table: Contains Value
Ess.Table.contains.desc: Is this value anywhere in the table? Checks every entry, numbered and named alike. Values are compared exactly, so two separate tables with the same contents do NOT count as equal.

t.desc: The table to search.

val.desc: The value to look for. Written as Lua, so put quotes around text; or wire in a value from another node.

returns.name: found
returns.desc: True if the value is in the table.

Ess.Table.copy.title: Table: Copy
Ess.Table.copy.desc: Makes a separate copy of a table so that editing one doesn't quietly change the other. It's a SHALLOW copy: any tables sitting inside are still shared between the two, not cloned.

t.default: { hp = 100, name = "Bravo" }
t.desc: The table to copy.

returns.name: copy
returns.desc: A new table with the same entries.

Ess.Table.count.title: Table: Count
Ess.Table.count.desc: How many entries a table holds in total, named keys included. Use this rather than Lua's # length, which only ever sees the numbered part and silently ignores named keys.

t.default: { hp = 100, name = "Bravo" }
t.desc: The table to count.

returns.name: count
returns.desc: Total number of entries.

Ess.Table.filter.skip_reason: takes a test function; a beginner has nothing sensible to type in a text field

Ess.Table.find.skip_reason: takes a test function; a beginner has nothing sensible to type in a text field

Ess.Table.indexOf.title: Table: Index Of
Ess.Table.indexOf.desc: The position (1, 2, 3...) of the first entry equal to this value, or nothing if it isn't there. Only looks at the numbered part of the table, so named keys are ignored.

t.desc: The list to search.

val.desc: The value to look for. Written as Lua, so put quotes around text; or wire in a value from another node.

returns.name: index
returns.desc: The 1-based position, or nothing if the value isn't in the list.

Ess.Table.isEmpty.title: Table: Is Empty
Ess.Table.isEmpty.desc: True if the table has nothing in it at all - no numbered entries and no named ones either.

t.desc: The table to test.

returns.name: empty
returns.desc: True when the table has no entries.

Ess.Table.keys.title: Table: Keys
Ess.Table.keys.desc: Gives you all of a table's key names as a plain numbered list, so you can walk through them or count them.

t.default: { hp = 100, name = "Bravo" }
t.desc: The table to read the keys from.

returns.name: keys
returns.desc: A numbered list of the table's keys (order is not guaranteed).

Ess.Table.map.skip_reason: takes a transform function; a beginner has nothing sensible to type in a text field

Ess.Table.merge.title: Table: Merge
Ess.Table.merge.desc: Copies every entry from src onto dst, overwriting where the two clash - the usual way to apply overrides on top of default settings. This CHANGES dst in place and hands it back to you, so pass a copy if you need the original kept.

dst.desc: The table being changed - it receives the entries.

src.desc: The table to copy entries from. Its values win any clash.

returns.name: dst
returns.desc: The same dst table, now with src's entries merged in.

Ess.Table.reduce.skip_reason: takes a fold function; no sensible node shape

Ess.Table.reverse.title: Table: Reverse
Ess.Table.reverse.desc: Gives back a new list with the order flipped back to front. The original list is left alone.

t.desc: The list to flip.

returns.name: reversed
returns.desc: A new list in the opposite order.

Ess.Table.slice.title: Table: Slice
Ess.Table.slice.desc: Pulls out a new list containing just entries i through j, counting from 1 and including both ends. Leave the numbers off to take the whole list; numbers past the ends are pulled back in rather than causing an error.

t.desc: The list to take a piece of.

i.desc: First entry to take, counting from 1. Defaults to the start.

j.desc: Last entry to take (included). Defaults to the end.

returns.name: slice
returns.desc: A new list holding just that stretch of entries.

Ess.Table.values.title: Table: Values
Ess.Table.values.desc: Gives you all of a table's values as a plain numbered list, throwing the keys away - handy when you only care about the contents.

t.default: { hp = 100, name = "Bravo" }
t.desc: The table to read the values from.

returns.name: values
returns.desc: A numbered list of the table's values (order is not guaranteed).

Ess.TextConsole.close.title: Text Console: Close
Ess.TextConsole.close.desc: Close the typing console and give the player back control of their character if it was locked. Safe to call even when nothing is open.

Ess.TextConsole.isOpen.title: Text Console: Is Open
Ess.TextConsole.isOpen.desc: Check whether the typing console is currently open and eating keystrokes. Use it to stop your own key handler from reacting to letters the player is trying to type.

returns.desc: True while the console is open.
returns.name: ok

Ess.TextConsole.open.title: Text Console: Open
Ess.TextConsole.open.desc: Open a yellow prompt line at the top-left of the screen for the player to type into -- no .gfx asset needed, just a plain text widget. Unlike UI: Text Prompt this is a REPL: Enter runs your onSubmit and clears the line but leaves the console OPEN, and only Escape closes it. By default it freezes the player's movement and actions while typing; set lockPlayer = false for a chat box that leaves the game running underneath.

opts.default: { prompt = "SAY: ", max = 200, lockPlayer = true, onSubmit = function(sText) Ess.Hud.banner(sText) end }
opts.desc: Settings table: prompt (text before the caret, default "> "), text (what it starts with), max (character limit, default 200), lockPlayer (default true), onSubmit(text), onCancel(), onChange(text).

Ess.Time.clock.title: Time: Clock
Ess.Time.clock.desc:
A self-advancing stopwatch for 'how long since the last tick', which is what you need to make movement or drain rates run at the same speed no matter how often your loop ticks.

Each reading gives the seconds since the PREVIOUS reading and is capped, so a pause or a stutter cannot hand you a huge jump that flings something across the map.

maxDelta.desc: The cap, in seconds. Any longer gap - a pause, a loading hitch - is reported as this instead of the real time. Leaving it empty means 0.25.

returns.name: clock
returns.desc: The clock. Reading it is a method, so there is no node for it - type clock:delta() into a Lua field inside your loop's action. Each call resets the measurement, so read it ONCE per tick and reuse the number.

Ess.Time.cooldown.title: Time: Cooldown
Ess.Time.cooldown.desc:
Builds a reusable 'am I allowed to do this again yet' checker, so you do not hand-roll a stamp, a comparison and a reset every time.

The FIRST check is always allowed - a freshly made cooldown is ready immediately, not blocked as though it had just been used. Asking while it is still cooling returns no and does NOT push the window back, so hammering the key cannot keep it locked forever.

Keep the checker somewhere that survives your script re-running, or every key press builds a brand new one that is ready again.

seconds.desc: How long the lockout lasts. Leaving it empty means one second.

returns.name: ready
returns.desc: The checker. Call it in a Lua field - ready() gives true and immediately starts the next window, or false if you must wait. Store it in an Ess.State table; a new one from a re-run is always ready again.

Ess.Time.elapsed.title: Time: Elapsed
Ess.Time.elapsed.desc:
How many seconds since that stamp was marked.

Reading it does NOT advance or reset anything, so it is safe to check on every tick and always get the true answer - only Time: Re-Mark moves the start. That is what makes 'has ten seconds passed yet' reliable here.

uStamp.desc: The stamp to measure from, wired in from a Time: Mark Now node.

returns.name: seconds
returns.desc: Seconds since the mark, as a decimal. Comes back as 0 if the stamp is missing - so a timer that reads 0 forever usually means nothing is wired in.

Ess.Time.format.title: Time: Format
Ess.Time.format.desc: Turns a raw number of seconds into a tidy display string, so a HUD stopwatch or countdown does not read as 87.43219. Feed it a Time: Elapsed value.

nSeconds.desc: The number of seconds to format, usually wired from Time: Elapsed.

bUseTenths.desc: Show tenths of a second as well - worth it for a tense countdown, distracting on a long timer.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The display string. Comes back empty if the engine's formatter is unavailable, so do not assume you always have text.

Ess.Time.mainStamp.title: Time: Mark Now (Game Clock)
Ess.Time.mainStamp.desc:
The same as Time: Mark Now, but on the GAME clock: it freezes while the game is paused and slows down with Time: Set Scale.

Pick this one for gameplay cooldowns that should stop counting while the player is in a menu, and the real-world one for UI timing that should not.

returns.name: stamp
returns.desc: An opaque handle to feed to Time: Elapsed or Time: Re-Mark.

Ess.Time.mark.title: Time: Re-Mark
Ess.Time.mark.desc: Resets a stamp you already have back to now - restarting that stopwatch without making a new one. This is how a repeating cooldown works: check elapsed, act, re-mark.

uStamp.desc: The stamp to reset, wired in from a Time: Mark Now node. Empty does nothing.

Ess.Time.restoreScale.title: Time: Restore Scale
Ess.Time.restoreScale.desc: Puts the world back to normal speed - the same as setting the scale to 1, under the name you will actually look for. Every slow-motion effect needs one of these, and it is worth running once at the start of a script too, in case a previous run died before it could clean up.

Ess.Time.scale.title: Time: Set Scale
Ess.Time.scale.desc:
Changes how fast the game world runs - slow motion for an explosion or a finishing move.

IT STAYS. This is a global setting with no timer on it: set 0.2 and the whole game is five times slower until something sets it back. Always pair it with Time: Restore Scale, and be careful in a script that can crash halfway through and leave the player stuck in slow motion.

n.desc: Speed multiplier: 1 is normal, 0.2 is five times slower, above 1 is faster. Very small values make the game feel frozen.

Ess.Time.since.title: Time: Since
Ess.Time.since.desc: Exactly the same as Time: Elapsed, under a name that reads better in some graphs ('since I started this'). Same behaviour, same numbers - pick whichever makes your graph clearer.

returns.name: seconds
returns.desc: Seconds since the mark, or 0 if the stamp is missing.

Ess.Time.stamp.title: Time: Mark Now (Real Clock)
Ess.Time.stamp.desc:
Marks this instant and hands you a stamp to measure from later - the start of a stopwatch. Ask Time: Elapsed how long it has been.

This is the REAL-WORLD clock: it keeps counting through pauses, menus and slow-motion. Use it for UI, cooldowns on your own tools, and anything that should not freeze with the game.

Remember the stamp somewhere that survives - in a script that re-runs on every key press, a plain local is gone by the next press, so put it in an Ess.State table.

returns.name: stamp
returns.desc: An opaque handle, not a number - you cannot subtract it or print it, only feed it to Time: Elapsed or Time: Re-Mark.

Ess.Track.add.title: Track: Track Custom Cleanup
Ess.Track.add.desc:
The escape hatch: register any cleanup of your own to be run when the tracker closes, for something Ess has no dedicated node for - resetting a variable, restoring time scale, putting a setting back.

Wire in the SAME tracker the rest of your feature registers into, or this lands in a fresh bin that never gets closed.

closeFn.desc: A no-argument action to run at teardown. Anything that is not actually a function is silently ignored - it is handed straight back to you but never registered, so nothing will run.

returns.name: closeFn
returns.desc: The same function back, unchanged, so it can be chained onward.

Ess.Track.any.title: Track: Track Anything
Ess.Track.any.desc:
The one to reach for. Hand it ANY of the things Ess gives you to turn something off and it will be torn down with the rest when the tracker closes - a stop from an On: node, a marker handle, a loop's name, or an object that knows how to cancel itself.

That is the whole point: you no longer have to remember which namespace spells cleanup which way. The typed nodes below are still better when you know exactly what you are holding, but this is the one that always works.

Wire in the SAME tracker every node registers into. The default builds a fresh empty one right here, which is valid Lua but puts this in a bin nobody will ever close.

x.desc: The thing to tear down later, wired in from whatever made it. A loop's name must be typed WITH quotes ('MyMod.tick') - without them it reads as a variable and tracks nothing. Anything empty is quietly ignored.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: The same thing back, unchanged, so you can carry on using it in the very next node instead of splitting into two steps.

Ess.Track.closeAll.title: Track: Close Everything
Ess.Track.closeAll.desc:
The payoff. Ends everything this tracker collected, in one action - every hook released, every spawned object removed, every marker cleared.

It works backwards, newest first, because things you made later usually depend on things you made earlier and tearing down in that order is what avoids surprises. Afterwards the tracker empties itself: safe to call twice, and safe to keep using, since anything registered later starts a fresh batch.

This MUST be the same tracker the things were registered into. The default builds a brand new empty one, which cheerfully succeeds and tears down absolutely nothing - if your cleanup 'does not work', check that first.

Ess.Track.contextAction.title: Track: Add Context Action And Track
Ess.Track.contextAction.desc:
The third that DOES as well as tracks: it attaches a context action - the on-screen 'press this to use it' prompt on an object - and registers its removal for teardown, so the prompt cannot linger on an object after your feature is gone.

Like the disposer, removal uses the SAME object handle you passed in, not a separate one.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.

uGuid.desc: The object to put the prompt on, wired in. Empty registers nothing.

sLabelOrKey.desc: The label shown to the player, or a localisation key.

....desc: Any further arguments the engine's context-action call wants, typed as raw Lua and separated by commas. Real examples vary a lot - anywhere from none to half a dozen - so only the object and label above are a fixed shape. Leave empty if you are unsure.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The same object handle back, so it can be chained onward.

Ess.Track.disposer.title: Track: Add To Disposer And Track
Ess.Track.disposer.desc:
Another that DOES as well as tracks: it hands an object to the engine's disposer under a category now, and registers the matching removal for teardown.

Worth knowing: unlike a hook or a marker, the removal here takes the SAME object handle you passed in rather than some separate handle the engine gives back - so there is nothing extra to hold on to.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.

uGuid.desc: The object to add, wired in. Empty registers nothing.

sCategory.desc: The disposer category to file it under - a plain piece of text you choose.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The same object handle back, so it can be chained onward.

Ess.Track.event.title: Track: Track Event Hook
Ess.Track.event.desc:
Registers an engine hook you ALREADY created so it gets deleted at teardown. Hooks are never cleaned up for you, and a hook left behind keeps firing into a feature that no longer exists.

Shortcut: the Event: Hook Engine Event node has its own tracker input that does exactly this in one step - use that instead unless you are tracking a hook made some other way.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.

handle.desc: The handle the hook handed back when it was created. An empty one is quietly ignored, which means nothing gets cleaned up.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The same handle back, so you can keep using it to unhook early if you want to.

Ess.Track.guid.title: Track: Track Spawned Object
Ess.Track.guid.desc:
Registers something you SPAWNED so it is removed from the world at teardown - the fix for a test script that leaves a field of abandoned vehicles behind after a dozen runs.

CAREFUL: this DELETES the object when the tracker closes. Only ever track things your own mod created. Tracking the player's car, or an NPC that belongs to a mission, means your cleanup destroys it.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.

uGuid.desc: The handle of the object you spawned, wired in from the node that spawned it. Left empty this registers nothing at all - which is safer than the alternative, so it is deliberately not filled in for you.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The same object handle back, so you can spawn, track and use it in one chain.

Ess.Track.marker.title: Track: Track Raw Marker
Ess.Track.marker.desc:
Registers a RAW engine marker handle so it is removed at teardown.

This is for the low-level marker layer only. A handle from Mark: Object or Mark: Zone is NOT one of these - it is a bundle of several surfaces plus possibly an anchor prop, and it needs Mark: Clear. Put those through Track: Track Anything instead, which routes them correctly. Passing one here fails quietly and your markers stay on screen.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.

handle.desc: A handle from a raw marker call. If it came from a Mark: node, use Track: Track Anything instead.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The same handle back, unchanged.

Ess.Track.new.title: Track: New Tracker
Ess.Track.new.desc:
One bin for everything a feature creates, so switching the feature off is a single action instead of a checklist you will get wrong.

WHY IT EXISTS: on this engine every Add has a matching Remove and there is no 'remove everything I made' for ANY of them - spawned objects, markers, event hooks, radar and PDA blips all leak if you forget one. A tracker is that missing function.

Its registrars are methods, so they have no nodes of their own - type them into any Lua field: tracker:guid(u) for a spawned object, tracker:marker(h), tracker:event(h), tracker:any(x) for anything at all, then tracker:closeAll() to tear the lot down. You can also wire the tracker straight into the Event: Hook node's tracker input.

returns.name: tracker
returns.desc: The bin. tracker:closeAll() runs every teardown in reverse order - newest first, which is the order that does not surprise - then empties itself. Safe to call twice, and safe to keep using afterwards: anything added later is a fresh batch.

Ess.Track.pda.title: Track: Track PDA Blip
Ess.Track.pda.desc:
Registers a PDA map blip you already added so it is removed at teardown. Like the radar one, it is tracked by the NAME you registered it under rather than a handle, and the name has to match exactly or nothing is removed.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.

sName.desc: The exact name the blip was added under - text, not a handle.

returns.name: sName
returns.desc: The same name back, so it can be passed straight on.

Ess.Track.qualityRef.title: Track: Add Quality And Track
Ess.Track.qualityRef.desc:
Different from most of the nodes here: this one DOES the thing as well as tracking it. It applies an engine quality to an object now, and registers the matching removal for teardown, so a temporary property cannot outlive the feature that applied it.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one, or the quality is never taken off again.

uGuid.desc: The object to apply the quality to, wired in. Empty simply fails quietly and registers nothing.

nQuality.desc: The engine's numeric id for the quality. These are engine constants, so look the right number up rather than guessing - a wrong one fails silently rather than erroring.

returns.name: ref
returns.desc: The reference the engine handed back, or nothing if it did not take. Nothing coming back means the quality was never applied, so check that before wondering why the effect is missing.

Ess.Track.radar.title: Track: Track Radar Objective
Ess.Track.radar.desc:
Registers a radar objective you already added so it is removed at teardown. Unlike most things here you track it by the NAME you registered it under, not by a handle - that is what the engine's remove call wants.

The name must match exactly or the teardown silently removes nothing and the blip stays on the radar for the rest of the session.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.

sName.desc: The exact name the objective was added under. This is text, not a handle, and a typo here is a leak you will not notice until the blips pile up.

returns.name: sName
returns.desc: The same name back, so it can be passed straight on.

Ess.Triggers.arm.title: Triggers: Arm
Ess.Triggers.arm.desc: Waits for something to happen in the world and then runs your code - the player walking into an area, a target dying, a building dropping below half health, an area being cleared out, or simply a timer. This is what turns a static set of spawns into an encounter that reacts. Most conditions work by quietly checking a few times a second and will keep checking forever until they fire, so hand it a tracker or hold on to the cancel handle.

spec.desc: What to wait for. Leave blank to fire immediately. {once = 5} fires once after 5 seconds. {recurring = 10, limit = 3, delay = 2} fires every 10 seconds, at most 3 times, starting after 2. {proximity = 25, at = {x,y,z}} fires when the player gets within 25 of that spot. {onDestroy = 'SomePlacementName'} fires when that named thing in the level dies - if the name is not found it is logged and this never fires. {onDestroy = {at = {x,y,z}, radius = 45, kind = ...}} finds the nearest matching object in the area and then watches THAT one die, re-checking every second until something is actually there, which is how you arm on a target that has not spawned yet. {onHealthBelow = {target = <handle>, pct = 50}} fires at half health, measured against the health it had when you armed this, not its maximum - arm it on an already-damaged target and the bar you are measuring from is that damaged value. {onCleared = {at = {x,y,z}, radius = 45, kind = ..., faction = ...}} fires when a populated area becomes empty, and it has to SEE something there first, so arming it over an already-empty patch waits forever.

onFire.desc: Your code, run once the condition is met. A recurring trigger runs it again on every tick.

tracker.desc: Optional but strongly recommended. Hand it an Ess.Track and every timer this schedules gets cleaned up with the rest of your setup, instead of a poll quietly running for the rest of the session.

returns.name: cancel
returns.desc: A stop handle. Keep it and feed it to an Ess.stop node to disarm the trigger, even if its condition is met later. Without it (and without a tracker) a waiting trigger cannot be called off.

Ess.Triggers.scope.skip_reason: Returns a namespace object whose whole point is the methods you then call on it (scope:armNamed, scope:gate), which node wiring cannot express - beginners should use the Triggers: Arm node instead.

Ess.UI.Bar.title: UI: Progress Bar
Ess.UI.Bar.desc: Show a labelled progress bar on screen -- fuel, health, a capture meter, a download timer. It appears immediately at whatever starting value you give it, and you move it afterwards with handle:set(0.75) or relabel it with handle:label("AMMO"). Values below 0 or above 1 are clamped. TRAP: needs the ui_bar.gfx movie deployed with your mod or nothing shows.

opts.desc: Settings table: x, y (position, default 20/330), w, h (size, default 300x36), label (text beside the bar), value (0 to 1).

returns.desc: The bar widget handle -- call :set(0..1), :label(s), :show(), :hide() on it.
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.Board.title: UI: Contract Board
Ess.UI.Board.desc: Open a big two-pane board: a scrolling list of 12 rows down the left, and a details pane on the right holding a category line, up to 4 reward lines, up to 8 objective lines, plus a progress bar and progress text. This is what the game-style contract-selection screen is built from. Fill the right-hand pane with handle:detail{...}; onSelect fires every single time the cursor moves, which is where you refresh it. TRAP: needs the contracts.gfx movie deployed with your mod, and needs focus = true to respond to keys.

opts.default: { x = 60, y = 60, title = "CONTRACTS", hint = "UP/DOWN MOVE   ENTER ACCEPT   LEFT BACK", focus = true, items = { { header = "AVAILABLE" }, { label = "Oil Field Raid" }, { label = "Convoy Ambush" } }, detail = { category = "OIL FIELD", rewards = { "$5000", "Fuel +200" }, objectives = { "Destroy 3 tanks", "Reach the LZ" }, progress = 0.4, progressText = "2/5" } }
opts.desc: Settings table: x, y (default 60/60), w, h (default 660x420), title, hint, items (same row shape as UI: Scrolling List), empty, detail (the right pane: category, rewards, objectives, progress 0..1, progressText), focus = true to give it the keyboard, onSelect(item, i, board), onChoose(item, i, board), onBack(board).

returns.desc: The board widget handle -- call :items(t), :detail(t), :select(i), :selected(), :title(s), :hint(s), :show(), :hide(), :focus() on it.
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.Chat.title: UI: Chat Log
Ess.UI.Chat.desc: Show a scrolling message log with 5 visible lines and an optional typing line underneath -- a chat window, or a running feed of what's happening. Add lines with handle:push("text") (long lines wrap at 52 characters) and start typing with handle:prompt(). Set autoHide to a number of seconds and the window fades out that long after the last message and pops back on the next one; it deliberately never fades while you are typing in it. Leave autoHide out and it stays on screen permanently. TRAP: needs the chat.gfx movie deployed with your mod.

opts.default: { x = 20, y = 400, title = "COMMS", autoHide = 8, onSubmit = function(sText) Ess.Hud.radio(sText) end }
opts.desc: Settings table: x, y (default 20/400), w, h (default 360x132), title, max (lines kept in the buffer, default 60), autoHide (seconds -- omit to stay visible forever), onSubmit(text) for what the player types.

returns.desc: The chat widget handle -- call :push(s), :prompt(), :title(s), :clear(), :show(), :hide(), :focus() on it.
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.Confirm.title: UI: Yes/No Dialog
Ess.UI.Confirm.desc: Pop a modal yes/no box in the middle of the screen and grab the keyboard: Left/Right switch between the two buttons, Enter picks, Escape counts as no. It deliberately starts with NO highlighted, so a stray Enter never confirms something destructive. Your onResult then runs with true or false and whatever had the keyboard before gets it straight back. Only one dialog exists at a time -- opening a second one reuses and overwrites the first. TRAP: needs the ui_confirm.gfx movie deployed with your mod.

opts.default: { title = "CONFIRM", text = "Blow the fuel depot?", yes = "YES", no = "NO", onResult = function(bYes) Ess.Hud.banner(bYes and "BOOM" or "STOOD DOWN") end }
opts.desc: Settings table: title (default "CONFIRM"), text (the question -- wraps at 44 characters onto 2 lines), yes / no (button labels), onResult(true|false).

returns.desc: The dialog widget handle (a single shared dialog).
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.Focus.title: UI: Give Keyboard Focus
Ess.UI.Focus.desc: Hand the keyboard to one widget -- exactly one widget at a time hears key presses. Any keys already buffered get thrown away, so the key you pressed to open the thing doesn't leak into it as a first keystroke. Pass nothing to take the keyboard away from everything.

w.default: Ess.UI.List{ title = "PICK ONE", items = { { label = "Option A" }, { label = "Option B" } } }
w.desc: The widget handle that should receive key presses. Leave empty to take focus off everything.

Ess.UI.Focused.title: UI: Focused Widget
Ess.UI.Focused.desc: Read back which widget currently owns the keyboard, if any. Handy for checking whether some Ess.UI window is already swallowing key presses before your own key handler reacts to them.

returns.desc: The widget handle that has the keyboard, or nothing if no widget does.
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.Input.title: UI: Text Prompt
Ess.UI.Input.desc: Pop a one-line typed prompt with a blinking caret and grab the keyboard: Enter submits and closes it, Escape cancels and closes it. One-shot -- unlike Text Console: Open it does NOT stay open after Enter. Only one exists at a time, and whatever had the keyboard before gets it back when it closes. Long text scrolls so you always see the last 40 characters. TRAP: needs the ui_input.gfx movie deployed with your mod -- for a text field that needs no asset at all, use Text Console: Open.

opts.default: { prompt = "NAME THIS SQUAD -- ENTER SUBMIT   ESC CANCEL", text = "", max = 120, onSubmit = function(sText) Ess.Hud.banner(sText) end }
opts.desc: Settings table: prompt (the header line above the field), text (what it starts with), max (character limit, default 120), onSubmit(text), onCancel().

returns.desc: The prompt widget handle (a single shared prompt).
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.List.title: UI: Scrolling List
Ess.UI.List.desc: Show a scrollable list the player drives with the arrow keys: 10 rows visible at once, a scrollbar, section headers the cursor skips straight over, and a body that resizes to fit the content. Up/Down move and wrap around at the ends (hold a key and it auto-repeats after a short delay), Enter or Right picks the row, Left or Escape backs out. TRAP: it only hears keys once it has the keyboard, so pass focus = true or nothing will respond. Second trap: needs the ui_list.gfx movie deployed with your mod.

opts.default: { x = 40, y = 60, title = "TARGETS", hint = "UP/DOWN MOVE   ENTER PICK   LEFT BACK", focus = true, items = { { header = "PRIORITY" }, { label = "Fuel depot" }, { label = "Radar tower" } }, onChoose = function(tItem) Ess.Hud.banner(tItem.label) end }
opts.desc: Settings table: x, y (default 40/60), w, h (default 320x360), title, crumb (breadcrumb line), hint (key-help line), items (rows -- { header = "SECTION" } or { label = "Entry", any = yourData }), empty (text shown when there are no rows), focus = true to give it the keyboard, onChoose(item, i, list), onSelect(item, i, list), onBack(list).

returns.desc: The list widget handle -- call :items(t), :select(i), :selected(), :title(s), :crumb(s), :hint(s), :show(), :hide(), :focus() on it.
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.Menu.skip_reason: Builder object: the returned menu shows nothing until you chain :entry()/:category()/:switch()/:header() and then :open() on it, so it has no single-node shape.

Ess.UI.Panel.title: UI: Info Panel
Ess.UI.Panel.desc: Show a titled box with up to 8 text lines under it, whose body smoothly grows and shrinks to fit however many lines you've actually filled -- a status readout or a stats board. It appears straight away showing just the title; you fill the rows with handle:line(0, "text") (rows are numbered 0 to 7) and wipe them with handle:clear(). TRAP: needs the ui_panel.gfx movie deployed with your mod or you get a handle and an empty screen.

opts.desc: Settings table: x, y (position, default 20/120), w, h (size, default 300x200), title, lines (how many rows tall to start, 0 to 8).

returns.desc: The panel widget handle -- call :title(s), :line(i, s), :fit(n), :clear(), :show(), :hide() on it.
returns.name: result

Ess.UI.Toast.title: UI: Toast
Ess.UI.Toast.desc: Pop a small notification on the right-hand side of the screen that fades away by itself after 4 seconds. Three can stack at once; a fourth replaces whichever is closest to expiring. The text wraps onto at most 2 lines at 46 characters. TRAP: this needs the ui_toast.gfx movie deployed with your mod -- if you want a notification with no asset at all, use HUD: Hint Popup or HUD: Banner instead.

opts.desc: Settings table: ttl is how many seconds it stays up before fading (default 4).

returns.desc: The toast handle -- call :dismiss() on it to take it down early.
returns.name: result

Ess.UI._attachCommon.skip_reason: Internal plumbing: bolts the shared show/hide/focus/destroy methods onto a widget while it is being constructed.

Ess.UI._ensureTick.skip_reason: Internal plumbing: arms Ess.UI's shared heartbeat, which every widget already does for itself.

Ess.UI._register.skip_reason: Internal plumbing: adds a widget to Ess.UI's live list during construction.

Ess.UI._setTarget.skip_reason: Internal plumbing: sets a widget's body-resize easing target; widgets drive it themselves.

Ess.UI.comma.title: UI: Format Number With Commas
Ess.UI.comma.desc: Turn a big number into readable text with thousands separators -- 1234567 comes back as "1,234,567". Decimals are dropped (it rounds down), so it's for money, kill counts and scores just before they go on screen.

returns.desc: The number as text with commas, e.g. "1,234,567".
returns.name: text

Ess.UI.fmt_time.title: UI: Format Seconds As Clock
Ess.UI.fmt_time.desc: Turn a number of seconds into minutes:seconds text for a countdown -- 125 comes back as "2:05". The seconds are zero-padded, the minutes are not, and it never rolls over into hours (3700 seconds reads as "61:40").

returns.desc: The time as text, e.g. "2:05".
returns.name: text

Ess.UI.navName.title: UI: Name A Nav Key
Ess.UI.navName.desc: Turn a Windows key code into the direction Ess.UI treats it as -- "up", "down", "left", "right", "enter" or "esc". It reads the remappable Ess.UI.KEYS table, so if you have rebound Up to W it answers using your new binding. Anything that is not a navigation key gets nothing back.

vk.desc: The Windows virtual-key code, e.g. 38 (0x26) for Up Arrow, 40 for Down, 13 for Enter, 27 for Escape.

returns.desc: "up", "down", "left", "right", "enter" or "esc" -- or nothing if that key is not a nav key.
returns.name: direction

Ess.UI.wrap.title: UI: Wrap Text
Ess.UI.wrap.desc: Break one long sentence into a list of shorter lines so it fits inside a widget. It breaks on a space where it can find one (looking back up to 15 characters), and only cuts mid-word when it can't. The default width is 46 characters -- each widget passes its own, so toasts wrap at 46, the chat log at 52 and the yes/no dialog at 44.

s.default: Get to the extraction point before the gunships arrive.

width.desc: Maximum characters per line. Defaults to 46.

returns.desc: The lines in order -- always at least one entry, even for empty text.
returns.name: lines

Ess.Vec.add.title: Vector: Add
Ess.Vec.add.desc: Adds two vectors together. Give it a position and an offset and you get the shifted position back - for example lifting a spawn point 5 units into the air.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: Summed X.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Summed Y.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Summed Z.

Ess.Vec.cross.title: Vector: Cross Product
Ess.Vec.cross.desc: Gives the direction at right angles to two others - camera-right from forward and up, a surface's facing from two of its edges, or "is B on my left or my right" from whether the Y answer comes out positive or negative.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: X of the perpendicular vector.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Y of the perpendicular vector.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Z of the perpendicular vector.

Ess.Vec.dir.title: Vector: Direction
Ess.Vec.dir.desc: Which way to aim or shove to get from A to B, as a length-1 direction with the distance stripped out. Scale it up for a knockback impulse, or add it to a position to take a step that way.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: X of the length-1 direction from A to B.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Y of the length-1 direction from A to B.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Z of the length-1 direction from A to B.

Ess.Vec.dot.title: Vector: Dot Product
Ess.Vec.dot.desc: Compares two directions and boils the answer down to one number: positive means they roughly agree, 0 means they are at right angles, negative means they oppose. The usual "is that thing in front of me or behind me" test.

returns.name: dot
returns.desc: Positive if the vectors point the same sort of way, negative if opposite, 0 if square on.

Ess.Vec.length.title: Vector: Length
Ess.Vec.length.desc: How long a vector is - for example how fast something is moving, given the x/y/z of its velocity.

x.desc: X part of the vector.

y.desc: Y part of the vector.

z.desc: Z part of the vector.

returns.name: length
returns.desc: The vector's length.

Ess.Vec.lerp.title: Vector: Blend Positions
Ess.Vec.lerp.desc: The point partway between two positions - t = 0 is the first, 1 is the second, 0.5 is dead centre. For gliding a camera or an object smoothly from one spot to another.

t.desc: How far along, 0 to 1.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: X of the in-between point.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Y of the in-between point.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Z of the in-between point.

Ess.Vec.normalize.title: Vector: Normalize
Ess.Vec.normalize.desc: Shrinks a vector down to length 1 while keeping its direction - a pure "which way" with the "how much" stripped off, ready to multiply by whatever strength you want. A zero-length vector safely comes back as 0,0,0 rather than breaking with NaN.

x.desc: X part of the vector.

y.desc: Y part of the vector.

z.desc: Z part of the vector.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: X of the length-1 direction.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Y of the length-1 direction.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Z of the length-1 direction.

Ess.Vec.scale.title: Vector: Scale
Ess.Vec.scale.desc: Multiplies a direction by a strength. Take a length-1 direction from Vector: Direction and scale it up to get a knockback impulse or a velocity.

x.desc: X part of the vector.

y.desc: Y part of the vector.

z.desc: Z part of the vector.

s.desc: How much to multiply it by.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: Scaled X.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Scaled Y.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Scaled Z.

Ess.Vec.sub.title: Vector: Subtract
Ess.Vec.sub.desc: Takes the second vector away from the first. Position A minus position B gives the vector that points from B to A - the raw "which way and how far" between two things.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: X of the difference.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Y of the difference.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Z of the difference.

Ess.Vec.toward.title: Vector: Point Toward
Ess.Vec.toward.desc: The spot a set distance from A along the line to B. Use it to move something a few units closer to its target, or to place a marker just short of a destination, without working out the direction yourself.

dist.desc: How far to travel from A toward B.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: X of the resulting point.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Y of the resulting point.

returns.name: z
returns.desc: Z of the resulting point.

Ess.Vehicle.driver.title: Vehicle: Driver
Ess.Vehicle.driver.desc: Gets whoever is behind the wheel or at the controls of a vehicle - also the way you get a helicopter's PILOT handle, which is what the flight and landing orders want.

returns.name: uChar
returns.desc: The driver's character handle, or nil if the seat is empty. A freshly spawned vehicle has no driver for a moment, so an immediate read can come back nil.

Ess.Vehicle.enterBestSeat.title: Vehicle: Enter Best Seat
Ess.Vehicle.enterBestSeat.desc: Puts a character into a vehicle, taking the best free seat automatically in driver, gunner, passenger, cargo order - the everyday 'get in' node.

uVeh.desc: The vehicle to board. CAUTION from live testing: spawning a vehicle and immediately boarding it from INSIDE the PMC HQ interior stalled the whole Lua tick for 30+ seconds, and needed the game killed. Do this out in the open world, and do not chain another query on the very next line - leave a beat.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the boarding call went through.

Ess.Vehicle.enterSeatExcluding.title: Vehicle: Enter Seat (Excluding)
Ess.Vehicle.enterSeatExcluding.desc: Boards a vehicle but skips seats you name - built for 'get in but never take the wheel', such as a co-op partner boarding a car the other player is already driving.

excludeSeats.desc: A list of seat codes to refuse: "d" driver, "g" gunner, "p" passenger, "c" cargo. The remaining types are tried in that same priority order. Blocking the driver seat is the usual case: { "d" }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the character actually got into a seat.

returns.name: sSeatTypeUsed
returns.desc: Which seat code they ended up in ("d"/"g"/"p"/"c"), or nil when every allowed seat was full or missing.

Ess.Vehicle.evictAll.title: Vehicle: Evict Everyone
Ess.Vehicle.evictAll.desc: Forces every occupant out of a vehicle at once - the bulk version of the exit node, for clearing an enemy truck or emptying a heli before you take it.

uVeh.desc: The vehicle to empty. This one wants the VEHICLE's own handle, not a rider's or a pilot's - confirmed live, the driver read as real before the call and nil after.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the call went through.

Ess.Vehicle.exit.title: Vehicle: Exit
Ess.Vehicle.exit.desc: Gets one named character back out of a vehicle - the missing other half of the boarding nodes.

uVeh.desc: The vehicle to get out of. Note the order here: the VEHICLE comes first, the person second.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the exit went through.

Ess.Vehicle.flyTo.title: Vehicle: Fly Helicopter To Point
Ess.Vehicle.flyTo.desc: Sends an AI helicopter to a spot in the sky, handling the two things that trip people up: a plain move-to order does not fly a helicopter, and a freshly spawned one has no pilot for a moment.

uHeli.desc: The helicopter to send. It needs a pilot - a crewed '(Driver)' or '(Full)' template. This node keeps checking every 0.15s until the pilot exists and only then issues the order, so it is safe to call the instant you spawn one.

x.desc: Destination east/west coordinate.

y.desc: Destination height. Y is up; give it real altitude or it will try to fly into the ground.

z.desc: Destination north/south coordinate.

opts.desc: Extra settings: height = the drop height (default 0.5), careless = true for a less cautious approach, onReady = a function run once the order is actually issued, handy for hanging a camera on the pilot.

returns.name: cancel
returns.desc: Call this to abort the wait-for-pilot loop early if you change your mind before the order goes out.

Ess.Vehicle.followGhost.title: Vehicle: Follow Ghost
Ess.Vehicle.followGhost.desc: Spawns a stand-in object you can keep moving around - a live preview marker for placement tools - and hands back a little object with the controls to move or delete it.

template.desc: The template name to spawn, exactly as the game spells it. A blank name is refused on purpose because an empty spawn crashes the game to desktop.

x.desc: Where to first place it: east/west coordinate.

y.desc: Starting height.

z.desc: Starting north/south coordinate.

returns.name: ghost
returns.desc: An object with ghost.guid (the CURRENT handle), ghost:update(x,y,z) to move it and ghost:remove() to delete it - or nil if the spawn failed. IMPORTANT: moving a spawned HUMAN by position silently does nothing on this engine, so update() detects that and quietly despawns and re-spawns instead, which CHANGES the handle. Always read ghost.guid fresh off the object, never cache it.

Ess.Vehicle.isFlipped.title: Vehicle: Is Flipped
Ess.Vehicle.isFlipped.desc: Tells you whether a vehicle has rolled onto its roof or side, so you can offer a respawn or a nudge.

returns.name: bFlipped
returns.desc: True when it is upside down. There is deliberately NO unflip node - no reliable way to right a vehicle has been verified on this engine, so the usual answer is an upward Impulse Push or a fresh spawn.

Ess.Vehicle.land.title: Vehicle: Land Helicopter
Ess.Vehicle.land.desc: Orders an AI helicopter to descend and set down on the ground.

uHeliOrPilot.desc: The helicopter, or its pilot directly - either works. BIG TRAP confirmed live: a heli still running its own combat AI simply IGNORES this and keeps flying. Send it somewhere with Vehicle Fly To first, then land it - that pattern gave a real measured descent.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True when the order was issued. That is not a promise it actually descended - see the trap above.

Ess.Vehicle.orbitFlight.title: Vehicle: Orbit Flight
Ess.Vehicle.orbitFlight.desc: Flies a crewed helicopter a few circular laps around a point - the 'victory lap' flight - by chaining a ring of timed waypoints for you.

uHeli.desc: The helicopter to fly. It must already have a pilot - a '(Driver)' or '(Full)' template - an empty airframe will not move.

cx.desc: East/west coordinate of the point to circle.

cy.desc: Ground height at the centre point. The orbit height below is added on top of this, and because the first leg is already up in the air the heli climbs into the circle by itself - no separate takeoff order needed.

cz.desc: North/south coordinate of the point to circle.

opts.desc: Flight shape: radius (90), height above the centre (45), orbits (2), points per lap (6), secPerLeg (2.2), startAngle in degrees, tracker to register the timers for cleanup, onDone = a function run after the last leg.

returns.name: totalSeconds
returns.desc: How long the whole flight will take, so you can time a camera move or the next beat to match it.

Ess.Vehicle.repair.title: Vehicle: Repair And Rearm
Ess.Vehicle.repair.desc: Fully heals a vehicle and refills its weapons in one go - the between-round fixup for a wave defence, an escort patch-up, or mercy on a smoking ride.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the heal went through. The rearm is best-effort and is not reported separately.

Ess.Vehicle.riders.title: Vehicle: Riders
Ess.Vehicle.riders.desc: Lists everyone currently aboard a vehicle so you can count occupants, heal a whole crew, or check whether it is worth blowing up.

returns.name: tRiders
returns.desc: A list of character handles. Always a real list, empty rather than nil when there is nobody aboard or the vehicle cannot be read.

Ess.Vehicle.seatOf.title: Vehicle: Seat Of Character
Ess.Vehicle.seatOf.desc: Tells you which seat a character is sitting in, if any - the quick way to check 'are they driving or just along for the ride'.

returns.name: sSeat
returns.desc: The seat they occupy, or nil if they are not in a vehicle.

Ess.lastError.title: Last Error
Ess.lastError.desc: This is how you find out why nothing happened. Ess fails silently on purpose - a stale handle or a missing argument gives you nothing back rather than crashing the game - so the last swallowed failure gets parked here. The routine: notice nothing happened, turn debug on with a Lua line reading Ess.DEBUG = true, do the thing again, then read this. Only failures recorded while debug was on carry a label saying which call it was.

returns.name: error
returns.desc: A small record: .msg is what went wrong, .label is which call (only filled in while debug was on), .count is how many failures there have been this session. Nothing at all if nothing has failed yet.

Ess.stop.title: Stop
Ess.stop.desc: Turns off anything Ess handed you - a hook, a marker, a running loop's name, a tracker, an objective. Ess ended up with 27 different words for 'turn this off', one per namespace, so 'how do I stop this' had no learnable answer. This is the one node that takes any of them. Every namespace's own stop still works; this is the one to reach for when you are just holding a handle and want it gone.

x.desc: Whatever the node that started the thing handed back - a stop function, a marker handle, a loop name in quotes, a tracker. Wire it straight in. Leaving it empty is harmless, it just does nothing.

returns.name: stopped
returns.desc: True if something was really torn down. False means it was empty or Ess did not recognise it - with debug on it logs exactly which.

Ess.stopAll.title: Stop All
Ess.stopAll.desc: Stops every handle in a list, working backwards from the end. Backwards is deliberate: things you set up later usually lean on things you set up earlier, so tearing down in reverse is the order that does not surprise. Use it when your mod keeps a list of everything it started.

tHandles.desc: A plain list of handles, e.g. { h1, h2, h3 }. It must have no gaps: if you emptied slots out by setting them to nil, Lua cannot be trusted to report the list's length and some entries may be left running without telling you.

returns.name: count
returns.desc: How many of them actually stopped.
